None of what I describe here should mean abandoning financial discipline or pretending that every worthwhile initiative delivers the same return, rather it means taking a fuller view of what makes Britain attractive for long-term investment and recognising that government, business, investors and civil society each have a part to play in creating those conditions. However, too many people persist in discussing these things separately, through narrow perspectives of individual sectors, industries or political priorities. 

There is another challenge, too, which is we have become very good at talking Britain down and whilst our difficulties are undoubtedly real, so too are our extraordinary strengths. I travel across the country and so I know there are people building remarkable businesses, developing groundbreaking technologies and strengthening their communities, but the truth is some of this happens despite wider government policy and not because of it. Perhaps, therefore we need to spend rather more time connecting the energy such individuals show, rather than hearing more about what is not working.

The ‘UK Davos’

This thinking is what led me to establish Anthropy, now the UK’s largest national leadership gathering, which has been nicknamed the “UK Davos”, but don’t blame me for that. It brings together leaders from all sectors at the Eden Project in Cornwall each March and what began as an experiment in national collaboration is now a gathering of 2,500 leaders, united not by political allegiance or profession, but by a shared determination to inspire a better Britain. For March 2027, we have chosen growth as our overarching theme but rather than simply focusing on GDP, we are asking four broader questions of growth in all its dimensions: How do we grow human flourishing? How do we grow vibrant places? How do we grow good prosperity? And how do we grow Britain’s global influence? 

Together is how we grow a nation and together these questions will inform a National Growthprint, with the intention of presenting practical proposals for a Westminster launch next summer. This is not an argument for replacing economic growth with worthy aspirations, quite the opposite: it is recognition that lasting prosperity depends upon the strength of the economy which in turn is based on its people, places, institutions and relationships.

Britain has no shortage of people talking about its future, but what we need are more people prepared to step forward to help shape it. That is why, next March, we will gather again at the Eden Project, not simply to discuss Britain’s challenges, but to explore what we might achieve together, because the most important question is not simply how much Britain can grow, but what kind of Britain that growth will create. 

John O’Brien MBE is founder and chairman of Anthropy. Anthropy27 takes place at the Eden Project, Cornwall, 10th to 12th March 2027

articles.title: Channel 4 in talks to sell London HQ to property developer Socius
articles.summary:
Channel 4 is in talks to sell its longstanding London headquarters for more than £50m as the broadcaster grapples with a cash squeeze and a downturn in television advertising.

Property developer Socius has entered exclusive negotiations to acquire the broadcaster’s Horseferry Road base in Pimlico, Sky News reported on Thursday.

A deal is not guaranteed, however, and the eventual sale price is expected to fall significantly short of the £90m valuation reported earlier this year.

The government-owned but commercially funded broadcaster put the building up for sale earlier this year as part of a wider restructuring under chief executive Priya Dogra.

Channel 4 has occupied the site for more than 30 years and has since established a separate national headquarters in Leeds, although it has yet to confirm where its London-based employees will relocate.

Socius specialises in mixed-use urban developments and is behind plans for a major cancer research district elsewhere in the capital.

Channel 4 and Socius have been approached for comment.

Channel 4 battles ad slump

The potential sale comes as Channel 4 faces mounting financial pressure from a structural shift in advertising spending away from traditional television and towards digital platforms.

Consumer goods giant Unilever had slashed its advertising spending with Channel 4 by around 92 per cent this year, as the company pivots towards influencer-led marketing.

The owner of Dove and Hellmann’s has more than halved its overall UK television advertising spending compared with 2025, with ITV and Sky also suffering significant declines.

Channel 4 is meanwhile cutting around a quarter of its workforce, equivalent to some 300 jobs, in one of the biggest rounds of redundancies in its history.

The cuts follow the loss of 200 roles under former chief executive Alex Mahon nearly two years ago.

The broadcaster suffered a further commercial blow earlier this month when it permanently axed Married at First Sight, one of its most lucrative programmes, following allegations of rape made by female participants.

The potential disposal of its London headquarters would mark another significant step in Dogra’s overhaul of the broadcaster as it seeks to cut costs and adapt to an increasingly digital advertising market.

articles.title: Heathrow expansion should be paused while government ‘makes the case’ – Transport Committee
articles.summary:
Plans for Heathrow’s multibillion-pound third runway should be put on ice for the government to “make the case” for expansion, according to the chair of the Transport Committee.

In an eagerly anticipated report, the group of influential lawmakers led by Labour MP Ruth Cadbury said that the pro-growth case for expansion had weakened substantially since previous analyses and should not go ahead in its current form.

“Our report should be a wake-up call for ministers,” Cadbury said, adding: “Plans for a third runway should be grounded for now and the government should go back to the drawing board before proceeding any further.”

The paper follows a months-long probe by the cross-party committee, whose members sought evidence from airline bosses, environmental campaigners and the two bidders vying to oversee Heathrow’s £50bn expansion.

Heathrow expansion ‘not given time for economic analysis’

In a major blow to the project’s cheerleaders, the report found there to be a lack of certainty over the cost of expansion, warning that passengers and airlines could face sky-high air fares should the build come in over budget.

Ministers had also failed to make adequate provisions to improve transport links to the west London hub, MPs added, namely from the south and west of England.

The report represents one of the most significant rebukes of Heathrow expansion since then-Chancellor Rachel Reeves fired the starting gun on its planning during a pro-growth speech last year. Since then, expansion has garnered near-universal support from industry and political parties, but it has also been beset by infighting over concerns over the financial costs associated with HAL’s blueprint.

Last week, the boss of British Airways-owner IAG said the current proposal was “doomed to failure” in a leaked letter to the Prime Minister published by the Sunday Times. Luis Gallego warned of a £19bn gap between the headline cost of expansion and the amount airlines and their customers would be willing to pay.

Under the current private financing model, Heathrow and rival suitor Heathrow West will recoup their costs for the megaproject by raising the charge added to travellers’ tickets.

Rachel Reeves fired the starting gone on the third runway expansion

Commenting alongside the report, Cadbury said the Department for Transport had “not given itself enough time to produce the most economic analysis”.

“If a third runway gets off the ground, then government also needs to strengthen the air quality test and noise tests, develop plans for improving public transport and bottom out how much it will cost airlines and passengers to use an expanded Heathrow,” she added.

Heathrow chief executive Thomas Woldbye said the weight of evidence remained “strongly behind Heathrow expansion”.

“The case for expanding Heathrow has been examined more thoroughly than almost any infrastructure project in modern Britain,” he added. “Successive governments, independent commissions and industry experts have repeatedly concluded that you either expand Heathrow so the UK can compete and grow, or you accept a steady erosion of the UK’s connectivity and global competitiveness.”

Officials are currently running the rule over responses to a Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement, which will act as a framework against which bidders’ applications will be judged. Under the current schedule, the Department for Transport will then publish a final version of the document, which will be put to an MPs vote early next year.

Should the vote pass, both HAL and Heathrow West are expected to submit planning applications. Transport secretary Heidi Alexander will then consider both blueprints before choosing which, if any, the government will rubber stamp.

“The Transport Select Committee’s report on Heathrow expansion is a recipe for yet more delay,” Viggo Terling, chief of staff at the Adam Smith Institute, said. “It calls for a national aviation strategy, further peer-reviewed economic analysis and a consultation on landing charges. Each may sound reasonable in isolation, but these demands must be weighed against the costs of prolonging a debate that has already lasted more than 20 years.”

articles.title: Nandy warns ‘jury is out’ on Ofcom’s ability to regulate online world
articles.summary:
Culture secretary Lisa Nandy has warned Ofcom over its ability to police the online world, saying that the “jury is out” on whether the regulator is capable of delivering on its expanding remit.

Speaking to Sky News on Thursday, Nandy said she was in active discussions with the watchdog’s new chair over its performance, as ministers prepare to introduce Britain’s under-16 social media ban.

“I think the jury is out about whether they can do what we’ve asked them to do,” she said.

“I think there’s an awful lot that Ofcom does and that we’re asking it to do, but this is a conversation that I’m actively having with the new chair of Ofcom, who was brought in to shake things up.”

Asked whether she was putting the regulator on notice, Nandy said she would prefer to take a “partnership approach”, but stressed the urgency of tackling online harms.

“I’d prefer that we all stepped up and understood the urgency and the responsibilities that we have,” she said.

In September, Nandy admitted there was “a problem” with the watchdog’s ability to enforce online safety rules, warning that “laws are only as good as the ability to enforce them”.

She also signalled an appetite for further regulation of technology companies, describing the forthcoming social media ban as a “staging post to what must be a very active interventionist state”.

Pressure mounts on Ofcom

The comments come ahead of Britain’s planned ban on under-16s accessing high-risk social media platforms, including Instagram, Tiktok, Snapchat and Youtube, from March.

Ofcom will be tasked with overseeing the restrictions, alongside additional safeguards for 16 and 17-year-olds covering addictive features such as infinite scrolling and algorithmic recommendations.

The regulator has already faced a series of legal challenges from technology giants over the scope of its powers under the Online Safety Act.

Earlier this month, the High Court rejected a challenge brought by Meta, Whatsapp, Tiktok and X against Ofcom’s demands for detailed information about their content moderation practices, strengthening its ability to scrutinise platforms.

Ofcom has also announced tougher requirements for technology companies to detect illegal content, including child sexual abuse material, amid concerns that artificial intelligence is accelerating its creation and distribution.

The watchdog can impose fines of up to £18m or 10 per cent of qualifying global annual turnover for breaches of the Online Safety Act.

But Nandy’s latest intervention suggests ministers are increasingly concerned about whether the regulator has the capacity to turn Britain’s expanding online safety legislation into effective enforcement.

articles.title: Cricket Australia to hire accountability expert for Sandpapergate probe
articles.summary:
Cricket Australia is set to turn to one of the country’s most decorated barristers, Fiona McLeod SC, to run its Sandpapergate “truth forum”.

McLeod has 35 years of experience as a barrister, is a former president of the Law Council of Australia and has written books on honesty and accountability in public life.

She is expected to be tasked with diffusing the toxic row over the Australian cricket team’s use of sandpaper to cheat and exactly who knew what about it, reports The Age.

The issue has erupted again this month, eight years after the notorious incident, plunging the country’s players past and present into open civil war.

Test captain Pat Cummins has continued to insist he did not know about the cheating, which saw three players – Cameron Bancroft, Steve Smith and David Warner – serve bans.

But calls for a fresh inquiry have grown louder since former batter Usman Khawaja alleged that the whole team – including Cummins – was in on the sandpaper scheme in his new book. Bancroft and Warner have since backed up those claims, which related to a Test series against South Africa in 2018.

It has led to suggestions that Bancroft, Smith and Warner were made scapegoats and that an initial investigation into the scandal was a whitewash.

That has pressured Cricket Australia into drawing up a new probe, although questions remain over the scope of the exercise and CA’s appetite to expose more wrongdoing.

Fiona McLeod: Barrister who wrote the book on lying

McLeod has been involved in high-profile inquiries before, including into the Monash IVF embryo transfer errors and the Yoorrook Justice Commission for Indigenous Victorians.

She also represented the Commonwealth in the Victorian Bushfires Royal Commission, the Queensland Floods Commission and the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse.

In her 2021 book, Easy Lies and Influence, McLeod wrote: “The issue of corruption and the failures of accountability continue to trouble me. Once seen in the political domain, they cannot be unseen. Once trust is lost, personal grievance festers.”

In another passage, she noted: “When listening to a lie, we can be confounded momentarily – we do not expect people to lie to us, especially those entrusted with authority. Many are unable or unwilling to discern the truth and act accordingly, despite overwhelming evidence.”

articles.title: Investment firm Xyra plots renewed bid for Poundland
articles.summary:
The little-known investment group which had been a frontrunner to buy Poundland is planning a fresh bid to buy the discount retailer out of administration.

A spokesperson for Xyra Group Holdings’ bid for Poundland, told City AM the investment firm will “engage with administrators” following the high street giant’s collapse.

Poundland fell into administration on Wednesday afternoon, marking one of the most significant high street failures in recent years and piling fresh scrutiny on whether its owner, Gordon Brothers, tried hard enough to protect its thousands of staff.

Xyra Group Holdings was among the four bidders locked in talks with the US investment firm in the hours leading up to its collapse, which was triggered after it was decided that a solvent takeover would not be possible.

In a statement issued to City AM, the spokesperson said: “We have worked tirelessly since the sale process began to put together what we believe remains the best bid. 

“It is very disappointing to see Poundland go into administration, so we will now engage with the administrators to see if we can still help save what is a wonderful business.”

Xyra’s enduring interest in the collapsed retailer will boost hopes that the high street titan and its employees could be saved, though a break-up of the company through administration remains the most likely outcome.

Tony Brown, a former executive at retailers including Beales, BHS and Peacocks, has been leading Xyra’s proposal to take over Poundland, which would have seen the retailer expand its store count and introduce more exclusive ranges to fatten its margins.

Xyra Group Holdings is an investment vehicle led by 23-year-old entrepreneur Manvedeep Singh. The group has never previously completed an acquisition but has called upon a number of City veterans, including Brown, in its attempts to get its bid over the line. 

The investment firm had previously told City AM that it had fully funded its offer. Xyra had been urging Gordon Brothers to force an extension to Poundland’s notice to appoint administrators, to allow it more time to put its takeover in place.

Bidder wanted more time

Poundland’s management told its near-12,000 staff on Wednesday that they had no choice but to file administration because Gordon Brothers had refused to provide any more of the funding needed to keep its shelves stocked.

Brown said earlier this week: “Pending customary due diligence by identified lenders and investors, Xyra has secured interest to cover the required funding to complete the acquisition of Poundland as a going concern.”

Each of the four bidders previously in the running had been attempting to buy Poundland as a going concern. It is not known whether the other bidders – which include Zachert Private Equity and Irish property firm MPG – remain interested in buying the retailer out of administration.

Dubai-based wholesaler Quality Premier Foods, which emerged as a potential buyer in the days before Poundland’s collapse, remains interested in the retailer, Sky News has reported.

Alix Partners, Poundland’s administrators, said on Wednesday: We appreciate this is a deeply concerning time for all involved – customers, suppliers and, in particular, Poundland colleagues. Our priority now is to work with all stakeholders, including representatives from government and USDAW, as we identify the best possible route forward. 

“We would encourage anybody interested in acquiring the business in part or as a whole, as well as UK retail operators with open employment opportunities, to contact The Administrators.” 

A spokesperson for Gordon Brothers said its attempted sale of Poundland “explored every avenue to secure a sale of the whole company.

“First and foremost, our thoughts are with Poundland colleagues. We recognise how difficult the continued uncertainty is for them. Efforts to preserve as many jobs and stores as possible will continue, led by the Administrators.”

articles.title: Bank of England sounds alarm on ‘opaque’ AI financing
articles.summary:
The Bank of England has warned that the “rapid expansion” and “opaque” financing of AI is amplifying the risk of shocks rippling across markets, even as investment in the technology helps drive global growth.

The central bank’s Financial Policy Committee (FPC) said “spillovers across markets have been limited” thus far and economic growth has been “resilient, in part supported by AI-related investment.”

But the 12-member committee – which includes Bank governor Andrew Bailey and Financial Conduct Authority boss Nikhil Rathi – cautioned the funding behind AI was becoming increasingly “complex, circular and opaque”.

“The very rapid expansion and broadening of its financing… is also contributing to a deepening of interconnections across the global financial system, making it increasingly likely for stress in one area to propagate to another,” the FPC said.

The committee pointed to “more complex financial structures” as driving the interconnected risk. It said financing was spanning equity markets, public bond markets and private credit as well as less transparent measures.

AI-related companies were providing finance to others in the sector, the FPC said, which was “strengthening sectoral interconnections”.

It added these “circular financing arrangements can make it more difficult to identify concentrations of risk and where exposures ultimately sit.”

Bank calls for firms to get prepared for quantum

Technology stocks have faced sharp swings in the last few months, exacerbated by the US midterm that saw AI-related stocks tumble as investors reassessed the pace development would move at.

The FPC said spillovers were “limited” across recent episodes but could lead to globally active investors deleveraging in other markets, including sovereign debt markets. It added equity valuations “remain stretched on some measures, despite recent falls”.

The committee also raised the alarm on the development of quantum technology and called for the industry to “accelerate long-term preparations”.

“They will also need credible arrangements to recover quickly from operational disruption, in order to maintain the provision of vital financial services. Taken together, these will place competing demands on technology skills and management capacity,” the FPC said.

“A failure to take action will compromise firms’ operational resilience with potential system-wide implications.”

It pointed to recent Google Cloud and Microsoft outages that illustrate how “operational dependencies” can mean disruption at one provider has a knock-on effect on several firms.

The Prudential Regulation Authority and Financial Conduct Authority published a joint consultation this month, ordering firms to ramp up their cyber protections. The watchdogs instructed financial institutions to be prepared to rebuild from scratch in the face of a major cyber attack on operations.

“The evolving operational risk environment reinforces the need for significant and sustained investment by the financial sector in building resilience,” the FPC said.

articles.title: ‘We need more dynamism’ – Healey urged to stay out of merger decisions
articles.summary:
Chancellor John Healey has been urged to avoid interfering with the competition and merger regulator as former Treasury officials blamed the UK’s lagging productivity on a lack of dynamism in the economy. 

A new paper by top economists who worked in senior roles at the Treasury claimes most of the UK’s slowdown in productivity growth can be attributed to a lack of competition. 

Research focused on the struggles faced by new firms to break into markets even as the likes of Octopus Energy, Lidl and Revolut have challenged larger businesses and helped make the economy “more productive”. 

John Kingman, the chair of Barclays and Great British Railways who was previously second permanent secretary at the Treasury, and Shriti Vadera, a former adviser to Gordon Brown, said the government should stay out of merger decisions. 

The senior business figures pointed out that the firms under five years old made 10 per cent of all business sales in 2021 compared to 18 per cent in 2005. 

The intervention challenges Treasury ministers’ growing interest in pushing the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) to force mergers through after former Chancellor Rachel Reeves directed the regulator to support growth and focus on industrial strategy sectors in 2025. 

Healey must ’embrace power of competition’

The paper, published by King’s College London, said the government should “reassert” the CMA’s independence and competition mandate while ministers should be kept out of individual merger decisions other than a small set which are key to public interest. 

Healey and business secretary Jonathan Reynolds were also urged to allow “failing firms to fail”. The paper explained that there should be special administration options for more critical sectors such as telecoms after ministers intervened to allow BT’s takeover of Talktalk, just as the government has considered bringing Thames Water under temporary public control given its financial struggles. 

Government decisions that potentially undermined growth included former Chancellor Jeremy Hunt’s criticism of the CMA’s decision to block Microsoft’s $69bn purchase of the games company Activision Blizzard and Reeves’ attacks against former CMA chair Marcus Bokkerink, according to the two prominent business figures.

At the time of a proposed takeover of Activision, which was later cleared by the CMA in late 2023, Microsoft chiefs hit out at the CMA as they said the decision showed the UK was “clearly closed for business”. 

They argued that such ministerial interventions set a precedent for other regulators to “not upset powerful firms”. 

“If the government wants higher growth, as it says it does, it needs consciously to embrace the power of competition and disruption and do everything possible to drive it,” Kingman and Vadera wrote.  

“UK economic history shows plenty of examples where competition authorities and economic regulators, often working alongside the government, have successfully done this, with large economic gains.

“More recent governments, however, appear to have lost this impetus and embraced a very different philosophy; they appear to have come to see active procompetition policy as a threat to growth, rather than a driver of it.”

“The implicit hope in all this seems to have been that if competition authorities can be reined in, incumbent firms would be happier and would respond by investing more in the UK.”

Public procurement strategy could push up costs

The paper also hit out at Healey’s push to ‘buy British’ in public procurement as it called for an overhaul of the system that currently “entrenches existing providers”. 

It said Healey and Louise Haigh’s efforts to boost UK firms by contracting them for government services could be costly for taxpayers.

Several firms have hit out at the CMA for heavy-handed interventions on business practices. Google executives said the CMA’s proposals to require the company to include AI assistants as alternatives to its search engine as “unlawful”, adding that it would “undermine competition”. 

A government spokesperson said: “We strongly support the CMA’s independent role in promoting competition for the benefit of consumers across the economy, as set out in the Strategic Steer.”

A CMA spokesperson said: “The CMA strategy puts competition and consumer protection at heart of driving growth and supporting household prosperity. Our independence in individual case decisions is enshrined in law and has not changed.

“We are actively focused on strengthening competition and economic dynamism, including through our work to remove barriers facing scale-ups and innovative firms and open markets to greater challenge. We will continue to use our powers independently and robustly to protect consumers, support innovation, and drive growth.”

articles.title: Net migration now in tens of thousands after exodus of young Brits
articles.summary:
Net migration has fallen into the tens of thousands of people for the first time this century outside of the pandemic, official data has shown, as young Brits leaving the country made up about a fifth of total emigration. 

Migration levels dropped to 77,000 in the year to June 2026, estimates by the Office for National Statistics showed. 

This represented the lowest level of migration since 1997 outside of the pandemic. 

Statisticians said the fall in the net migration of non-EU nationals was the main reason for the decrease. 

Immigration of people outside of the EU dropped by more than 100,000 after tougher rules on visas, including higher salary thresholds for workers, limited people from around the world from moving to the UK. 

Total immigration of non-EU nationals in the 12-month period was 550,000, compared to 79,000 for EU nationals and 109,000 for Britons arriving. 

Emigration levels of about 661,000 helped bring the net migration figure down significantly. In the previous 12-month period, net migration was at 204,000. 

Migration drops as outflow of young Brits increases

The figures will likely relieve Labour government figures as immigration concerns have been pushed down the list of the British public’s voting priorities in recent months. 

For years, the previous Tory government pledged to bring net migration down to the tens of thousands although figures peaked at about 944,000 in the year to March 2023. 

Separate Home Office figures showed on Thursday that the number of people claiming asylum dropped by 33 per cent in one year although there were record high numbers in applications for British citizenship. 

But official data showed that about 19 per cent of total emigration came from British nationals aged between 16 and 34 leaving the country. 

About 65,000 people aged between 25 and 34 left in the 12-month period. Young adults between the age of 16 and 34 made up about half of the total number of British emigrants. 

According to the official body, the net outflow of those aged between 25 and 34 has grown by about five times since 2022. The difference has been driven by British nationals choosing not to return to the country.

Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, said that “British and European people are leaving in their droves” due to a higher tax burden. 

“The fall in net migration is mainly a result of changes made by the previous Conservative government,” Philp said. 

“We now need to go even further with a legally binding annual cap, set by Parliament, at a far lower level. 

“Mass low-skilled immigration must end completely as it is bad for our economy and corrosive to our society.”

articles.title: Unilever perfume suppliers fined €500m over ‘beer and curry’ cartel
articles.summary:
Perfume suppliers to FTSE 100 giant Unilever have been fined more than €500m for running a “beer and curry” cartel in which bosses colluded to fix prices.

The UK’s competition watchdog said three of the world’s biggest perfume makers, who have admitted to breaking the law, collaborated in WhatsApp groups and in person to keep prices high.

Bosses at the Swiss and American perfumers shared sensitive information about their dealings with Unilever, one of the world’s biggest consumer products groups and the owner of brands like Domestos, Dove and Cif.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said the perfume executives used these covert meetings and group chats to collectively refuse Unilever’s requests for them to lower prices. 

The regulator said the suppliers used “WhatsApp messages, telephone calls and other communications” to discuss “how to respond to commercial negotiations, rather than deciding their approaches independently”.

The watchdog added that some of these conversations took place at in-person “beer and curry” meetings in London. The years-long investigation into the perfume companies included raids on their offices in March 2023.

The CMA fined the three manufacturers, Firmenich, Givaudan and International Flavors & Fragrances (IFF), £85m. This is in addition to the €471.9m in penalties imposed by the European Union’s (EU) competition watchdog, bringing the total fines to more than €500m.

Cartels ‘can push up prices’

Juliette Enser, the CMA’s executive director of competition enforcement, said: “Suppliers must set their prices and commercial strategies independently of each other. Exchanging sensitive information with competitors can weaken competition and leave business customers facing costs.

“These were major international suppliers discussing information that should have remained confidential. Today’s fines should be a clear warning for all businesses: competitors must compete, not coordinate behind closed doors.”

The perfume makers’ actions warned that cartel activity can also “ultimately feed through to higher prices” for customers. 

The fines imposed on all three companies were discounted after they co-operated with the UK and EU investigations and settled with the authorities.

Christian Stammkoetter, chief executive of Givaudan, said the behaviour regulators identified was “unacceptable”.

An IFF spokesman said that the company “has accepted responsibility for improper conduct involving certain individuals, none of whom remain with the company”.

DSM-Firmenich said its settlement was not an admission of liability. Their spokesperson added it had “cooperated fully” with investigators and said the settlement represented “the company’s commitment to maintaining the highest standards of compliance and business conduct”.

articles.title: Institutional clients shield CMC from market volatility
articles.summary:
CMC reported a surge in profit before tax, after its pivot towards institutional clients and multi-asset investing shielded it from wider market volatility.

The investment platform saw profit before tax jump to £106m in its half-year results, up from £49.3m the prior year.

CMC chief executive, Lord Peter Cruddas, pinned its progress on its move away from being a “business whose performance is principally driven by the retail trading cycle”.

“That investment now allows us to serve consumers, financial institutions and distribution platforms,” he said.

Headwinds

Group net trading revenue climbed 67 per cent to £230.9m, led by a sharp uptick in activity across its institutional channel.

But further growth was offset by a 31 per cent rise in operating expenses to £177.6m. 

This was primarily driven by a 47 per cent jump in staff costs to £83.8m, following higher performance bonuses, as well as increased spending on technology and its shirt partnership with Everton football club.

CMC warned that the UK government’s decision to increase the banking surcharge from January 2027 will also lift its domestic tax rate to 31 per cent.

Scaling operations

The firm continued to strengthen its position as a global provider of financial services, expanding across major financial hubs.

Its Dubai business now acts as CMC’s strategic base for its institutional business, alongside the UK, Australia and Singapore. 

The firm sees the Dubai hub as able to attract “further substantial growth”, adding the Middle East presents “significant long-term opportunities”.

The firm has also enhanced its “local distribution”, offering products for institutional investors in Europe, Asia Pacific and North America. 

Extending product reach

Alongside its institutional expansion, CMC has broadened its mutli-asset offerings, rolled out fractional investing and 24/5 equity trading, as well as launching a tax-free spread betting product called Spectre.

The FTSE 250 firm also secured regulatory approval to operate as a cryptoasset business in the UK.

Management reaffirmed its full-year guidance of net operating income reaching at least £550m, while earnings before tax are anticipated to climb to £250m. 

The investment platform confirmed a record interim dividend of 10.1p per share, up from 5.5p last year.

articles.title: Babcock lands Burnham backing with record contract win
articles.summary:
Defence giant Babcock has secured the backing of Prime Minister Andy Burnham as it landed its largest contract award in history.

The FTSE 100 engineering group has inked a five-year term agreement worth £8.7bn to support the UK’s submarine availability and deterrents at sea.

It is expected to create 3,000 new full-time roles and more than 2,500 apprentice and graduate opportunities for the period, Babcock said.

The contract, dubbed the Gateway Agreement, was signed with the Ministry of Defence and follows on from Babcock’s previous martime support agreement. 

Burnham said the new contract was a “clear demonstration” of the government’s commitment to keep “the public safe”. He added it would protect jobs and help young people into work as well as protect national security. 

A separate Memorandum of Understanding was signed alongside the deal that could take its lifespan up to 15 years, Babcock said. 

Babcock rides high on defence demand

“Babcock will continue to strengthen sovereign, industrial capabilities, bringing benefits to communities across the country, including SMEs and local supply chain. Together we will further strengthen the UK’s defence readiness and national strategic resilience,” the group’s boss Harry Holt said.

The defence firms’ revenue edged up to £2.7bn in the first half of the year, a climb from £2.5bn in the same period last year.

Its contract backlog stood at £8.9bn, while its debt had narrowed to £267m from £351m.

London-listed defence stocks rallied following the Budget, where Chancellor John Healey announced extra funding for defence through the use of public finance institutions (PuFins) at the Budget.

The Chancellor used the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank as a means to borrow cash for defence, without explicitly breaching the government’s fiscal rules.

Healey resigned as defence secretary under Sir Keir Starmer after a row over funds for the Defence Investment Plan. He had demanded a timetable to increase defence spending to three per cent of GDP by 2030, ahead of Nato’s wider target of 3.5 per cent by 2035.

No specific timetable has been set for the three per cent benchmark.

articles.title: Halfords shares motor after profit target lifted again
articles.summary:
Halfords shares jumped after it improved its profit target for the second time in a matter of months, as the motoring retailer continues to benefit from the surge in sales it saw during the hot summer.

The FTSE 250 firm said it plans to reinvest some of the £8m extra revenue it took during this year’s heatwaves, as record temperatures drove demand for seasonal products like camping equipment and cycling gear. Shares in Halfords jumped more than seven per cent in early trading.

The decision to use this extra proceeds to “accelerate planned investment” will help Halfords reach an underlying pre-tax profit of between £60m and £65m in the full year, the group told shareholders. 

The retailer and garage operator had already boosted its target to a range of £55m and £65m, despite the market initially expecting a return of about £53m. The group is on track to comfortably beat last year’s underlying pre-tax profit of £45m.

The firm notched a £35.5m pre-tax profit in the six months to October, it told shareholders on Thursday, more than doubling last year’s £17.2m. Its revenue grew by 7.1 per cent to £953m, helped by volume increases in categories like motoring accessories and tyres.

Halfords, which was founded in Leicester in 1892, is known for being Britain’s biggest bicycle retailer. But, after the Covid-era surge in demand for bikes faded, new boss Henry Birch has pushed the group to focus on expanding its garage business.

These efforts, which the company pitched to investors as its “Fit for the Future” strategy, were given a lift over the summer when it posted “very strong performance in seasonal categories, in part reflecting unusually warm summer weather”. 

Halfords overhauls retail ranges

Halfords said on Thursday that it expects this unexpected sales boost to “normalise somewhat” in the second half of the year. “Our focus on execution is nevertheless delivering sustainably improved returns,” the group added.

The company is now starting work on its “Evolve” agenda, which will see the group target between £10m and £15m in annual efficiency costs by simplifying its supply chain and operations.

Halfords has already started work on this programme by exercising closer control of the hours worked by its garage staff in a bid to cut labour costs, it said. “[By] ensuring we have the right technician doing the right job in the right location, we are reducing our cost to serve,” the group said.

The firm, which sells cycling and motoring accessories alongside its garage network, has started overhauling its product ranges in a bid to drive margins growth. Halfords hopes to achieve an operating profit margin of between five and six per cent in the coming years.

Birch said: “We continue to make strong progress as we deliver the ‘Optimise’ phase of our strategy, and our focus on improved execution also meant that we were well set up to capitalise on the warm summer weather.

“Looking ahead, we see clear opportunities to invest for long-term shareholder value creation. To this end, we are pleased to be announcing investment in a new, national distribution centre which will support the next phase of Halfords’ growth and drive attractive shareholder returns, ensuring we keep the nation moving for many years to come.”

articles.title: Putin's grip on Crimea tested amid major blackout as Zelenskyy warns of looming Russian strike
articles.summary:
Russian President Vladimir Putin's control over Crimea faced renewed pressure Thursday as a massive blackout crippled the Russian-occupied peninsula, disrupting public transport and leaving people without heat, according to reports.

The blackout came after Ukrainian strikes had damaged the Kerch Strait Bridge last week, disrupting a key Russian military supply route, and as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Moscow was preparing another large-scale attack on Ukraine.

Russian-controlled utilities blamed the Crimea blackout on an accident at energy facilities outside the region, after reports of explosions and air raid sirens sounded across the Black Sea peninsula, according to the Kyiv Post.

PUTIN LAUNCHES UKRAINE BARRAGE HOURS AFTER TRUMP MEETING AMID ALLEGED RUSSIAN MISSILE BREACH OF NATO AIRSPACE

Meanwhile, Zelenskyy said Ukrainian intelligence suggested that Russia was preparing to target the country's energy infrastructure, logistics networks and essential services.

"Unfortunately, the Russians are already completing preparations for a new massive strike," Zelenskyy wrote on X Thursday following a coordination meeting. "According to intelligence, energy facilities and logistics infrastructure, as well as essential services facilities in cities and communities, will once again be the targets."

The Ukrainian leader also urged residents to remain vigilant, warning of renewed missile attacks.

"In the coming days, please pay attention to the alarms of missile threats," Zelenskyy said in his nightly video address Thursday, according to Reuters. "And in Russia, they should know that we will rebuild what is ours and retaliate against every Russian strike."

In Crimea, Russian-controlled electricity provider Sevastopolenergo said that Sevastopol had lost power, while electricity restrictions affected Simferopol, Kerch, Alushta and Yevpatoria, according to Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda.

ZELENSKYY SAYS RUSSIA STRIKES HOMETOWN, CRITICIZES PUTIN-TRUMP MEETING

Streetcar services were also suspended in Yevpatoria and buses replaced trolleybuses on some routes in Simferopol. Parts of Kerch were also reportedly left without heating.

Russian-installed authorities had issued air raid alerts Thursday morning amid reports of explosions.

The blackout is the latest in a series of disruptions that have hit Crimea since late October, with Russian authorities blaming damage to power infrastructure.

The disruptions come amid mounting pressure on Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014 and has since used as a military and logistics hub for its operations against Ukraine.

The Kerch Strait Bridge, which connects the peninsula to mainland Russia, serves as a critical transportation link for Russian forces and has been targeted by Ukraine since Putin launched his invasion in 2022.

KUSHNER ENTERS UKRAINE PEACE TALKS AS TRUMP EYES SECURING SAFEGUARDS AGAINST ANOTHER RUSSIAN INVASION

The bridge was built after the Russian annexation and opened in 2018, serving as a symbol of Moscow's control over the peninsula.

Meanwhile in Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko also said seven people were wounded in an overnight Russian attack on the Ukrainian capital that damaged a shopping center and two other buildings, Reuters reported.

Zelenskyy also called for additional air defense assistance Thursday, emphasizing the need for interceptors for Patriot air defense systems and National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile Systems (NASAMS).

"I expect a report from Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry on the results of its communication with our partners regarding the supply of air defenses — interceptors for Patriots and NASAMS are the key priority," Zelenskyy wrote.

It was the second time this week Zelenskyy had warned of preparations for another major Russian attack, according to Reuters.

articles.title: Iran accuses Zelenskyy of 'false flag' Kuwait drone strike op to get Trump's attention
articles.summary:
A former adviser to Iran's nuclear negotiating team accused Ukraine on Thursday of orchestrating a deadly drone attack in Kuwait to prove its worth to President Donald Trump, as Tehran continued to deny responsibility.

And while Kuwaiti and Italian officials blamed Iran for the strike, which killed two Italian defense technicians and wounded two others, Iran’s embassy in Rome warned against "false flag" operations it said were aimed at widening the Persian Gulf conflict and now drawing Europe into the crisis.

Mohammad Marandi, who served as an adviser during talks with the U.S. in Pakistan and has been dubbed Iran's "English-language mouthpiece," claimed Ukrainian forces were operating across the Middle East, including in northern Iraq and Syria, also in remarks reported by the Fars News Agency, which is affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

IRAN TARGETS US AIR BASE IN KUWAIT AFTER US DEFENSIVE STRIKES AMID CRITICISM FROM GULF STATES

"It is widely believed in Iran that the attack on Kuwait was a false flag operation, likely carried out by the Ukrainian regime, because its operatives are now present across the region, including in northern Iraq and Syria. Ukraine aims to demonstrate its potential to Trump," Marandi said on X.

Fars also cited a security source who claimed Ukrainian operatives had deployed thousands of drones and other unmanned aircraft in several Middle Eastern countries, including Iraq's Kurdistan region, according to Iran International.

Kuwait's Defense Ministry said falling debris from the interception of Iranian drones struck a military facility Thursday, initially wounding four people. Two Italian nationals later died of their injuries.

A Kuwaiti national and a Pakistani national were also wounded and taken to a hospital for treatment. The ministry did not disclose the facility's precise location.

Italy's Foreign Ministry confirmed that the two Italian nationals were employees of Rheinmetall Italia, the Italian subsidiary of German defense manufacturer Rheinmetall.

"An explosion caused by a drone attack ... occurred at a site where two Italian technicians from the company Rheinmetall Italia were working," the ministry said in a statement.

The victims were identified as Antonio Saccoccio, 65, of Formia, Italy, and Emanuele Lo Russo, 36, of Rome, Italian news agency ANSA reported.

EUROPE ASSASSINATION SCHEME EMERGES AS IRAN DENIES DC 'DIRTY BOMB' PLOT AMID TRUMP WARNING

The men had been performing maintenance on detection antennas for the Skyguard air defense system.

Iran's embassy in Rome rejected allegations that Tehran was responsible for the attack, warning of alleged efforts to draw European countries into the Middle East conflict.

"The Embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran also draws the international community's attention to 'false flag' activities and operations aimed at expanding the scope of the conflict, linking disputes in other regions to the Persian Gulf crisis, drawing Europe into the crisis, and exacerbating the current critical situation, and calls on everyone to remain vigilant in this regard."

Meanwhile, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he had spoken with his Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts and offered to cooperate in an investigation into the deadly incident.

"In calls with my Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts, expressed condolences over deaths of Italian citizens in Kuwait," Araghchi wrote. "The incident is suspicious and looks like a precooked recipe for war.

"We stand ready to cooperate with Kuwait and Italy to determine the cause of the incident," he added.

TOP GULF OFFICIAL OFFERS GLIMMER OF HOPE ON TRUMP-IRAN NUCLEAR TALKS AS THREAT OF WAR HANGS OVER REGION

Kuwait, a key U.S. ally in the Persian Gulf, has repeatedly come under Iranian attack since the U.S. and Israel launched military operations against Iran on Feb. 28.

Ukraine has deployed drone specialists and interceptor drones to the Middle East to help defend against Iranian attacks, expanding its regional defense cooperation by sharing technology and military expertise developed during its war with Russia.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in March that Kyiv had sent interceptor drones and specialists to help protect U.S. military installations in Jordan at Washington's request.

Ukraine also announced that teams of military specialists had been deployed to Kuwait, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia to help defend against Iranian drone attacks.

"Ukraine has the greatest experience in the world in countering attack drones," Zelenskyy said in March, adding that "without our experience, it will be very difficult for the Gulf region, the entire Middle East, and partners in Europe and America to build strong protection."

articles.title: UK shields fighter jets, contacts reservists in Cold War-scale push amid Russia threat
articles.summary:
The United Kingdom is bolstering its military readiness amid growing threats from Russia, contacting former service members to assess its reserves as the Royal Air Force reportedly strengthens defenses against potential drone attacks.

Britain's Ministry of Defence has written to former service members to verify their contact information and military skills to ensure the country is prepared for a national emergency or potential conflict, Secretary of State for Defence Wes Streeting confirmed Friday.

The outreach comes as the International Institute for Strategic Studies warned Thursday that suspected Russian-directed sabotage across Europe could trigger a "mass-casualty event."

NATO WARNS PUTIN COULD STRIKE BEFORE EUROPEAN ARMY RESPONDS, POINTS TO US AS MILITARY MODEL

The think tank found that sabotage incidents rose 16% in the year through September 2026, with Germany and Poland accounting for more than half of the cases. Researchers warned that a major attack could spark calls for retaliation and divide European governments.

"I want the country to be alert, not alarmed," Streeting told BBC Radio 4's "Today" program.

"You can't not look at what's going on in Europe and not be concerned about a threat environment which has deteriorated in recent years and is sadly increasing," he said.

Streeting said the government needed updated records of its strategic reserve in case former service members were called upon to respond to a domestic disaster or overseas conflict.

He cited Russian incursions into Polish airspace, suspected Russian-sponsored sabotage across Europe and Iran-linked threats to British military bases.

Last week, a suspected Russian projectile landed in eastern Poland about 60 miles from a British-led military exercise. The incident happened the same day Britain's defense secretary and chief of the air staff visited troops.

INSIDE THE PENTAGON'S DOOMSDAY PLAN TO KEEP AMERICA FIGHTING IF GLOBAL WAR ERUPTS

"And so against that backdrop, against that threat environment, the government and the country has to be ready to face down those risks," Streeting said. "Because the more ready we are, the less likely we are to find ourselves in a conflict, in a war. That is my goal. That is the goal of this government."

The Ministry of Defence said in a news release it was contacting thousands of former military personnel this week as part of a drive to "strengthen the UK’s readiness and deliver on recommendations made in the Strategic Defence Review."

"Service Chiefs are writing to members of the Strategic Reserve, asking them to stay connected and update their details, providing Defence with a better understanding of the skills and experience it could draw upon if needed."

"In the coming months, Strategic Reservists will have the opportunity to volunteer for training and exercises, such as the UK’s participation in NATO’s flagship Steadfast Defender next spring."

The outreach marks the first time since the Cold War that Britain's defense ministry has contacted reservists on such a scale to encourage participation in military exercises, according to The Telegraph.

TRUMP’S PROPOSED RUSSIA DEAL RAISES NATO ALARM AS EX-COMMANDER WARNS PUTIN SEEKS INFLUENCE OVER EUROPE

Meanwhile, Britain's domestic intelligence agency, MI5, and the defense ministry have reportedly warned British companies supplying military equipment to Ukraine that they could be targeted by Russian saboteurs.

The Royal Air Force is strengthening security at military bases, using hardened aircraft shelters and installing anti-drone netting to protect exposed fighter jets, according to The Times.

The measures follow Iranian threats against military bases in England that prompted tighter security and the relocation of U.S. military aircraft.

Suspected drone incursions over European airfields have also heightened concerns about Russian aggression.

"We take the security of our bases, equipment and personnel very seriously and are always adapting to counter any potential threats," a Ministry of Defence spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

US MILITARY BASES ARE ‘ILL-EQUIPPED’ TO STOP DRONE SWARMS, TOP COMMANDER REVEALS AFTER RUBIO'S UAP WARNING

"This includes investing an additional £470 million to strengthen security at military sites, including better physical protection, surveillance and counter-drone capabilities.

"We have already invested £15 million in drone and counter-drone technology and introduced restricted airspace over 44 critical Defence sites."

The developments come as President Donald Trump said Thursday he had asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to "pull back all military aggression" against Europe, signaling a shift in tone toward the Russian leader, whom he called a friend last week.

Trump said he made the request during a meeting with Putin in China last week, adding that he believed it could help secure a deal to end Russia's war in Ukraine.

Trump's comments came a day after he hosted NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte in Florida. The two leaders issued a joint statement urging Russia not to expand its war in Ukraine.

"During my conversations in China with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, I spent a lot of time talking about the fact that I would like to see President Putin pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe," Trump said on Truth Social.

articles.title: Ukrainian intelligence says North Korea paused missile deliveries to Russia amid friction over South Korea
articles.summary:
North Korea has temporarily halted shipments of ballistic missiles and artillery shells to Russia following diplomatic friction between the two allies over Moscow's outreach to South Korea, Ukrainian military intelligence said Thursday.

According to Ukraine's GUR military intelligence agency, North Korean Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui announced the freeze on KN-23 ballistic missile and artillery deliveries last month after Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko suggested Moscow would help de-escalate tensions between Seoul and Pyongyang, Reuters reported.

Choe demanded that Russia clarify its policy toward South Korea, GUR said, though Reuters noted it could not independently verify the report or confirm public remarks from either official.

PUTIN'S WAR DEATH TOLL REPORTEDLY TOPS 700,000 AS RUSSIA SCRAMBLES FOR RECRUITS

The reported pause also suspends Russian military flights over North Korea and stalls a Kremlin request to expand North Korea's troop deployment in Russia from roughly 8,500 to 50,000, according to the outlet.

Rudenko, who oversees Asian relations, said last month that Seoul had signaled interest in normalizing ties and resuming direct flights with Moscow once the Ukraine war ends.

Despite the reported freeze, North Korean troops remain active in Russia, with 11th Corps units serving in the Kursk region and a missile unit operating in Voronezh since mid-summer, GUR said. Russian President Vladimir Putin also hosted top Kim Jong Un aide Jo Yong Won at the Kremlin last week, where both men reportedly praised bilateral cooperation.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned on social media Thursday that Moscow is "completing preparations for a new massive strike" on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, logistics and critical services.

TRUMP'S HISTORIC SUMMIT WITH XI, PUTIN MARKS DIPLOMATIC MILESTONE, BUT BREAKTHROUGHS REMAIN ELUSIVE

Crews are already working to restore power in six regions after overnight Russian missile and drone strikes damaged an apartment building, a hospital and businesses, according to Zelenskyy, who also renewed appeals for U.S.-made Patriot air defense interceptors.

In Washington, President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social Thursday that he urged Putin during talks in China to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe, in the hopes that a deal can be made between Russia and Ukraine, and made quickly."

U.S. envoy Jared Kushner, who is mediating talks with Steve Witkoff, said on the "MD Meets" podcast that Putin has "shown restraint" by agreeing not to use nuclear weapons, though negotiations remain deadlocked over Ukrainian territory.

Ukrainian forces also struck a Russian military airfield and an oil pumping facility overnight, while Russia claimed it intercepted 343 Ukrainian drones.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: FlyDubai to resume Tel Aviv flights following attempted hijacking incident
articles.summary:
FlyDubai announced Thursday it will resume flights to Tel Aviv, Israel, next week, ending a suspension in place following an attempted hijacking incident in late September, according to media reports.

A source familiar with the matter told The Times of Israel that the airline is being allowed back into Israeli airspace "under new security arrangements."

The development comes after Transportation Minister Miri Regev decided this week that FlyDubai flights to Israel can resume pending clearance from Shin Bet, Mossad and Israel's National Security Council, the outlet reported.

A FlyDubai spokesperson told Reuters that the flights will begin again on Dec. 3. FlyDubai flights to Israel have been suspended since FlyDubai Flight FZ1073 on Sept. 30, when a co-pilot allegedly attacked his captain.

FLYDUBAI CO-PILOT ALLEGEDLY PLANNED TO CRASH ISRAEL-BOUND JET AT BEN GURION AIRPORT

That plane was diverted to Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, where it made a safe landing.

"Captain Smit Machchhar, the Indian captain of FlyDubai Flight 1073, fought back after being stabbed in the cockpit," according to the Israel Foreign Ministry. "Despite being severely injured, he managed to unlock the cockpit door – allowing Israeli passengers and the Emirati crew to intervene and save all the passengers."

FLYDUBAI PILOT SHOWED WORLD 'THE HIGHEST FORM OF COURAGE,' INDIA'S PM SAYS

Israeli broadcaster Channel 12 reported that Hamam al-Hammami told investigators he intended to continue Flight FZ1073 toward Israel as though nothing was wrong, obtain the necessary clearances to approach Ben Gurion Airport and then crash the aircraft into a building or another plane at the airport.

UAE Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said investigators determined that the co-pilot attempted to carry out a terrorist act by attacking the captain with a crash axe and attempting to take control of the aircraft.

Fox News Digital's Bradford Betz contributed to this report.

articles.title: Bangkok oil refinery explosion injures at least 9, Thailand company monitoring air quality
articles.summary:
At least nine people have been injured in an oil refinery explosion in Bangkok, Thailand, on Thursday, with three in critical condition.

The explosion occurred at a Bangchak Corporation-owned facility, the company confirmed in a statement posted to Facebook.

The company also claimed it was able to control and extinguish a large blaze caused by the explosion within 30 minutes of the blast.

EMERGENCY CREWS RESPONDING TO MASSIVE EXPLOSION AT NEW ORLEANS-AREA OIL REFINERY: SHERIFF

Additionally, it claimed monitoring showed no reduction in normal air quality.

"Since the incident occurred, the company has continuously monitored air quality in real time using automatic ambient air quality monitoring (AQM) stations, which the company has installed in the Phra Khanong, Bang Na, and Bang Nam Phueng areas to measure air quality around the refinery resulting from operations," the company wrote.

TWO INJURED AFTER EXPLOSION RIPS THROUGH CHEMICAL PLANT, SPARKING HAZMAT RESPONSE, SHELTER-IN-PLACE ORDER

"It was found that the air quality in the surrounding area of the refinery is within normal standards. Furthermore, at 5: 30 PM (17: 30 hrs.), the Pollution Control Department measured the air quality within a 3–4 km radius around the refinery—the same radial area—and confirmed that the measurement results are within normal standards," the statement added.

The company said it has also paused all production operations at the facility.

'PURE HELL' IN MOSCOW AS UKRAINIAN DRONES STRIKE MAJOR REFINERY SUPPLYING CAPITAL'S FUEL MARKET

Local authorities issued a mobile phone alert to nearby residents around 3 p.m. local time advising them to avoid the area.

Officials later told residents they could return home but advised those living within 5 kilometers (3 miles) of the facility to be wary of air pollution.

CALIFORNIA OFFICIALS WARN MASSIVE CHEMICAL TANK WILL LIKELY SPILL THOUSANDS OF GALLONS OR 'BLOW UP'

Thailand's Pollution Control Department also said it was monitoring air and water pollution levels in the area.

The country's energy minister, Akanat Promphan, said the fire likely started at one of the refinery units, which is hundreds of feet away from where oil is stored.

OFFICIALS SAY POSSIBLE CRACK IN UNSTABLE CHEMICAL TANK MAY RELIEVE PRESSURE AT AEROSPACE PLANT

"If we’re not a hundred percent certain that the oil storage is safe, we won’t allow them to resume operations," Promphan said.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Housefishing could fool you with AI real estate photos
articles.summary:
You find a beautiful house online. The driveway looks brand new, and the landscaping could be straight out of a home magazine. You get excited, schedule a showing and start thinking about where your furniture might go. Then you pull up to the address and wonder whether you're looking at the same house.

That's the growing concern behind housefishing, a term for real estate listings that use digitally altered or AI-generated photos to make properties look better than they actually are. A recent report highlighted complaints from homebuyers and renters who described misleading property pictures as "false advertising." With AI tools becoming more convincing, it's getting harder to know whether you're looking at a home's actual condition or a digital makeover. So how can you tell whether a listing photo shows the home you're actually getting, and what should you check before scheduling a tour?

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

HIS HOME CHANGED HANDS FOR $5. COULD IT HAPPEN TO YOUR FAMILY?

Housefishing happens when property photos create an unrealistic impression of a home. AI can make an outdated property appear freshly renovated without anyone doing the actual work. For instance, two photos can show the same two-story house, but create very different impressions. 

The original photo can show a home with a dark asphalt driveway and large shrubs covering much of the front porch. But an AI-enhanced version can show a clean concrete driveway and a newly styled entrance.

This example shows how digital alterations can make a property appear to have undergone an expensive makeover. If those improvements exist only in the edited photo, someone visiting the property could be in for an unpleasant surprise.

Virtual staging has been around for years. Adding digital furniture to an empty living room can help buyers understand how they might use the space. AI simply makes those transformations easier and more realistic. But replacing a worn-out kitchen with an AI-generated renovation is another story. Laurent Cardinal, founder of real estate technology company Planpoint at planpoint.io/, believes agents need to be upfront about what they've changed. "The line is drawn where the intent is," Cardinal explains.

He supports using AI to show what a home could look like after renovations, provided agents clearly disclose the changes. His recommendation is straightforward: Show the original photo alongside the edited version so prospective buyers can compare them. However, digitally hiding property defects or replacing an unattractive view crosses that line. "That's cheating and it's hurtful to everyone in the market," Cardinal says. A misleading listing can waste someone's time and influence important financial decisions. For renters, the consequences can be especially serious if they send a deposit based on photos that fail to reflect the property.

You might think you'd recognize an AI-generated photo immediately. Maybe the furniture looks strange or a window seems out of place. Unfortunately, today's tools can produce convincing results. Sometimes the changes are subtle enough to escape a close look. Cardinal warns that even people familiar with AI-generated content can struggle to identify it. "But there's no silver bullet here, and anyone can get caught," he says.

Unusually perfect rooms can raise questions, especially when architectural details appear inconsistent between photos. However, traditional real estate photography can also be misleading. Wide-angle lenses make rooms appear larger, while carefully chosen lighting can minimize visible imperfections. AI creates an additional concern because it can alter the features of the property itself. That makes it increasingly difficult to judge a home's condition from listing photos alone.

FAKE VACATION RENTAL SITES USE LIVE CHAT TO STEAL YOUR DATA

The rules depend on where the property is located and which listing service an agent uses. California has already taken action. Under Assembly Bill 723, which took effect Jan. 1, 2026, real estate professionals must disclose covered digital alterations in advertisements for properties for sale. They must also provide access to the original, unaltered photos. The law covers changes made using traditional editing software or AI. Routine adjustments to lighting or color generally fall outside the requirements when they don't misrepresent the property. California has also approved Assembly Bill 2025. Starting Jan. 1, 2027, the state will require disclosures for digitally altered rental advertisements, with access to original photos when existing pictures have been changed.

Meanwhile, New York has warned agents about misleading AI property pictures. In November 2025, the New York Department of State reminded real estate professionals that advertisements must accurately represent properties for sale or rent. Agents who publish deceptive advertisements can face disciplinary action. Multiple listing services have their own restrictions. Stellar MLS, for example, requires disclosure of virtually staged photos and prohibits edits that conceal property defects or alter permanent features. There is currently no single nationwide law requiring every AI-edited real estate photo to carry a disclosure. Still, existing advertising laws and professional rules can apply when pictures mislead prospective buyers.

Interestingly, the same technology creating misleading property photos may also help identify them. Cardinal's company, Planpoint, connects listing photos to interactive floor plans. That allows prospective buyers to see how rooms fit together instead of relying on individual pictures that may be difficult to interpret. Its Planpoint Visit platform also offers AI photo detection. The technology checks newly uploaded property photos for signs of AI generation and displays a warning when it finds something suspicious. Cardinal says the company achieved a 98% success rate in its internal testing.

Before scheduling a showing or putting money down on a property, there are several ways to check whether the listing photos tell the whole story.

If a home looks suspiciously polished, ask the agent whether any pictures have been digitally altered. Request the original photos so you can compare them. Pay particular attention to kitchens and bathrooms, where expensive renovations can significantly affect a home's value. If an agent cannot explain what was changed, ask more questions before moving forward.

Cardinal recommends a simple way to verify a property's appearance. "The easiest way is to request a live video call with the agent or the owner," he says. Ask to see the areas you're most interested in, including anything that looks unusually perfect in the listing. A live walkthrough can reveal details that edited photos might hide. However, it cannot prove that the person showing the home has authority to rent or sell it.

Look carefully at the room dimensions and window locations. Then compare those details with the photos. Cardinal suggests asking, "Do the rooms and angles add up?" If a small bedroom appears enormous in a listing, ask whether the pictures were digitally altered. Remember that wide-angle photography can also exaggerate the apparent size of a room.

Search the property's address in Google Maps and look at the exterior using Street View. Compare the driveway and surrounding homes with what's shown in the listing. You might notice changes that deserve a closer look. However, Street View pictures can be outdated, so differences don't automatically mean an agent used AI.

Use Google Lens or another reverse-image search tool to check whether the same property pictures appear elsewhere online. You may find older listings showing the home before it was digitally enhanced. You could also discover that someone copied photos from another property to create a fraudulent rental advertisement. For help getting started, see our guide on how to reverse search an image on your phone.

Never rely solely on listing photos when making a financial commitment. If you're renting, independently verify the identity and authority of the landlord or agent before sending a deposit. For a home purchase, arrange an in-person showing and an independent inspection before committing to buy. A polished listing photo cannot tell you whether the property has hidden problems.

Those example of the two photos of the same house really show how far AI has come. The updated version looks fantastic, and I can see why someone would want to schedule a showing. But what happens when you arrive and discover that the beautiful driveway and landscaping don't actually exist? I think AI can be a great tool for helping buyers see a home's potential, especially if they're considering renovations. The problem starts when agents present those digital upgrades as the real thing. Buying a home is a major investment, and people deserve to know exactly what they're getting before they fall in love with a property online. I'd like to see more transparency from real estate agents, with original photos available alongside any AI-enhanced versions. There's nothing wrong with showing what a house could become, but buyers should never have to guess what it looks like today.

Would you walk away from a home if you discovered the agent had used AI to make it look better than it actually was, or would you consider that acceptable marketing? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com
