articles.title: Unvaccinated Pennsylvania resident dies of measles in state's ninth fatal case this year
articles.summary:
Pennsylvania health officials announced Monday that a resident unvaccinated against measles died from the virus after testing positive, making it the ninth measles-related death in the state this year.

The Pennsylvania Department of Health confirmed the death less than a week after the United States lost its measles elimination status, ending a public health achievement that had been maintained since 2000.

Officials said the victim was a resident of Centre County, located in the middle of the state and most known for being home to Penn State University.

The state has 1,638 confirmed measles cases across 46 counties this year, including 49 new infections that were reported Monday.

CHILD’S MEASLES DEATH MARKS NEW YORK STATE’S FIRST IN MORE THAN 30 YEARS AMID OUTBREAK

Hospitalizations rose from 315 to 330, according to the state’s measles dashboard. Just five of the confirmed infections involved vaccinated residents.

Last week, officials confirmed the state’s eighth measles death, an unvaccinated Clinton County resident.

Pennsylvania and federal health authorities continue to urge residents to get the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, saying it the best defense against the disease.

Pennsylvania has been battling a measles outbreak since April and now leads the nation in cases, accounting for more than a quarter of all U.S. infections.

TRUMP SURGEON GENERAL PICK BACKS MMR VACCINE, REJECTS LINK BETWEEN CHILDHOOD VACCINES AND AUTISM

The sharp rise in cases — largely in rural and Amish communities with historically low vaccination rates — has prompted state health officials to ramp up immunization efforts.

The state health department has administered more than 7,400 doses of the MMR vaccine at nearly 300 pop-up clinics. Officials plan to set up dozens more of these temporary immunization sites over the coming weeks and months.

For months, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have sparred over the response to the ongoing measles outbreak in the state.

Shapiro has accused Kennedy of spreading misinformation about the MMR vaccine and vaccines in general, something the nation's top health official has denied.

AMISH FACE NEW YORK VACCINE MANDATE IN SUPREME COURT FIGHT, MIGHT HAVE TO ‘PACK THEIR WAGONS’

Overall, Kennedy has given a mix of answers about his stance on the MMR vaccine. When testifying before the House in May 2025, he said he would "probably" vaccinate his children against measles.

When he was asked the same question in August 2024, prior to becoming HHS secretary, Kennedy said he would not give his kids the MMR vaccine.

Kennedy, meanwhile, has accused Shapiro of politicizing the outbreak and suggested that some of Pennsylvania’s reported measles deaths may have been "fabricated."

The Pan American Health Organization’s decision last Wednesday to revoke the U.S.’ measles elimination status means the virus is once again considered endemic in the country. This means it is circulating regularly at a relatively predictable level, much like the seasonal flu and chickenpox.

The difference is, measles is around 12 times more contagious than the flu and twice as contagious as chickenpox, according to Unicef.

People infected with measles — especially babies and young children — also face the risk of severe complications, including a weakened immune system or encephalitis, a type of brain swelling that can cause seizures and intellectual disabilities.

articles.title: Apple tightens Mac security as AI agents seek your files
articles.summary:
Ever download an app on your Mac and click through the permission requests without giving them much thought? You're certainly not alone. But what if one of those approvals gave an AI assistant access to your private messages, financial documents or even files you thought were protected?

That's the concern behind Apple's latest Mac security controls. As AI agents become more capable of performing tasks on your computer, they're also requesting access to more personal information. And once you grant certain permissions, an app could potentially see far more than you intended.

Now, Apple is introducing new protections in macOS 27.3 that give you greater control over what these apps can access. The changes arrived in macOS 27.3 beta 2 on Nov. 16, with the broader software release still to come. Here's what Apple is changing and why you may want to check your Mac's privacy settings now.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

MALICIOUS BROWSER EXTENSIONS CAN HIJACK AI ASSISTANTS

AI assistants have become increasingly useful, especially when you want help getting through a long list of tasks. An AI agent can go further by interacting with apps and taking actions on your behalf. For example, you might ask an AI agent to organize your Downloads folder or find a receipt buried in your email. To complete those tasks, the software may request permission to access information stored on your Mac. That's where things can get uncomfortable. Some apps request a powerful macOS permission called Full Disk Access, which can give them access to nearly everything stored on your computer, including information from other apps.

Apple warns that an app with this permission can read or modify sensitive files. It may also be able to delete or export information without asking you again. And the potential exposure goes beyond documents. Another powerful permission, called System & App Protection Override, can allow an app to control your Mac and monitor activity, including keystrokes, when you grant unrestricted access. That's a lot of trust to place in software, especially when an AI agent can take actions without asking you to approve every step.

Apple's upcoming update introduces several changes designed to make powerful permissions easier to understand. It also gives Mac owners more opportunities to limit access before an app starts working.

Apple is separating its existing Device Control and Data Access permission system into two settings: System & App Protection Override and Accessibility. The change helps clarify when an app is requesting permission to bypass built-in protections. Apple is also introducing more detailed warnings about the information an app could access if you approve its request. Instead of clicking through a vague permission prompt, you'll have more information about what you're allowing.

One of the biggest changes involves Full Disk Access. Starting with macOS 27.3, some apps requesting this permission will let you choose specific protected folders instead of granting access to everything. Other apps may continue using the existing approval process, depending on their purpose.

For example, an AI tool helping you organize work documents may only need access to one folder. You could grant that limited permission while keeping other protected information off-limits. Apple is also introducing a more consistent process for granting these permissions. You'll select the requesting app from a list rather than navigating different approval methods.

Another important addition gives you more control over how AI agents interact with other apps. When configuring System & App Protection Override, you can choose which apps an AI tool may control. For each approved app, you can select Ask First or At Any Time. Choosing Ask First means the AI agent must request permission before controlling that app. That extra confirmation may slow down some automated tasks, but it also gives you an opportunity to catch unwanted actions.

Apple is adding a transparency indicator that appears when an app controls another app through this permission system. That could make it easier to recognize when software is acting on your behalf.

MAC MALWARE CAN HIDE COMMANDS IN YOUR ICLOUD CALENDAR

Apple's announcement follows growing scrutiny over how much information AI-powered software can access. In September, a journalist claimed that Meta's Muse AI app had read his private messages without his permission. Meta disputed that account, saying the Messages integration requires explicit permission. Separately, a security vulnerability in OpenAI's ChatGPT Mac app could have allowed attackers to access sensitive information. OpenAI patched the flaw before it was publicly reported.

These incidents highlight the security concerns surrounding increasingly capable AI software. Even legitimate applications can create privacy risks when they receive broad access to personal information. Apple's response focuses on making those permissions more visible and giving people greater control over what they approve. Importantly, the changes won't prevent you from installing AI agents or using apps that genuinely need broader permissions.

There's something worth knowing before assuming the update will automatically protect everything on your Mac. Apple says permissions you've already granted will remain in effect after the update. The new approval experience primarily applies when apps request permissions going forward.

That means an AI app you installed months ago could still have access to information you previously approved. You'll need to review those permissions yourself if you want to change them. Apple is also allowing developers of certain backup and accessibility applications to request special permissions that preserve their existing functionality. This should help prevent legitimate tools from losing features they need to operate.

You can review your Mac's privacy permissions now, even before macOS 27.3 becomes widely available.

Steps may vary slightly depending on your version of macOS.

If you find an app with permissions it no longer needs, you can revoke its access. Depending on your macOS version, you may see a toggle or an option to remove the app from the permission list. For macOS 27.3: Select an app and click the Remove (−) button to revoke access. To replace broad access with a more limited permission, remove the app and add it again. When prompted, choose the specific protected folders or apps it needs.

Keep in mind that some legitimate applications, including backup software and security tools, require extensive access to function properly. Removing their permissions could prevent certain features from working.

AI CHATBOT PRIVACY: WHAT YOUR AI MAY KNOW ABOUT YOU

You don't have to stop using AI assistants to protect your information. A few precautions can help you take advantage of these tools while reducing unnecessary exposure.

When an app requests access to your files, consider whether it needs permission to browse your entire Mac. If the new macOS controls offer a Choose Folder or Choose Apps option, use it to limit the information the software can reach. You can adjust those permissions later if the app needs additional access.

If you're using macOS 27.3, look for the Ask First setting when granting an AI agent permission to control another application. This gives you another opportunity to review what the software wants to do. It's especially useful when an AI tool interacts with apps containing sensitive personal information.

Be careful when installing new AI agents, particularly from unfamiliar websites. We've previously reported how AI-related scams target Mac owners through convincing fake download pages. Stick with official developer websites or the Mac App Store whenever possible. Keep your installed apps updated to receive security fixes.

Your Mac includes built-in malware protection, but reputable antivirus software can add another layer of security. It can help detect malicious downloads and other threats, including malware disguised as legitimate AI tools. However, antivirus software can't reliably prevent an app from accessing information you've already given it permission to use. That's why reviewing your Mac's privacy settings remains important. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Even when an app has limited access to your files, you should understand how it handles information you choose to share. Check whether the developer stores your data or sends it to cloud servers. Apple's permission controls can restrict access to protected information on your Mac, but they don't replace an app's privacy policy.

An AI tool may have needed access to a particular folder when you first installed it. That doesn't mean it needs the same permission indefinitely. Periodically check Privacy & Security and remove access that no longer serves a purpose. This is particularly important for AI apps you rarely use.

If you're allowing an AI agent to organize or modify files, make sure you have a recent backup. An automated task could accidentally delete something important or change a document you wanted to keep. Apple's built-in Time Machine can automatically back up your Mac and help you recover files if something goes wrong. For step-by-step instructions, check out our guide on how to back up your computer.

I'm glad Apple is taking a closer look at how much access AI agents can have on our computers. These tools are becoming more capable, and I can see why people would want an assistant that handles repetitive work. But giving an app permission to see everything on your Mac seems like a steep price to pay for convenience. I particularly like the option to make an AI agent ask before controlling another app. That's a level of oversight I would want, especially when personal information is involved. My biggest concern is that previously granted permissions will remain active. Apple can introduce better warnings, but those warnings won't change the decisions you've already made. I'd encourage Mac owners to spend a few minutes reviewing their settings rather than waiting for the next update.

Would you trust an AI assistant with unrestricted access to your Mac if it could save you hours of work, or does the thought of software reading your private information cross a line? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

articles.title: Ex- Ukraine prosecutor general accuses Zelenskyy's office of interfering in anti-corruption investigation
articles.summary:
Ukraine's former prosecutor general is accusing President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's administration of interfering in a criminal investigation involving the head of the country's anti-corruption bureau after the president demanded his removal from office in September.

In an extensive interview with Fox News Digital, Ruslan Kravchenko alleged that Zelenskyy's decision to remove him came under pressure from the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO), whose officials he said his office had been investigating.

"The signature on the resignation letter was mine. The decision was his," Kravchenko said. "You do not have to put handcuffs on the president himself to tie his hands. It is enough to put the people he relies on at risk."

BILLIONS IN US AID TO UKRAINE UNDER MICROSCOPE AS CORRUPTION ROCKS ZELENSKYY’S INNER CIRCLE

Kravchenko's most serious allegation concerns what happened afterward. He claims the president's office instructed prosecutors to close a criminal case involving NABU Director Semen Kryvonos.

"The Office of the President began issuing instructions to the Office of the Prosecutor General to immediately close the criminal case against the head of NABU," he said. "In my assessment, that amounts to deliberate interference in an investigation."

"The authority to investigate crimes becomes the ability to determine government policy and even geopolitics," he argued.

Kravchenko did not identify who allegedly issued those instructions or provide documentary evidence of the communications in the materials supplied to Fox News Digital. His allegation of presidential interference has not been independently verified.

UKRAINE'S ZELENSKYY ON DEFYING US IN ATTACKING RUSSIAN OIL: 'OUR RESPONSE MUST BE PAINFUL'

Kravchenko's departure followed a September investigation known as Operation Carthage, in which NABU and SAPO accused officials connected to the Prosecutor General's Office of helping protect fraudulent call centers and laundering criminal proceeds.

According to a Sept. 8 report in The Guardian, the investigation centered on fraudulent call centers whose employees impersonated banks, police officers and investment advisers to steal money from victims in Ukraine, Russia and Europe. NABU alleged that a senior official in the Prosecutor General's Office protected the operation and helped launder its proceeds. 

Law enforcement sources told Ukrainska Pravda that individual call centers paid approximately $7,000 a month in protection money. Investigators also released recordings suggesting that the principal suspect had overseen repairs at Kravchenko's home while allegedly collecting bribes.

Kravchenko, who has not been charged in the investigation, denies wrongdoing and rejects the allegations against his office. He claimed the operation was intended to seize investigative materials concerning misconduct by anti-corruption officials and prevent him from pursuing those cases.

He said he initially refused to resign but changed his position following a Sept. 7 meeting with Zelenskyy, attended, according to Kravchenko, by Davyd Arakhamia, leader of the president's parliamentary faction.

"When the president wants your resignation and the leader of his parliamentary faction, which commands a majority, is sitting beside him, believe me: a prosecutor general's room for maneuver is extremely limited," he said.

Zelenskyy publicly confirmed that he had demanded Kravchenko's removal.

"There is only one path for this Prosecutor General: removal from office. That is what I told him," Zelenskyy said in a Sept. 14 statement, according to Reuters.

Zelenskyy also said that if Kravchenko considered the decision political pressure, he was free to characterize it that way. The president suspended him on Sept. 14, and parliament approved his dismissal the following day.

ZELENSKYY PRESSES US FOR EXPANDED RUSSIA TALKS AS KUSHNER ANNOUNCES BREAKTHROUGH

The confrontation intensified when Kravchenko announced on Sept. 14 that he had signed a notice of suspicion against Kryvonos over alleged misconduct predating his appointment as NABU director.

Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office disputed the validity of the notice, stating that Kryvonos had not been formally notified of suspicion under Ukrainian law and that relevant entries in the investigative register had been deleted.

Kravchenko alleges those actions followed pressure from the president's administration. The claim remains unverified.

NABU and SAPO have rejected Kravchenko's broader accusations, describing them as a campaign against independent anti-corruption institutions. In a Nov. 4 announcement, the agencies said Operation Carthage had uncovered an alleged criminal network involving senior law-enforcement officials accused of protecting fraudulent businesses. Those allegations have not been proven in court.

The controversy comes amid widespread public concern about corruption. A September survey by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology found that 72% of Ukrainians held Zelenskyy politically responsible for corruption among his associates, although the findings did not suggest respondents believed he was personally involved.

Zelenskyy has publicly condemned the widening investigation's allegations. In a Nov. 7 address, he described alleged misconduct involving senior security officials as "frankly shameful, absolutely unacceptable," according to Reuters, and called for a full investigation.

His former chief of staff, Andriy Yermak, defended him in an interview with the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, amid an earlier corruption scandal in November 2025, describing Zelenskyy as "not corrupt" and saying he had allowed independent anti-corruption investigations.

Zelenskyy's office did not respond to multiple requests from Fox News Digital for comment on Kravchenko's latest allegations.

The former prosecutor general maintains that his removal prevented him from pursuing investigations into the leadership of the anti-corruption agencies. Ukrainian authorities, meanwhile, have publicly defended the investigation that preceded his dismissal.

articles.title: Former Florida mayor urges American Jews to fight back against rising antisemitism
articles.summary:
As antisemitism surges across the United States and around the world in the wake of Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, massacre, policy strategist and public speaker Gabe Groisman is urging American Jews to stand their ground and fight for the future of their community — and the soul of the nation.

In his new book, "The Jewish Fight for America," Groisman, a former mayor of Bal Harbour, Florida, explores the history of American Jews and their contributions to the country, arguing that despite rising antisemitism, they should confront the tide of hate and stand firm in their rightful place.

"The first fight we have to take on here in the U.S. is to strengthen the community, to try to teach our brothers and sisters about who we are as a people," Groisman told Fox News Digital. "Then we can get to the part of why the Land of Israel is important to us, why Jewish sovereignty over the Land of Israel, which is the State of Israel today, is an integral part of who we are as Jews in America or anywhere in the world."

CHRISTIAN ZIONISTS TAKE ON ANTI-ISRAEL ‘PROPAGANDA’ FROM BIBLICAL HEARTLAND

One of the book’s chapters opens with quotes from Genesis. Groisman explained that powerful forces are seeking to distance American Jews from Israel. On the left, he said, a movement is seeking to "unlearn Zionism," while on the right, critics attack Zionism through the lens of dual loyalty.

"These days, people are afraid to connect things to the Bible, but it is critical to do so. It is the only way to honestly understand where our connection to that land begins. It begins with the Bible and the words of God himself," Groisman said.

He noted that only 26% of American Jews say they believe in "God as described in the Bible," per a Pew Research Center study published in May 2021. According to the study, another 50% believe in some other spiritual force.

"Most American Jews don't hold a biblical or Judeo-Christian understanding of God, and I think that's a huge reason why most don't look to the Bible for their connection to the land," said Groisman.

"When they are asked to defend their connection to the Land of Israel or to the State of Israel, they can’t begin to respond in a proper way because they don’t believe in God," he added.

Groisman has practiced law for more than 20 years, litigating cases nationwide and participating in legal challenges on behalf of the Jewish community.

A NEW CHAPTER FOR AMERICA’S 250TH: 'J250' INITIATIVE PUTS JEWISH CONTRIBUTIONS IN THE SPOTLIGHT

During his tenure as mayor, Groisman passed what he describes as the nation's first anti-Israel boycott ordinance, as well as the first municipal ordinance adopting a definition of antisemitism.

Groisman said the book seeks to address a question American Jews across the country are asking privately: What is the future of Jews in America, and is it time to leave? His answer, he said, is an emphatic no.

"Jewish American history is not well taught, not even in Jewish circles. We need to understand that this community has been here since before day one and has played integral roles in this country. The religious liberties established in this country from the beginning were meant to benefit groups explicitly like the Jews, who were here from day one," he said.

For American Jews, Groisman said, the solution lies in helping young people reconnect with their identity. He argued that a strong sense of identity and purpose, rooted in their Jewish religion and national heritage, can help them become confident American Jews and thrive in the United States.

"America is not about freedom from religion; it’s about freedom of religion. You are allowed to be who you are as an American and still be as American as everybody else," he said.

In his book, Groisman examines developments over the past several years that he believes have contributed to the surge in antisemitism, including the rise of intersectionality and critical race theory on the left and their growing influence in academic and intellectual circles, which he says have received significant funding from foreign actors.

SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER

Groisman pointed to foreign funding flowing into American universities, warning that "that money comes with strings attached" and is intended "to create chaos in our country." He argued that foreign actors unable to defeat the United States militarily seek to weaken it by creating internal divisions, with antisemitism serving as "a useful tool" in that effort.

"When we saw actors in this country, in the aftermath of Oct. 7 and even before Israel responded in Gaza, being coordinated and directed by foreign actors in the United States, all the way down to small chapters on college campuses across the country, that requires years and years of coordination," he said.

Groisman said his book offers a message of optimism, emphasizing his faith in America, its political system and the American people’s ability to confront these challenges.

"For the American Jewish community, this book will hopefully help swing the pendulum back, encouraging people to recalibrate and put our country — and the American Jewish community as an integral part of it — back on track," he said.

articles.title: Black Friday hype stems from a desire 'to be part of a collective event', expert says
articles.summary: Once a strictly US affair, it's become a truly global phenomenon. From shoppers hunting for bargains in Louisiana, to queues forming outside stores in Venezuela, the Black Friday sales event has become the biggest day of the year for retail foot traffic. FRANCE 24's Sharon Gaffney speaks with Olaya Moldes Andres, Associate Professor in Marketing and Strategy at Cardiff Business School. She explains that, beyond the sales, the success of Black Friday may also be due to a desire by shoppers to "join the collective action. Whether it is spending money or going to the mall, shoppers feel part of a collective event, so perhaps this is where the whole hype comes from, to feel that we're being part of something, same thing as Christmas or any other social event".

articles.title: RN’s antisemitic past ‘coming back to haunt them’: Will Le Pen ‘distance herself’ from Bardella?
articles.summary: Could new allegations of antisemitism damage Jordan Bardella’s standing and the far-right National Rally’s electoral prospects? Charli James is pleased to welcome Paul Smith, Associate Professor in French and Francophone Studies at the University of Nottingham. Smith examines the far-right leader’s continued denials and considers whether Marine Le Pen might eventually distance herself from him. In the meantime, Smith suggests that Bardella needs to “make his mind up” about how to respond to these latest troubling allegations published by Le Monde and Mediapart. “It’s very difficult to deny. Le Monde and Mediapart, certainly Le Monde, wouldn’t be publishing these details if they didn’t have some pretty substantial evidence.” Could this prove to be the Achilles’ heel of a far-right party with its sights set on the second round of the presidential election?

articles.title: Is Spain's snap election being rigged? Debunking viral claims
articles.summary: Ahead of Spain's snap election on Sunday, allegations of vote rigging - known in Spanish as "pucherazo" - are spreading widely on social media. From claims that undocumented migrants are being illegally registered to vote, to allegations that postal ballots and vote counts could be manipulated, internet users are accusing Pedro Sánchez's government of attempting to rig the election. But these claims misrepresent how Spain's electoral system works, as Vedika Bahl explains in Truth or Fake.

articles.title: 'Citizens angry with the establishment' as Spain heads to the polls
articles.summary: Three party leaders are vying in Spain's general election on Sunday, which leftist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called following a parliamentary setback over housing legislation that underscored the fragility of his minority coalition government. Speaking with FRANCE 24's Sharon Gaffney, Javier Carbonell, Policy Analyst at the European Policy Centre, says that despite solid economic growth in Spain the population "have suffered a housing crisis and inflation, citizens are still angry with the government and the economic system regardless of macroeconomic data", adding that "in the end citizens are angry with the establishment, in this case it will be Sanchez, but to be honest I think they will be angry at PP and Vox very soon".

Spain's Socialist prime minister dogged by incumbent fatigue and nepotism allegations. articles.title: Hamas weighs response after Israel kills 10 people in Gaza

A strike on a residential apartment in Deir Al-Balah in central Gaza killed a man and his wife, the officials said. articles.title: Bank of England boss warns AI must benefit humans
articles.summary:
LONDON — Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey has warned governments need to reassure the public about the benefits of increasingly powerful artificial intelligence models, amid rising fears the technology is advancing at a pace beyond human control.

As the U.K. prepares to take over the G20 presidency, Bailey backed Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s plan to put AI at the heart of the country’s plans.

But the U.K. central banker said lawmakers, not regulators, would have to set the guardrails for the technology.

“It’s a bit like rearing children. You have to give them the chance to do things, but you also have to set some sort of boundaries as it were,” he said in an interview from his office in the Bank of England.

With the G20 presidency fast approaching, Burnham has said he wants to use the U.K. to establish “a single set” of global standards for AI.

U.S. President Donald Trump shot down any global oversight of the giant American companies dominating the development of the technology, which he has rebranded as “super intelligence.”

Against that backdrop, Bailey called for more international testing and access to AI giants’ frontier models, which he said are “critical questions” as the U.K. takes on the G20 presidency.

The U.K. central banking chief will make that push internationally in his role as chair of the Financial Stability Board, a global watchdog for the financial system.

With the number of cyber incidents already rising, Bailey said AI models are being built on “the good, the bad, and the ugly” of human behavior, and are now training themselves.

But the governor argued it was reasonable for the public to ask what the benefit is from the rapid growth of a technology which could be used to blow holes in the financial system, but also order the Christmas shopping.

“The public needs to trust this technology,” he said. “There needs to be greater transparency, explanation of what the things do, how they do it, what we’re doing.”

He added: “It’s sensible to come at it from that angle and say, we’ve got to have stronger government understanding, stronger government coordination on this stuff. Regulation may follow it.”

The U.K. central banker is acutely aware of the threats the new technology could bring to the financial system. The Bank’s Financial Policy Committee report on Thursday spelled out risks including increasingly interconnected and opaque financing that could spread the pain should a potential stock market AI bubble burst.

But Bailey said he would put himself in a camp of people who want AI to succeed to improve productivity and well-being.

“But it has to be under human control,” he said. “We want AI to be used by humans, as it were.”

articles.title: Ukraine cajoles allies to keep Putin’s athletes out
articles.summary:
BRUSSELS — Kyiv is stepping up its bid to keep Russian athletes out of global sports tournaments.

“We cannot allow international sport to become the weak link in the democratic world,” Ukrainian Minister of Youth and Sports Matvii Bidnyi told POLITICO from Brussels, where he met EU sports ministers, as legal and political momentum builds for Russian competitors to return.

International Olympic Committee President Kirsty Coventry has said athletes should not pay for governmental actions; top sporting organizations have eased restrictions instituted in 2022 after the Kremlin’s full-scale invasion began; and a Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling overturned ice hockey’s ban on Russian teams.

Ukraine has near-unanimous EU backing for keeping Russian athletes out of European sport, and wants the bloc’s new visa ban on Moscow’s combatants also applied to soldiers who compete on national teams, Bidnyi added.

With the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics on the horizon, the dispute is becoming a test of who’ll shape Russia’s return to world sport: governments, or federations and courts. Kyiv is desperate for Europe to coordinate its response before more restrictions are lifted.

Bidnyi said he presented three demands to EU sports ministers on Nov. 20: a ban on Russian symbols; verified neutral status for athletes; and funding cuts for federations that let Russians compete. He added that the proposals found “wide support.”

“I have heard no voice against it,” Bidnyi said. Asked whether all 27 EU countries are on board, he said that “almost all of them” had expressed willingness to make it a common position.

No propaganda in sport

On Monday, the European Commission proposed barring Russian teams and athletes from competing in the EU, which would also restrict financial flows from Russian sponsors to European sports and cultural associations. The sanctions package needs the approval of all 27 member countries.

In addition, seven EU countries had written to European Council President António Costa and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen before the sanctions package was presented asking for tougher visa rules on Russian nationals.

The countries wanted the Commission’s guidelines on visa applications by Russians to prevent nonessential travel, including to sporting events, rather than wait for a revised Visa Code that is not expected before the first quarter of 2027. They also encouraged fellow EU countries not to grant visas to Russian or Belarusian athletes.

Bidnyi said his three points are designed to stop Russia from using sport for propaganda, while Moscow maintains a relentless bombing campaign against Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure.

The first measure is a ban on Russian symbols, such as flags or the national anthem. “It’s unacceptable that the anthem of a country that kills peaceful people in Europe today sounds in such a cheerful manner in European arenas,” he said.

A photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik showing Vladimir Putin meeting young ice hockey players while visiting the VOLGA Arena multifunctional sports complex in Nizhny Novgorod on Aug. 28, 2026. | Kirill Zykov/Pool/AFP via Getty Images

The second is to make “neutral athlete” status something that is actually verified. “The neutral status should be maintained by detailed checking,” Bidnyi said. “We must check all aspects.”

The third is money. Bidnyi pointed to the new EU restriction on Erasmus+ funding — the bloc’s main program for education, training, youth and sport — for organizations that allow Russian state symbols, calling it a “first concrete result.” He wants the same model widened to organizations that let Russians use sport as a “tool of propaganda,” whether or not symbols are involved.

Bidnyi also raised the issue of soldiers that have become athletes, which touches the EU’s newest migration measures. The Commission’s visa guidelines, published this week alongside the sanctions package, tell national authorities to refuse visas to anyone who has served in Russia’s armed forces and fought in the war.

Bidnyi said the International Paralympic Committee has tolerated combatants taking part in its events, and that Russia is now trying to put soldiers who fought in Ukraine on its Paralympic teams. He called that “absolutely unacceptable.” Europe, he said, already refuses visas to combatants, and “it should be like this.”

The IPC said it has no rules barring former soldiers from competing, pointing to the movement’s origins in rehabilitating injured war veterans after World War II.

Nor is it its role, the IPC added, “to make moral judgments on which injured soldiers should or should not be allowed to compete.” It said former soldiers from countries including the U.S., Britain, Iraq, Bosnia and Iran have competed, and that it expects more at the 2028 Los Angeles Games.

The IPC said its responsibility is to decide which national Paralympic committees and athletes are eligible and to enforce its conduct rules. It said accreditation for the Games is the final decision of the organizing committee and national authorities, which handle security and background checks. Their organization’s answer did not mention Russia or Ukraine.

Russia’s sports minister, who the EU has also sanctioned, stated in September that more than 70 war veterans were already on national teams. Bidnyi also alleged that the Russian Union of Martial Arts recruits on behalf of units fighting in Ukraine and trains drone operators, and said that should be prohibited.

The Kremlin did not immediately respond to a request for comment about Bidnyi’s assertions about Russia’s military recruitment and wider propaganda strategy.

Ice hockey backlash

Sporting institutions, however, are gradually moving toward Russian reinstatement.

On one side of the confrontation, Bidnyi said, are governing bodies, courts and federations, which are “gradually opening the door to Russians hiding behind claims of neutrality.”

His primary example is the Oct. 30 decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) to overturn the International Ice Hockey Federation’s ban on Russian teams for the 2026-27 season. “The hockey case is the most outrageous example of Russian influence,” Bidnyi said.

Russian Alexander Ovechkin celebrates during the charity hockey “Match of the Year” between Russian players of the National Hockey League and the Kontinental Hockey League at the CSKA arena in Moscow on July 13, 2025. | Alexander Nemenov/AFP via Getty Images

Asked for comment, CAS said that the case, brought by the Russian Ice Hockey Federation against the IIHF, “was decided on a strictly legal basis” and that it is not aware of any circumstance that could have affected the panel’s independence.

Ultimately, that ruling set off a backlash. Finland, Sweden, Czechia, Norway, Austria, Denmark and Latvia have said they will play at next May’s men’s world championship in Germany but not against Russia — which means almost half of the 16 teams are refusing to face Russia. Canada’s government said Russia will not be allowed to play at the world juniors there next month.

Sponsors are also balking, with Skoda, the tournament’s main sponsor, saying it will reassess its backing. The IIHF says it still disagrees with the ruling.

Sanctions have also been lifted in gymnastics, weightlifting and chess, and the international ski federation has cleared more than 400 Russian and Belarusian athletes and support staff to compete as neutrals this season.

Bidnyi expects more of the same. The IOC’s decision to reinstate the Russian Olympic Committee, he said, “has set a dangerous precedent. International federations may now begin lifting restrictions one after another, hiding behind the autonomy of sport.”

Moscow, Bidnyi said, will keep going back to CAS and present every readmission as a propaganda win, with Putin personally overseeing the effort.

On the other side, he said, are governments, which can take a “principled stand” and refuse to let Russian representatives or the symbols of an aggressor state onto their territory. Russian participation “has long ceased to be merely a matter of sporting regulations,” he said. “It is a question of national security.”

The next chance to build a common position is a meeting of sports ministers in Tallinn in January. Bidnyi said it could bring in non-EU countries such as Canada and Norway, which have already taken firm action.

articles.title: Spain’s looming right-wing pivot on climate is already playing out in Valencia
articles.summary:
VALENCIA — Spain’s climate agenda could be in for a radical shake-up if conservative leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo takes power alongside the far-right Vox party after Sunday’s election — a prospect already playing out in Valencia.

Feijóo has pledged to scrap what he calls “unrealistic” timelines for climate goals, arguing that Spain must pursue decarbonization at a more pragmatic pace. His center-right People’s Party argues that climate ambitions must not come at the expense of economic competitiveness, industry or households.

His likely coalition partners, the far-right Vox party, want to go further — promising to dismantle what they call “climate impositions” from Brussels, remove low-emission zones and reverse restrictions on combustion-engine cars and CO₂ emissions.

The two parties’ dismantling of climate policy can already be seen in Spain’s Valencia region, where the PP has governed with Vox’s backing since 2023, coinciding with a rollback of environmental protections and the deadly floods of October 2024.

“The dangerous climate skepticism that will define a PP-Vox government at the national level has been on display here in Valencia from the moment they took power,” warned Raül Camacho Segarra, a spokesperson for the Valencian grassroots movement working to rebuild flood-damaged areas responsibly.

The floods put the government’s approach to land use, environmental regulation and climate adaptation under intense scrutiny. Yet shortly after, PP politician Juanfran Pérez Llorca was sworn in as the region’s new president and reaffirmed his opposition to parts of the climate agenda, describing the center-right European People’s Party’s Green Deal as a “threat” to Valencia’s farmers.

Local critics like Camacho accuse the right-wing government of failing to learn the lessons of the disaster and endangering the region’s communities.

“The policies they instituted ahead of the floods made us more vulnerable, and instead of recalibrating after the tragedy, they’ve actually doubled down since 2024,” he said, pointing to the allocation of public funds to bullfighting events instead of emergency response and promoting construction in areas needed for flood prevention.

Ana Camarasa, a physical geographer and regional flood risk expert at the University of Valencia, questioned politicians’ ability to pursue effective long-term resilience strategies while casting doubt on the threat posed by climate change.

“Governments that deny climate change ultimately aren’t obliged to take measures to address it, because it’s a problem that officially doesn’t exist,” she said.

Controversial climate record

With its millions of voters, Spain’s fourth-most-populous region is a coveted prize in the country’s political battle for power.

After eight years of left-wing rule, in 2023 the PP teamed up with Vox to take control of Valencia, forming one of its first regional coalition governments with the far right.

Under regional president Carlos Mazón, the new administration moved to scrap plans for a regional emergency response unit, dismantled key elements of Valencia’s climate law and emissions taxes, and disbanded a newly created agency to monitor climate change. His government also eased rules governing development on flood-prone coastlines and protected agricultural land.

Those decisions came under renewed scrutiny on Oct. 29, 2024, when Valencia was hit by one of the deadliest floods in modern Spanish history. The regional government downplayed the threat posed by a powerful storm that swept through the region, unleashing torrential rain that inundated towns and killed 229 people.

President of Valencia’s Region Carlos Mazón gives a press conference to announce his resignation at Valencia’s Palau de la Generalitat on November 3, 2025. | Jose Jordan/ AFP via Getty Images

For months after the disaster, Mazón — who controversially remained at an hours-long private lunch as the floodwaters rose — refused to take responsibility for his government’s handling of the catastrophe. Although crisis management is a regional responsibility, the PP shifted blame onto the national government and then-Deputy Prime Minister Teresa Ribera.

But Spanish courts exonerated both national authorities and Ribera, noting the regional government was the only entity authorized to manage the crisis. After being denounced as an “assassin” by victims’ relatives one year on, Mazón finally stepped down.

His successor, Pérez Llorca, took office promising to rebuild the region and leave it better prepared for future disasters. Yet key climate-protection measures have been further weakened since the floods.

Weeks after the disaster, the government pressed ahead with legislative changes to allow construction closer to shorelines. More recently, other controversial proposals have surfaced, including a plan to build more than 1,200 homes on farmland that critics say is instrumental to absorbing water during torrential rainstorms.

In an interview, Raúl Mérida, the technocrat appointed to oversee the region’s recovery, defended its reconstruction and adaptation efforts while playing down the significance of the Valencian government’s climate-skeptic statements.

“Our actions are based on science,” he said, adding that politicians across the political spectrum had backed his proposals to build floodable parks and carry out environmentally conscious river-restoration schemes that aim to better protect communities against future storms.

According to Mérida, 98% of infrastructure damaged in the disaster has been rebuilt. But he acknowledged that rebuilding did not necessarily mean the region was now better protected against flooding.

“The emergency contracts only allowed us to restore the infrastructure that was there, not improve it,” he said, citing roads and bridges. “We had to rebuild some infrastructure that had proved inadequate in reducing the severity of the floods in the same way.”

He added that the government had reinforced foundations and added protective stone embankments. When it came to private homes, he said, things were more complicated: Residents often had deep family roots and longstanding ties to the communities where they lived.

Like other rapidly growing Spanish regions, Mérida said Valencia was under pressure to build more housing and had enough land to do so as long as flood-zone regulations were respected. But he insisted that the priority would be ensuring “regulations governing flood-prone areas are respected” and that “citizens and territory are protected.”

“Adaptation measures work just as well in a left-wing municipality as they do in a right-wing one,” he said, adding that protecting communities from extreme weather should transcend party lines.

The limits of green consensus

In a September POLITICO poll carried out by PF Global, 60% of Spanish respondents described climate change as either the most important or one of the most important issues of our time.

But the poll also suggests Spaniards are wary of climate action overshadowing other national priorities. Nearly half — 49.2% — said the country’s energy and environmental policies were diverting resources from other pressing issues, including the cost-of-living crisis, healthcare and housing. Just over half — 50.3% — said Spain should act on climate change but not more than other countries.

That national ambivalence could give the PP and Vox room to argue for a slower, less costly green transition — even as voters continue to regard climate change as a major concern.

Widespread anger over the deadly 2024 floods doesn’t seem to have weakened the right-wing bloc’s electoral prospects in the region: A range of polls project the PP and Vox could win 19 of the region’s 33 seats in Spain’s 350-seat parliament.

Cars are piled in the street with other debris after flash floods hit the region on October 30, 2024 in the Sedaví area of Valencia, Spain. | David Ramos/Getty Images

In Valencia’s central province (excluding Castellón and Alicante), where 16 seats are up for grabs, Vox is projected to double its representation, from two seats in 2023 to four in 2026.

David Ribó, a candidate for the left-wing regionalist Compromís-Front Valencià coalition, said he was dismayed by the polling: “It boggles the mind that in a region that is the epicenter of climate change, political options that are openly denialist are still attracting votes.”

Ribó argued that Vox’s success did not reflect public apathy to climate change, but rather frustration with mainstream parties, as seen in the immediate aftermath of the floods, when the populist slogan “sólo el pueblo salva el pueblo” (“only the people can save the people”) was directed at political leaders and institutions perceived to have abandoned the region.

“People are struggling to make ends meet — especially because of the insane prices they’re having to pay for housing — and naturally, there is a sense of discontent,” he said. The “inequality crisis,” he argued, is pushing disillusioned voters toward populist leaders.

The University of Valencia’s Camarasa expressed concern over the increasing climate skepticism in Spanish politics, arguing certain topics “shouldn’t be treated as an ideological matter: The data is there, and we’ve also seen the consequences that come when you ignore it.”

The issue, she added, was particularly relevant amid the country’s housing crisis, which has put politicians under pressure to fast-track construction. Pointing to the deadly consequences of homes being built in flood-prone areas, she warned that leaders’ dismissive attitude toward the climate threat could lead to further “deficient and ineffective land management.”

But she conceded that Spain’s political system was perhaps not built to address the threat the country faces. “A government lasts as long as it lasts, but the solutions have to last longer,” she said.

articles.title: Swingin’ on the flippity-flop with chicken nuggets: The perils of young people’s slang
articles.summary:
Welcome to Declassified, a weekly humor column.

In August 1992, this writer put on his wack slack, fuzz and kickers before swingin’ on the flippity-flop watching popular rock combo Nirvana in a muddy field in southern England.

Fear not, the water at POLITICO Towers hasn’t been laced with ketamine. I’m just reliving a journalistic nightmare: young people and their new words.

Three months after I stood in a field listening to “Smells Like Teen Spirit,” a journalist from The New York Times called up Sub Pop, the record label that released Nirvana’s first album and did more than any other to give the world grunge, and fell victim to a prank.

Megan Jasper, a one-time receptionist at the label who went on to become its CEO, proceeded to make up a list of fake slang terms being used by the kids of the day. The NYT published the list in full*.

When it comes to politics, it’s hard to know what’s worse: pretending to be down with the kids when you’re old enough to know better or being clearly out-of-touch and missing out on what the youth really care about.

This week, Andy “have I mentioned I like The Smiths” Burnham was stung after getting too close to the TikTok generation (a bit like Icarus flying too close to the sun, if Icarus was the British prime minister and the sun was people doing shitty dances).

Burnham invited a bunch of creators to an event earlier this month (what’s the collective noun for influencers? A virus?) but footage only emerged this week of one miming the words “bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets” outside the famous black door of No. 10 Downing Street.

Bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets is a) an unwieldy name for a pet, b) a good name for a punk band, and c) offensive if you understand what young people are talking about (‘bomboclaat’ is a Jamaican profanity referring to a menstrual cloth, ‘pussy’ is a slang term for female genitals, and some accounts reckon ‘chicken nuggets’ refers to women being ‘cheap white meat’ — although it could also just mean chicken assholes and eyelashes mashed up, breadcrumbed and deep-fried).

Social media influencer Max Balegde, who posted the offending video, has 3.6 million followers on TikTok and 640,000 on Instagram. To put that into perspective, this column sometimes reaches the dizzying heights of eight readers.

The EU is so desperately uncool that no one has ever shouted “bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets” outside the Berlaymont. Despite a campaign to get countries to put forward the names of influencers to attend European Councils, a grand total of zero turned up at the October summit because of an overwhelming lack of interest from all sides.

* Wack slack = old ripped jeans

* Fuzz = heavy wool sweater

* Kickers = boots

* Swingin’ on the flippity-flop = hangin’ out

articles.title: Spain’s right turn: What a PP-Vox government would mean for Madrid — and Brussels
articles.summary:
MADRID — After eight years of Socialist rule, polls point to an incoming right-wing government in Spain — but exactly what it’ll do in office will depend on the balance of power between the conservative People’s Party and far-right Vox.

The right-wing parties’ manifestos are light on specifics. In the PP’s case, that is a deliberate strategy, according to one official, so that party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo can avoid overpromising in the campaign.

The exact agenda would depend on how ministries are carved up in a coalition between Feijóo’s traditional center-right party and Santiago Abascal’s Vox, which is still weighing how involved it wants to be in a potential Feijóo administration.

But a rightward shift after eight years of Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist government would shake up Spain’s policy agenda in several key areas, from migration to data centers, and certainly draw attention in Brussels.

One thing is clear, though: Spain is unlikely to turn into a euroskeptic at the top EU table.

Vox may be fiercely critical of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and the EU institutions, but it knows there are limits to how far you can press euroskepticism in Spain. The country is, at heart, very pro-European: Its path to EU membership ran alongside its transition to democracy after the death of fascist leader General Francisco Franco, and Europe is part of the country’s democratic identity.

Here are six ways Spain’s policy agenda could change under the PP-Vox government.

Migration: Spaniards first?

Migration is one area where Sánchez-era policy is likely to be reversed.

Both PP and Vox have strongly criticized the current government’s mass regularization of migrants, and the PP also advocates for a legal ban on this type of measure.

Since the last election in 2023, migration has risen to second on Spaniards’ list of top concerns, behind housing. The Ceuta crisis — where tens of thousands of mainly young men from Morocco poured into Spain — has hardened the rhetoric of both Vox and the PP, which have embraced the term “invasion.”

Vox’s flagship policy on migration is known as “national priority,” essentially a Spaniards-first approach that gives preferential access to public services, from housing to schools and benefits. Feijóo’s party manifesto includes “priority criteria for access to certain benefits, services and public resources,” but the PP doesn’t limit the criteria to nationality, saying it should also cover long-term legal residents in Spain.

Vox has also made remigration — a term imported from far-right circles in Germany and Austria — one of its core election campaign proposals. But the European Commission has already found that remigration proposals cannot be squared with EU law and the PP distances itself from the idea.

Workers clear debris from a dismantled migrant settlement at the entrance to the Tarajal warehouses, in Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta on Oct. 18, 2026. | Antonio Sempere/AFP via Getty Images

On almost all other migration-related issues, the PP and Vox would align with the new mainstream in an EU that takes a much tougher line, including the idea of return hubs.

Agriculture: Vox’s turf

The far right frames rural Spain as the true heart of the nation. Abascal’s party has always tried to secure the agriculture departments in regional governments where it rules jointly with the PP — and the agriculture ministry would likely be one of its top targets in a coalition government.

A significant proportion of immigration in Spain is linked to the agricultural sector, which relies on a vast pool of cheap migrant labor. Vox has spoken of extending the national priority principle to this sector as well, calling for pay rises to make these jobs attractive to Spaniards, although it has avoided making it a central issue of its immigration policy. The PP proposes temporary visas and hiring in the workers’ home countries.

Spain could end up clashing with the EU over trade if a PP-Vox government seeks to restrict imports from countries it thinks undercut the local market. In the past, Abascal’s party has also sought the suspension of a farm goods deal with Morocco, arguing that Moroccan producers were creating “unfair competition.” The PP pledges that “imported foodstuffs will meet food safety and production standards equivalent to our own,” a call for so-called mirror clauses in trade deals.

Vox rejects the EU Mercosur trade deal with South America as an attack on Spanish producers, while the PP tries to avoid the Mercosur debate, but is generally in favor of the pact.

However, the PP and Vox are completely aligned with the current Socialist government in their rejection of cuts to the Common Agricultural Policy — the EU’s all-important subsidy scheme for farmers — in the next 7-year EU budget, so there will be continuity on that.

Tech: no more crusades against Big Tech

Sánchez has made his testy relationship with what he calls the “technoligarchs” an important part of his election message. That public crusade against Big Tech will disappear with a PP-Vox government. Abascal has met Elon Musk, who has publicly supported Vox.

But on some issues, the PP is not far from the Socialist Party. For example, Feijóo pledges to bar social media access to those under 14 and accuses Sánchez’s government of being too soft on child protection on social media. On the other hand, Vox opposes this type of age limit.

Data centers could prove a bigger change. A Socialist decree that establishes limits on data centers’ energy consumption and sovereignty conditions was just approved by the government and ratified by parliament. Alberto Nadal, Feijóo’s industry guru, has promised to repeal this law once in government, clearing the way for potential sectoral expansion.

Energy and climate: from vanguard to mainstream

Energy and climate change have been major political priorities of the Socialist government, putting Spain among the most ambitious countries in the EU on green issues. Expect that to change substantially under a PP-Vox government.

Just by how much will depend on support for Vox. Abascal’s party links many of Spain’s agricultural problems to climate rules and has been mobilizing its supporters against the climate agenda for years. Vox has, for example, criticized the uprooting of olive trees to make way for solar panels.

The PP is firmly in the new EU mainstream on climate and energy, aligning with the European People’s Party to advocate a relaxation of climate rules and “an end to the imposition of unrealistic timelines.”

An olive tree stump in the Andalusian village of Lopera, where growers have struggled to prevent the uprooting of olive trees to make way for the installation of photovoltaic plants. | Cristina Quicler/AFP via Getty Images

On the energy front, both parties agree on extending the lifespan of nuclear plants. But even if Vox tries to pull Spain away from the energy transition, renewable energy is already a reality: Renewable electricity increased from 35% of total generation in 2015 to 56% in 2025, according to the International Energy Agency.

China: harder stance?

Under Sánchez’s government, Spain became one of the EU’s biggest advocates for closer ties with Beijing and established a strategic dialogue with China’s Xi Jinping.

Feijóo has promised he would abide by any EU-level agreement to harden the bloc’s stance towards Beijing. And some of Feijóo’s closest aides on foreign policy, such as veteran diplomat Ildefonso Castro, are committed Atlanticists who could steer a PP prime minister toward a tougher position if that aligned with Washington.

Vox is hawkish on China and in 2025 accused Sánchez of flattering “the communist Chinese dictatorship.” Both parties on the right support excluding high-risk suppliers from public procurement, citing Huawei as an example, and have strongly criticized the current government’s renewal of contracts with the Chinese company.

But it’s not an easy call. Some of the biggest Chinese investments in Spain are in regions with PP-led governments, such as Galicia, Andalusia and Valencia.

Women’s rights and culture wars

Sánchez’s government has sought to champion progressive values on the international stage, and a Spanish government with Vox as junior partner would mark a sharp contrast with that.

During his campaign, Feijóo promised to strip the ministry of equality of its ministerial status and incorporate its responsibilities, which are mainly focused on gender, into another department. If Vox’s model for regional governments is followed, Abascal’s party will seek to establish a family ministry.

In a radio interview, Feijóo also opened a debate on a possible reform of Spain’s abortion law, arguing that the parents of minors who decide to have an abortion should be informed of this decision. Vox, which in 2023 advocated repealing the law, is now more vague.

But there are points of friction between the two parties on equality. The PP maintains the consensus on gender violence laws, while Vox usually talks about intrafamilial violence and calls for the repeal of laws that have criminalized men.

Equality aside, expect to see culture war battles over rural heritage come into government. Vox supports measures to protect hunting, and both the PP and Vox agree on hunting wolves to protect livestock in the north of the country.

But the biggest battleground has been over bullfighting. Current Culture Minister Ernest Urtasun, from the left-wing Sumar party, scrapped the national bullfighting prize in 2024. Both PP and Vox plan to reinstate it.

articles.title: Budget summit walkout leaves EU one month to salvage deal
articles.summary:
BRUSSELS — A summit of EU leaders descended into crisis after governments demanding a smaller seven-year budget snubbed European Council President António Costa by walking out of his negotiation sessions.

The dramatic late-night move at Thursday’s gathering in Brussels heaps pressure on Costa, who was tasked with brokering a deal between the EU’s 27 governments and who is desperate to reach a positive outcome before the end of the year. While EU officials with knowledge of the process were caught off guard by the severity of the division, many had predicted some kind of political theater and still didn’t rule out a compromise emerging when leaders meet again on Dec. 17.

“All that effort, all the political fanfare, all the big announcements — and absolutely nothing to show for it,” Bernd Lange, chair of the European Parliament’s trade committee, said in a post on X.

Costa hadn’t organized Thursday’s summit to get a deal. Rather, his goal was to bang heads together and try to bridge splits between the two main rival camps: those like Spain and Italy, that want a bigger budget and to protect “traditional” EU spending in areas such as farming and poorer regions, and those like Germany and Sweden demanding the bloc scales down its ambitions and refocuses investment toward defense and security.

But after hours of meetings among small groups of leaders, several countries pushing for budget cuts — Denmark, Sweden, Belgium and Austria — walked out, claiming this negotiating method was aimed at pitching them against each other.

“It was obvious this was a move to divide us, to buy each of us seven off with a gift,” a diplomat from a country that wants a smaller budget said. “It just went really badly. It was not a real discussion.” They were granted anonymity, like others in this article, to speak candidly about the dramatic unfolding.

European Parliament’s trade committee chair Bernd Lange, who said there was “absolutely nothing to show for it” after all the buildup. | Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP via Getty Images

Costa abandoned plans to return for a second day and cut his concluding 1 a.m. press conference with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to just 11 minutes.

‘Strategic mistake’

The EU’s 27 leaders will now make a push to secure a deal at December’s summit, which multiple diplomats and officials said will probably last several days and nights.

While technically the bloc has an entire year to reach agreement on what’s called the Multiannual Financial Framework for 2028-2034, the current leadership are determined to get it settled before April’s election in France, where the far-right leader Marine Le Pen is the favorite to become president.

A visibly angry Emmanuel Macron criticized Costa’s proposed cuts as “a strategic mistake”for Europe ― a signal that threading the needle between the two camps won’t be easy.

Macron warned that dragging negotiations into the new year “is not democratically possible” as it would be too close to the election.

Underscoring that direction of travel, Costa indicated in the closed-door meetings with leaders that he will put forward a new budget proposal — envisaging fresh cuts — over the coming weeks to try to bring the EU closer to a deal, said two EU diplomats.

‘Mr. Blackmail’

But in a further sign the choreography was getting derailed, other leaders started to distance themselves from the year-end deadline.

“I don’t have a deadline, I have conditions,” said Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who frequently disagrees with Macron but who’s on the side of a larger budget.

“When there is an agreement that I consider fair for Italy, I will sign it. Until then, I am not prepared to sign anything.”

In another rebuke of Macron’s ultimatum, one EU diplomat nicknamed the French president “Monsieur Chantage” (Mr. Blackmail).

“It’s rich to come here and take hostage the negotiations because of your national election,” the diplomat said.

The Commission initially proposed a budget of around €2 trillion. Ahead of this week’s summit, Costa proposed to slash it by €204 billion. But that won’t be the end of it.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni speaks to the press during a break in the EU budget talks on Nov. 26, 2026. | John Thys/AFP via Getty Images

Costa told leaders that he’s planning to cut the Commission’s proposal by between another €220 billion to €230 billion — which is not far from the demands of the “frugal” countries, the diplomat said. He indicated that reductions will overwhelmingly affect competitiveness and foreign aid, as opposed to regional spending and agriculture.

“We’re not hugely far apart, but those last-minute solutions will matter a lot,” Petteri Orpo, prime minister of Finland — a country in the smaller budget camp — told reporters. He proposed €250 billion cuts from the Commission’s plan.

‘Really angry’

Costa’s tactics at the summit seemed to have disappointed both sides. His strategy of bringing together small groups of leaders “was not the best idea” because governments felt reluctant to reveal their red lines in front of their rivals, a diplomat from a country pushing for a larger budget said.

The decision to boycott the later meetings came after Finland’s Orpo grew “really angry” with Costa’s approach during one session, one EU diplomat said.

“Members of the S7 [the self-declared “Sensible Seven” of governments wanting a smaller budget] attended two breakout sessions, after which we concluded that further sessions would not bring us closer to a solution,” Austria wrote in a statement.

After the summit, Costa played down the apparent fiasco and said that the 10-hour discussion with leaders “was very useful to figure out the parameters of a possible landing zone in December.”

By the time Costa confirmed to reporters in the early hours of Friday that leaders “didn’t reach an agreement” most had already left for the night.

“We will continue to work,” he said.

Sebastian Starcevic, Aude van den Hove, Kathryn Carlson, Bjarke Smith-Meyer, Marianne Gros, Martina Sapio, Gerardo Fortuna, Jacopo Barigazzi, Hans von der Burchard, Tim Ross, Agnes Rønberg, Max Griera, Bartosz Brzeziński, Thibault Krause and Camille Gijs contributed reporting.

articles.title: EU leaders brave clash with Trump over tech tax, defense, Ukraine
articles.summary:
BRUSSELS ― EU leaders are warming to the idea of a possible fight with U.S. President Donald Trump over everything from digital taxes to defense procurement rules and financing for Ukraine.

As tense talks on the EU’s long-term budget descended into political theatrics on Thursday night, leaders including French President Emmanuel Macron continued to push for these measures.

“France defends this [digital tax] idea and has done so since 2018,” Macron told reporters. Europe was “very legitimate” in imposing such a levy because the U.S. wasn’t respecting international tax agreements agreed by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, he added.

Such proposals put Brussels on a collision course with Washington, which has repeatedly railed against policies that are seen as discriminating against U.S. interests. Trump has also taken issue with Europe’s continued support for Ukraine, just as leaders prepare to sign off on a €45 billion loan for Kyiv before the end of this year.

“The digital tax is not really an item which the U.S. side accepts so there will be some trouble coming, I’m sure,” said Bernd Lange, chair of the European Parliament’s trade committee. Referring to wider possible restrictions on European goods, he added: “All these tariff issues might also lead to some conflict.”

But in conversations with POLITICO, EU diplomats, experts and lawmakers said that many countries are now less wary of a possible clash with the U.S. following the Republican Party’s defeat in mid-term elections, and after years of trade battles and tension over Ukraine policy that have inured leaders to static with Washington.

‘Tide is turning’

Not improving the overall mood, Washington said it was planning to roll out new tariffs against the EU in a separate investigation. Still, more investigations are coming, for instance on “digital discrimination,” adding to a sense that tensions with the U.S. are inevitable — and so to be feared less.

“The Americans are paying the price for having been so aggressive toward us,” said an EU diplomat granted anonymity to speak frankly about a sensitive topic. “If we don’t do it, we’ll pay the price anyway. That’s where the tide is turning,”

As always in Europe, the view is not monolithic. Several countries have serious reservations about antagonizing the U.S. and could block risky measures. Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden said on his way into Thursday’s gathering that he had “some concerns” about the impact of a digital tax on relations with the U.S.

The talks are focusing on a proposal from European Council President António Costa for the bloc’s next seven-year budget, which targets firms that have a global turnover of more than €750 million of which €50 million is in Europe. Google, Meta and Amazon are among the tech giants that would face the tax.

The idea has particularly strong support in the European Parliament, which must sign off on any long-term budget deal from leaders. “The digital levy is the solution to a sufficient budget without additional burden upon member states,” said Siegfried Mureșan, Parliament’s co-rapporteur on the long-term EU budget.

But the proposal has already prompted an angry response from the Trump administration, which singled out “unjustified digital trade barriers” as a threat to the U.S. in its National Security Strategy published in December 2025. 

“We oppose the EU proposal for an EU-wide digital levy just as we have opposed (and continue to oppose) other digital services taxes that discriminate against U.S. companies while hurting consumers as well,” a spokesperson for the U.S. State Department told POLITICO in a statement, reiterating Washington’s years-long opposition.

Some EU countries are wary of the idea too. Swedish Europe Minister Jessica Rosencrantz told POLITICO that Stockholm has a “principled position against new own resources” — EU-wide taxes — and opposes the digital services tax.

The prime minister of Ireland, home to the EU headquarters of several big EU tech firms, has spoken out against such a tax, while Malta, Luxembourg and the Netherlands are all on the fence.

Yet, significantly, Germany has voiced openness to the tax, despite previously opposing it on the grounds it would provoke the U.S. Other nations with close transatlantic ties, such as Denmark and Finland, have not spoken out publicly against Costa’s proposal.

“The U.S.-EU trading relationship is already under tremendous pressure,” said Ivana Zuzul, senior vice president, Europe, at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce in Washington. “Proposals to levy a digital services tax and push Buy European preferences that shut U.S. companies out of EU-funded procurement programs and investment opportunities only irresponsibly add to that strain.”

At a meeting of European ambassadors on Monday evening, no delegations came out strongly against the digital service tax, according to three EU diplomats either attending or briefed on the meeting, but many requested further concrete details on how the levy would be rolled out.

Democratic Party control over Congress is also being seen as a positive factor in Brussels. “I think [Europe] should be active with your tools,” U.S. Dem Rep. Pramila Jayapal said on Saturday. “You have always been ahead of us in regulating big tech. And so I think for us, it’s important to keep that strong.”

Ukraine, defense tensions

Another problematic area is Costa’s proposal to enshrine European preference defense procurement. The seven-year EU budget proposal enforces such preferences in the fields of defense and space, excluding U.S. firms from bidding winning contracts funded by the EU budget, drawing criticism from American officials.

“Measures that exclude the United States … will weaken the EU’s competitiveness and security,” the U.S. government wrote in a discussion paper circulated in September.

NATO member Romania has sounded the alarm about European preference, with Defense Minister Ştefan-Radu Oprea telling POLITICO this week: “We need the American technology in Europe, and from my perspective we should identify ways to collaborate and have the American presence.”

But such public protests are the exception rather than the rule among EU countries bracing for drawdowns of U.S. troops and matériel in Europe.

‘Already come to pass’

Finally, there’s the growing chasm between Trump and Europe on Ukraine. 

In a Nov. 19 call with U.S. leaders and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Trump lamented what he called a waste of billions to provide Ukraine with weapons and cash for a conflict that is killing many people, according to three European officials aware of the meeting.

That complaint has barely registered with EU leaders, who are reviewing a proposal to lend Ukraine an additional €45 billion for 2027. 

The budget contains €100 billion earmarked for Ukraine, and senior EU officials say discussions are under way for potential further loans for Kyiv.

“With the United States … much of what we feared has already come to pass,” said the first EU diplomat. “We don’t have much support for Ukraine. We had to accept an unbalanced trade deal … and they are still putting a lot of pressure.”

“They aren’t letting up, so what do we have to lose?”

Jacob Parry and Mathieu Pollet contributed reporting.
