articles.title: FACT CHECK: Suan did not propose parliamentary gov’t if VP Sara isn’t impeached
articles.summary:
Claim: A video shows Cagayan de Oro 1st District Representative Lordan Suan saying that if Vice President Sara Duterte is not impeached, the law should be changed to shift the Philippines into a parliamentary form of government with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. as prime minister.

Rating: ALTERED

Why we fact-checked this: Multiple trending posts used a clip of Suan delivering a speech during the Cagayan de Oro Press Club’s 75th Anniversary Gala on November 23.

The video shows Suan supposedly saying, “Kung hindi man ma-impeach si Sara, gumawa na lang tayo ng batas para walang election sa 2028. (If [Vice President] Sara [Duterte] is not impeached, let’s just enact a law to cancel the 2028 elections.) Let’s transform the Philippines into a parliamentary form of government so that President Bongbong Marcos can become prime minister.”

A Facebook page called Defense Lawyers, one of the accounts that posted the video, wrote this as a caption: “Ano daw? BBM as Prime Minister?!!” (Say what? BBM as prime minister?)

The post garnered 11,700 reactions, 4,700 comments, and 1,700 shares as of writing.

Facebook user Amy Ugay also posted a vertical version of the video with a text overlay that says, “Oi Suan ikaw na lang kaya mag prime minister bakit si BBM pa tigilan mo ‘yan kahibangan mo.” 

(Hey Suan, why don’t you just become prime minister yourself instead of BBM? Stop this nonsense of yours.)

This post had 2,000 reactions, 742 comments, and 301 shares as of writing.

The facts: The audio used in the video is fake – Suan did not make any statement regarding Duterte, Marcos, or scrapping the elections in 2028.

A video shared by iFM CDO radio station showed Suan’s speech at the event, where he discussed the importance of the press amid widespread misinformation. He also mentioned House Bill No. 9397, or the proposed Right to Information Act, which seeks to institutionalize Filipinos’ right to access information on matters of public concern.

During his four-minute speech, Suan did not mention anything about the elections, Duterte’s impeachment, or proposing the country’s transition to a parliamentary form of government.

Suan’s office also categorically denied the claims, saying in a statement to Rappler on November 27 that the lawmaker remains an advocate of democracy and upholds Filipinos’ right to vote and choose their leaders.

His office added: “Walang puwang sa ating demokrasya ang sinadyang pagpapakalat ng kasinungalingan upang linlangin ang taumbayan.” 

(There is no place in our democracy for the deliberate spreading of lies to deceive the public.)

The Cagayan de Oro Press Club refuted the false claims in a Facebook statement published on November 26, clarifying that the congressman joined the event to show solidarity with local journalists and that he never uttered those statements.

“We call on vloggers and netizens to stop spreading unverified information that confuses the public and damages the reputation of our guests,” the statement read further.

Previous fact-checks: Rappler debunked multiple false claims about the 2028 elections:

FACT CHECK: ‘No 2028 election’ claim has no basis 

FACT CHECK: Marcos statement claiming to cancel 2028 election is taken out of context

FACT CHECK: ‘No 2028 election’ claim is ‘fake news,’ Malacañang says

FACT CHECK: Jonvic Remulla did not say Marcoses are ‘sure to be jailed’ after 2028

– Eirene Manatlao/Rappler.com 

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: Digital detoxing: When was the last time you took time off your screens?
articles.summary:
There was a time when I realized that I had become more unfocused and forgetful. Whether it’s misplacing my phone or wallet, or needing to take multiple breaks during work, these issues all started occurring more frequently. 

I took a step back to understand what had changed. But in fact, nothing changed; I connected my scattered attention to the time I spent on screens and realized what felt like harmless scrolling was starting to spill over into my everyday life.

Doomscrolling in the afternoon or watching movies while eating never seemed like a problem. Still, looking back, it seems like everything that I did always had a digital or auditory companion. Otherwise, every task would feel long, boring, or exhausting. That dependence made me reflect on how my screen time is starting to catch up with me mentally.

This research paper on social media’s impact on the human attention span, published earlier this year, describes my lack of focus and forgetfulness as a result of regular consumption of short-form content. The study suggests that my brain has been wired to feel rewarded by a simple scroll, making activities that require sustained attention feel unrewarding. This becomes problematic when the behavior becomes repetitive, and we begin to use doomscrolling as a way to regulate emotions. Moreover, short-form content was also shown to increase my potential risks of impulsivity, addiction-like behaviors, and depressive symptoms.

Realizing how attached I’ve become to my screen and how it has affected me mentally, I decided to make a change by making two simple promises to refocus and slow down: reduce my screen time by planning my day, and stick to the plan. 

What is digital detoxing?

Going through a digital detox was one of the most life turning points for me as it shaped a lot of my interests and who I am today. Beyond reducing my time online, it became an act of getting to know myself and finding the right balance of being online and offline. 

Finding this balance was the goal of my detox; it involved considering what I did throughout the day and making sure it was a healthy balance I could stick to. I knew simply reducing my screen time wouldn’t work, so I made small daily commitments to activities that would replace my time online.

My first commitment was to take time for physical activity, whether it was a short walk, a run, or a workout; it was my first non-negotiable to do for at least an hour a day. As someone who is already active, I knew it was something I could start with rather than trying to change my entire routine all at once. At first, it was a tiring conscious adjustment I had to keep in mind: tracking my online time and figuring out when and what activity to do. It was a challenging start, but after doing it consistently for a while, it became something that didn’t feel out of the ordinary.

I continued stacking up these commitments, ones that I knew I would enjoy and stick to, such as reading even just a page a day, drawing a simple sketch, learning a new song on the guitar or piano, and taking a short meditation in the morning. They all followed the same strategy: start small, do it every day until it becomes part of the routine, and repeat to the next commitment.  

With relationships and work to consider, I knew some days would be too busy for me to follow through on all my commitments, and I allowed myself that flexibility. Detoxing wasn’t a prison I put myself in; it was a way to make room for things that mattered to me, and my relationships and work are part of those. That meant adjusting my commitments around my responsibilities and energy; even if I could only manage a few minutes of an activity or had to skip it for the day, it was all okay. After all, detoxing was an act of self-care for me.

Even though I started this detox a while back, I still find myself sticking to the habits I built. It was a life-changing experience as it taught me how to find a balance between staying connected online and making meaningful time for myself offline. That balance looks different each day, but what mattered to me was being more intentional and mindful about how I spend my time.

Should you try digital detoxing?

Digital detoxing is not a “fix” that could work for everyone. It’s a highly personal journey that you need to commit to that can bring some benefits to your life. What it has done for me is that I have become more mindful of the way I spend my time every day, taught me how to manage my mental health, and most importantly taught me a lot about who I am.

You don’t have to wait until you see signs of excessive digital consumption, as I did. Give it a try, starting with one small, screen-free break in your day. Spend that time doing something you enjoy, and notice how you feel afterward. From there, you can decide which boundaries fit your responsibilities and which habits are worth keeping. – Rappler.com

References:

Masri-zada, T., Martirosyan, S., Abdou, A., Barbar, R., Kades, S., Makki, H., Haley, G., & Agrawal, D. K. (2018). The Impact of Social Media & Technology on Child and Adolescent Mental Health. J Psychiatry Psychiatr Disord. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12165459/

Ramadhan, R. N., Rampengan, D. D., Yumnanisha, D. A., Setiono, S. B., Tjandra, K. C., Ariyanto, M. V., Idrisov, B., & Empitu, M. A. (2024). Impacts of digital social media detox for mental health: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Narra J. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11392003/

This piece was written by Rappler intern Sebastian Vincent U. Ngo. Basti is a multimedia creative storyteller who focuses on the everyday details that make ordinary moments feel special. He seeks stories and uses design, words, and motion to help people see the familiar in a new light.

articles.title: Wesley So tops Jerusalem Masters, bags P6.4 million
articles.summary:
MANILA, Philippines – Filipino-American Super Grandmaster Wesley So notched pulsating back-to-back wins to claim the Jerusalem Masters 2026 title and $101,000 (P6.4 million) late Thursday, November 26, at the Museum of Tolerance in Israel’s capital. 

Striking in his last listed major tournament for the year, the Bacoor, Cavite-born So bested Russian Alexey Sarana in the deciding Armageddon for a 3-2 victory in the final of the 12-man all-GM tournament. 

They wound up tied after two rapid games and two blitz tiebreakers. 

In the semifinal, the 33-year-old So tamed fellow Team USA member Hans Moke Niemann, also via Armageddon when he secured a draw with black. 

So clinched his fourth crown this year, including his fourth United States championship, the GCT (Grand Chess Tour) Sinquefield Cup, and the American Cup. 

“I’m very happy, no more pressure,” said So in the post-game interview. So disclosed in the semifinals that he plays best when “ultra relaxed” and free from result pressure. 

After the round-robin qualifying stage, So was tied with Sarana at 7.0 points, trailing defending champion Arjun Erigaisi, with 9.0 points, and Niemann, with 8.0 points. Russian top seed Ian Nepomniachtchi tallied 6.5 points and missed the knockout semifinals. 

It was a remarkable recovery for So, who finished 13th out of 24 participants in last week’s Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot in Budapest, Hungary. 

If any consolation, So fared better than perennial world No. 1 Magnus Carlsen, who landed 17th. 

Following his Jerusalem triumph, So gained 10 points and climbed to ninth in the FIDE Live Rapid rating. So is ranked sixth in classical play. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Trend Intel: How the Filipino-inspired Glico Man became a brand mascot blueprint
articles.summary:
Hey trendsetters,

“A dancing Jollibee!”

This is what my newfound media friends from different parts of Southeast Asia blurted out when I introduced myself during the Glico Fam Trip, where I was the only representative from the Philippines. All of them gushed about how the Bee’s versions in their respective home countries aren’t as chaotic as the one from back home (I bet they saw those unhinged TikToks).

It’s interesting how their knee-jerk reaction to knowing where I come from is to associate me with a popular fast food chain’s mascot. But even more amusing is to realize how the impact of brand mascots is ultimately having a global resurgence.

The brand mascot renaissance

Previously “cringe,” brand mascots are now taking over the spotlight (again), said Little Black Book. The Wall Street Journal recently reported a rise in new mascots even from unexpected industries. Tech giants are no exception, with Meta recently unveiling an AI agent called Jolly, who might be intentionally made cute to grow people’s trust amid skepticism. And of course, we can’t deny the massive online impact of Duolingo’s Duo.

Screenshots from @duolingo on TikTok, showing funny videos of Duo the mascot

Here in the Philippines, we’ve seen Potato Corner’s Poco get its own talking plushie and blind box toys. 

In other parts of Asia, Butterbear of Coffee Beans by Dao (Thailand) is a pop culture sensation, Mixue’s Snow King (China) is having an amusement park based on him, and Buldak (South Korea) is introducing a “next-generation character.” The emotion even evolves from love to grief. Take, for example, people’s sentimental reaction to the retirement of Suica, the penguin fronting Japan’s JR East transportation smart card system.

“Mascots work when you need people to remember you even when they’re not paying attention. Children, tired parents, anyone scrolling half asleep. What connects them? Brands that win by being liked, not just respected,” said Jacopo Pesavento, CEO of Branding Records, in Marketing-Interactive.

The Glico Man’s iconic status

But if there’s a total hall of famer in the brand mascot department, it would have to be Japan’s Glico Man – the runner almost every Osaka visitor poses with. 

Whether you’re taking a well-timed photo in the Dotonbori River or shooting a Reel along with a thick crowd of tourists along the Ebisubashi Bridge with Anri’s I CAN’T STOP THE LONELINESS playing in the background, the Glico Man always makes an appearance, seemingly adding to the major city’s vibrancy.

People on TikTok posing with the Glico Man as backdrop in different spots

Before its 2014 version with LED lights, the Glico Man was established in 1935 to promote Ezaki Glico’s first product in 1922: A heart-shaped caramel candy with the slogan, “300 metres in a single piece,” implying that this health booster would give you enough energy to run 300 meters.

In case you didn’t know, the Glico Runner is actually inspired by a Filipino. Enter Fortunato Catalon, a track and field legend. 

“Not many people know this, but Glico Runner has a Filipino connection. The runner’s pose is said to have been inspired in part by Fortunato Catalon, the Filipino sprinter once celebrated as Asia’s fastest man, together with two Japanese runners – marathon pioneer Shizo Kanakuri and top sprinter Sasago Tani,” said a representative from Glico Philippines.

More than a face of a brand

These days, Osaka tourists are “last chance rushing” their way to Glico Man’s photo spots. The multinational confectionery company announced that the iconic sign will be covered starting December 1, as it’s up for a revamp, marking its seventh redesign since 1935. Don’t fret, as the runner will remain and is planned to be unveiled by spring (approximately March to May) in 2027.

How people on TikTok are documenting their final sight at the landmark is testament enough to the Running Man’s impact as a brand mascot – it no longer just represents a brand, but has already become synonymous with an entire city. 

The brand mascot to cultural landmark pipeline rarely happens, but when it does, it’s pretty worth it. In this case, a successful brand mascot is one that acts on its own, without needing constant deliberate action from its creators, as the audience has already become a huge player in promoting it through organic user-generated content. Plus, the accessibility it offers has allowed it to become an unofficial tourist spot.

We may chalk this phenomenon up to the “kidult” economy or people’s sudden drive to add whimsy to their mundane lives. But this interesting era of brand mascot renaissance in the age of AI may ultimately remind us that we might just need something overwhelmingly physical to see – or maybe even touch.

Which brand mascot pulled you in recently? Share your stories (or photos!) with us.

Until the next scroll!

Jelou Galang

Culture Desk Content Producer

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Photos of Duterte in the hospital are AI-generated
articles.summary:
Claim: Former president Rodrigo Duterte was taken to the hospital ahead of the start of his trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC), as shown in photos circulating online.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A collage of images depicting an individual resembling Duterte lying in a hospital bed has circulated on Facebook since November 24.

On November 25, Facebook user “Atty. Shiela Sison” shared the collage in a post that garnered 2,900 reactions, 926 comments, and 61 shares as of writing. The page “Sen. Rodante Marcoleta Supporters” posted it a day earlier, receiving 699 reactions, 126 comments, and 10 shares as of writing.

Both posts use the caption: “Get well soon po Tatay Digong sinugod sa hospital matapos…”

(Get well soon, Father Digong. Rushed to the hospital after…)

The caption did not specify the reason for Duterte’s alleged hospitalization. The phrase “See more” is also manually typed into the caption rather than generated by Facebook, and the collage is embedded in a link instead of an album.

Many commenters appear to have accepted the images as authentic, posting prayers and messages wishing Duterte a swift recovery.

The facts: The photos were generated using artificial intelligence. AI detection tools Hive Detect and Sightengine assessed the images as 99.5% and 87% likely to be AI-generated or deepfake content, respectively.

Duterte has been held at the ICC detention facility in The Hague, The Netherlands since his March 2025 arrest. Neither the ICC nor any credible news outlet has reported that he was transported to a hospital. 

Duterte at the ICC: The misleading posts emerged shortly before Duterte’s trial, which is scheduled to begin on November 30.

Trial Chamber III will determine whether the former leader is guilty beyond reasonable doubt of murder and attempted murder as crimes against humanity, related to his anti-illegal drug campaign in Davao as mayor and vice mayor, allegedly carried out through the Davao Death Squad, and subsequently nationwide after he became president in 2016.

Prosecutors plan to present around 100 witnesses, with five expected to testify before the court recesses for the holidays on December 18. (READ: Here’s what to expect at the opening of Rodrigo Duterte’s ICC trial)

Supreme Court update: On November 24, the Supreme Court dismissed petitions questioning Duterte’s arrest. The High Court ruled that the petitions were moot because a writ of habeas corpus cannot be enforced beyond Philippine jurisdiction and Duterte is already in ICC custody. Nine justices voted to dismiss the petitions, while four dissented. 

The Court clarified that the dismissal does not imply that Duterte’s arrest and transfer to The Hague were necessarily legal, and that any claims of rights violations must be pursued through other legal proceedings.

Debunked: Rappler has fact-checked claims regarding Duterte’s health condition:

FACT CHECK: No proof of Duterte in ‘critical’ condition

FACT CHECK: Photo of bedridden Duterte is fake, digitally altered

– Agatha Gonzalvo/Rappler.com

Agatha Gonzalvo is a Research and Data volunteer at Rappler. She is a fourth-year Applied Economics student at De La Salle University Manila.

articles.title: [Vantage Point] The Legarda-Leviste solar empire: Who opened the doors?
articles.summary:
The AMLC’s investigation into renewable-energy contract awards, a sprawling corporate network, and billions in financial transactions raises pressing questions about political influence, regulatory discretion, and private wealth.

On August 22, 2017, the Department of Energy (DOE) during the Rodrigo Duterte administration took two contradictory actions that defy conventional regulatory logic. 

On the exact same day, the DOE threatened to cancel a Leviste company’s solar contract for failing to deliver—yet awarded brand-new solar contracts to other Leviste-linked firms. Despite facing default, the developer was handed an even bigger share of the country’s renewable energy projects

That same year, according to the findings by the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC), P170.32 million in cash deposits entered the bank accounts of then-Energy secretary Alfonso Cusi. By 2022, his final year in office, Cusi’s annual cash deposits had climbed to P195.25 million. (READ: Cusi is sole billionaire in Duterte Cabinet at end of 2021)

The AMLC identified 243 cash deposits amounting to P434.85 million during his tenure—with 84.1% of the deposit value concentrated in 2017 and 2022. Whether any link exists between those cash inflows and the energy contracts remains an evidentiary issue that investigators must resolve. (READ: Duterte’s wealth remains secret until the end of his term)

Nearly a decade after those controversial awards, the AMLC’s reported allegations extend beyond Batangas Representative Leandro Leviste to his mother, Senator Loren Legarda, alongside Cusi.

According to reported Court of Appeals records, investigators allege that the three acted in concert to facilitate the acquisition, retention, and transfer of exclusive solar development rights to Leviste-linked corporations.

For more than a year, Vantage Point (see links below this paragraph) has examined how state-awarded development rights formed the bedrock of a multibillion-peso corporate empire. The latest disclosures examine the individuals who helped assemble those corporate vehicles and the public officials whose decisions enabled their expansion.

[Vantage Point] The Leviste gambit: Monetizing clean energy for political gains?

[Vantage Point] The solar tale: Jurisprudence slays Leviste’s thinly veiled tact

[Vantage Point] The Leviste solar saga – why markets should be worried

[Vantage Point] Consumers pay for DOE’s delayed action on Leviste firms 

[Vantage Point] The Leviste sting: The risks of trading farmland for megawatts

[Vantage Point] As Leandro Leviste cashes out of SPNEC, his private companies remain at the table

Between 2013 and 2021, Leviste reportedly incorporated 35 companies, many sharing the same incorporators and shareholders. Among the recurring names flagged by the AMLC were Legarda’s relatives, former Senate staffers, and even her former nanny.

Figure 1. Recurring names in Leviste’s corporate network

Source: Reported AMLC findings in Court of Appeals records. Appearances are not ownership percentages or proof of wrongdoing.

Were these individuals beneficial owners risking their own capital, or were they holding shares under arrangements benefiting someone else? Who supplied the equity, exercised effective control, and reaped the financial rewards? AMLC’s allegation of coordinated intervention warrants a rigorous examination of those relationships.

Cusi, meanwhile, faces questions about his role in regulatory approvals. Reported court records state that he personally approved and signed solar energy service contracts for Leviste-associated firms, including awards granted despite alleged defaults on prior commitments. What technical assessments, financial vetting, and compliance reports justified those approvals? Were competing developers held to the same standard?

An exclusive solar service contract reserves a geographic development opportunity, generally barring rival investors from developing the covered area. Granting those exclusive rights to entities unable to deliver can deprive the economy of investments and much-needed generating capacity. According to the AMLC, the 26 contracts which were eventually terminated carried roughly P10.44 billion in unfulfilled obligations. (READ: Duterte approves franchise for solar firm of Loren Legarda’s son)

The financial trail surrounding Cusi extends well beyond cash deposits. Investigators reportedly flagged 735 financial transactions totaling P11.05 billion during his term, spanning inter-account transfers, checks, fiduciary placements and withdrawals, investments, and cash deposits. Transaction volume is not necessarily income or illicit proceeds, but the origins and counterparties demand inspection.

Figure 2. Cusi’s reported cash deposits: P434.85 million

Source: Reported AMLC findings. 2017 and 2022 account for 84.1% of deposit value; no source of funds is established by this chart.

Investigators also noted substantial activity in Cusi’s accounts after he left public office, coinciding with Leviste’s sale of major shareholdings in SP New Energy Corp. (SPNEC). The reported contract approvals and subsequent financial activity necessitate a thorough review of banking and government records.

Cusi has challenged the accuracy of the Court of Appeals freeze order, categorically denying that he maintained a joint bank account with Golden Sun 999 Realty and Development Corp. He claims the same account number appears twice in the document, with the second entry identifying the correct account holders. The AMLC must address this alleged error and determine whether it affects its financial findings. His denial, however, does not by itself resolve the broader questions surrounding his reported P11.05 billion in financial transactions and the award of solar development contracts to Leviste-associated companies.

Self-made billionaire?

Leviste’s widely celebrated entrepreneurial rise merits scrutiny. Beneath the narrative of clean-energy innovation lay a corporate strategy that transformed government-granted development rights into lucrative commercial assets before some projects delivered electricity. 

The rising son

As early as January 2026, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla was examining whether Leviste’s corporate maneuvers circumvented statutory restrictions governing the transfer of congressional franchises.

Although congressional franchises and DOE service contracts are legally distinct instruments, the reported AMLC findings give urgency to that inquiry. Leviste-linked firms accumulated exclusive development rights, consolidated project stakes into the publicly listed SPNEC, and leveraged institutional investments that allowed early shareholders to monetize their positions. (READ: Leandro Leviste sells another P3 billion in SPNEC shares as solar controversies mount)

Across Leviste’s own accounts, the AMLC reportedly traced P57.89 billion in cumulative financial transactions. Investigators separately identified 1,044 checks worth roughly P14.99 billion issued to him by his solar companies, prompting the AMLC to flag potential commingling of personal and corporate funds. Gross transaction totals do not establish personal profit or unlawful enrichment, but they do justify accounting reconciliation.

Leviste maintains that his business dealings were lawful and conducted in the ordinary course of business. Cusi has declined further comment, citing pending court proceedings, while PDP-Laban has dismissed the probe as politically motivated. Yet the DOE’s reported termination notices and payment demands date back to December 2024—predating the flood-control controversy cited in claims of political persecution. 

Must Read

Leviste denies he made money from selling franchise to Pangilinan’s Meralco group

The Court of Appeals’ freeze orders remain provisional safeguards, not judicial convictions. Allegations involving Legarda must be weighed against official communications and corporate filings; Cusi’s actions, against departmental records and bank transaction records; and Leviste’s operations, against contractual compliance, capitalization, and monetization records.

Entrepreneurial ambition is no crime. But when private wealth is built partly upon exclusive development rights conferred by the state, the public is owed a full accounting of how those rights were secured, who opened the doors, who profited, and why billions in obligations went unmet. 

Where wrongdoing is proven, accountability must follow—regardless of surname, fortune, or public office. – Rappler.com

(To be concluded on Saturday, November 28)

articles.title: Nobel Committee chair emphasizes human accountability for AI’s potential harms
articles.summary:
MANILA, Philippines – Nobel Committee chair Jørgen Watne Frydnes at Rappler’s Social Good Summit 2026, Saturday, November 21, emphasized that, ultimately, people behind AI technologies as well as governments that utilize them must be held accountable if these systems inflict harm.

Already, these artificial intelligence systems are developing and moving faster than institutions and laws can respond, the chair said. These technologies are reshaping how people work, how wars are fought, and how societies form opinions. 

Algorithms determine what people see while advanced surveillance technologies are giving governments more oppressive ways to monitor journalists, citizens, and activists. 

This is a technology that is unique in that it is capable of making a decision for itself. “An atomic bomb could not decide who to bomb. AI can,” Frydnes said.

Who’s responsible? 

Frydnes’ attempt to answer the question of how the technology can be shaped for good is rooted in two principles that have routinely surfaced throughout the prize’s history. 

First, responsibility should always belong to people. Citing the Nuremberg trials after World War II, he recalled how those established that the responsibility for crimes should always fall on specific individuals and not abstract entities. 

“A machine cannot stand before a court, cannot feel remorse, and cannot answer to their victims. But those who design it, own it, deploy it, and profit from their existence, they can, and they should. And so can the states that use them. If we allow technology to become a new abstract entity behind which power hides, we will have undone one of the most important achievements of the last century,” he said. 

The second principle is that no one is above the law. 

This, he said, “must now also apply to the companies and individuals who hold power over information on a scale that rivals that of many states. A legal order enforced only when it’s politically convenient is no legal order at all.” 

Looking back at Nobel’s history

Further expounding his point, Frydnes looked to previous laureates, what they represent, and what they mean in the age of AI. 

He said the prize’s past offers lessons for understanding the challenges of the present. 

Cited were René Cassin, who helped draft the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and received the 1968 Nobel Peace Prize, and Carl von Ossietzky, the German journalist imprisoned in the 1930s by the Nazi regime for exposing its secret rearmament, and more recent laureates such as Maria Ressa and Dmitry Muratov.

He also cited the people behind the Pugwash Conferences who challenged the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction; the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons, which was recognized in 2017; and 2024 awardee Nihon Hidankyo, the Japanese organization of atomic bomb survivors from Hiroshima and Nagasaki, whose members have spent decades sharing their experiences to prevent the world from forgetting the consequences of nuclear warfare.

These specific awardees are a reminder that artificial intelligence too, is something that society can challenge if it runs counter to the good of humanity. 

While Frydnes acknowledged that the Nobel Peace Prize cannot regulate artificial intelligence or independently protect journalists from threats and intimidation, what it can do, he said, is to direct the world’s attention toward people who demonstrate that humanity can confront forces that appear greater than itself.

Frydnes offered a promise of his own, on behalf of those who continue to defend these principles: “We will not duck.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Duterte’s ICC trial: How to watch and follow the proceedings
articles.summary:
MANILA, Philippines – Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte will finally face trial before the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, Netherlands after years of calls for accountability over his violent war on drugs. 

The proceedings that will start on Monday, November 30, will put Duterte’s bloody anti-drug campaign under scrutiny. The charges cover alleged killings carried out by the Davao Death Squad when he was mayor of Davao City and those linked to his national drug war during his presidency.

Duterte has been detained at the ICC detention center since his arrest in Manila in March 2025. 

Hearings for 2026 are scheduled to run until December 17 before the court’s winter recess. Proceedings will resume on January 11, 2027.

Rappler justice reporter Jairo Bolledo and correspondent Michelle Abad will be in The Hague to cover the trial. They will bring updates from the courtroom and report on activities outside the court and detention center.

Here are the ways to follow Rappler’s coverage and stay on top of the latest developments:

1. Join the Justice and Crime chat room

The trial will raise questions about accountability and justice that deserve careful discussion. Join Rappler’s Justice and Crime community to follow the latest developments and exchange views with other readers.

articles.title: Dutch groups ask court to halt Meta smart glasses sales over privacy concerns
articles.summary:
AMSTERDAM, The Netherlands – Dutch consumer and digital rights groups asked a court on Thursday, November 26, to halt sales of Meta AI-powered smart glasses in the Netherlands, arguing they violate European privacy laws by allowing wearers to film people without their knowledge.

While limited in scope to the Netherlands, a summary ruling in the civil suit against Meta at the Amsterdam District Court could set a precedent amid growing public backlash, venue bans and regulatory warnings across the world.

A decision is expected by December 24 at the latest.

The rights groups, which include the Netherlands’ main consumer association Consumentenbond and Offlimits, which campaigns against online sex abuse, argued that the glasses developed by Meta and Ray-Ban owner EssilorLuxottica both violate privacy laws and force people to constantly worry in public places, with a chilling effect on society.

The plaintiffs want Meta to prevent its glasses from being used to record people without their knowledge, stop using recordings to train AI models and halt sales until Meta complies. They sought penalties of €100,000 ($109,600) per day per defendant for non-compliance, capped at €100 million.

Offlimits’ lawyer Karlijn Han said the glasses were used for what she described in court as “creep shots.” “Covert recordings are undoubtedly also being made during exams, in changing rooms, at swimming pools, in hotel rooms and hospitals, but also in playgrounds and on beaches,” she said in opening remarks. “Each invasion of privacy is worse than the last.”

Meta denies images are used to train AI

Meta’s lawyer Bastiaan Kemp said the court should reject the suit. He said the measures demanded would harm legitimate users, damage Meta’s competitive position and amount to a product recall without resolving concerns about similar devices.

“Providers of products cannot be held responsible for every instance of deliberate misuse,” he told the court. He said that a recording light on the frame makes it obvious when they are being used for recording.

And he denied allegations made by Consumentenbond’s lawyer in court that Meta processes images recorded by the smart glasses in Europe or uses them to train AI models in violation of European law. Meta and manufacturing partner EssilorLuxottica sold more than 7 million smart glasses in 2025, around 80% of the global market.

A lawyer for EssilorLuxottica argued that it neither processes nor has access to footage and that a sales ban would be disproportionate and ineffective given the availability of similar products from other manufacturers.

Backlash extends worldwide

From proposed restrictions in Australia and Norway to bans in courts across England, Wales, and New York state, governments and judicial authorities are increasingly seeking to prevent covert recording and protect sensitive information. Cinema operators in the UK are also introducing restrictions over privacy and film piracy concerns.

On Tuesday, Germany’s national consumer federation announced legal action against Meta and Ray-Ban over alleged privacy violations, arguing that the glasses make it nearly impossible for consumers to comply with European data protection rules when using them in public.

The European Data Protection Board warned in October that smart glasses raised serious privacy concerns and called for stronger safeguards.

Dutch privacy regulator AP this month advised consumers to not buy smart glasses, saying they are unsafe for both users and bystanders. In October, Dutch retail chain Hans Anders suspended sales of Meta’s ​Ray-Ban smart glasses in the Netherlands and Belgium.

Meta also faces proposed class-action lawsuits in the United States over alleged improper sharing of private images gathered by the glasses. – Rappler.com

articles.title: For a mother who lost 2 sons, Duterte’s ICC trial is a birthday gift
articles.summary:
Llore Pasco, a mother who lost her two sons, is traveling to The Hague to attend the trial of ex-president Rodrigo Duterte that will open on her 73rd birthday. She said she had never imagined she would see Duterte in the dock.

“This is the greatest and most beautiful gift you could give me,” she said hours before boarding a plane to the Netherlands.

“My only wish is not just justice for my children, but for all those killed during the time of Rodrigo Duterte. I hope the killings stop for the next generation.”

Must Read

Here’s what to expect at the opening of Rodrigo Duterte’s ICC trial

The former Philippine leader goes on trial at the International Criminal Court on Monday, November 30, for alleged crimes against humanity during a six-year anti-drug campaign in which thousands of people were killed.

“For those who have suffered the most egregious abuses during the war on drugs, this will be a welcome moment in their quest for justice,” said Priya Pillai, an international lawyer who runs the Asia Justice Coalition. It “is a significant moment in Philippine history.”

Duterte, 81, faces allegations relating to 85 murders and two attempted murders from 2011 to 2018, including when he served as the mayor of Davao City and the early years of his presidency. The court’s prosecutors say the victims are only a sample of as many as 30,000 people killed by death squads targeting users and sellers of illegal drugs.

Must Read

Rodrigo Duterte at ICC: A cheat sheet on understanding his case, trial

It is one of the highest-profile cases to come before the court in its more than two decades of existence, and the biggest since US President Donald Trump’s administration imposed sanctions that could imperil the court’s ability to function.

If convicted of any of three counts of crimes against humanity, Duterte could face life in prison.

Duterte’s supporters have called for his release. His daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte said on Wednesday that “no foreign court or nation should ever stand above the sovereignty of our country.”

Test of embattled ICC

The proceedings will test the court’s ability to conduct a high-profile trial amid an ongoing campaign by the United States to force its closure. Washington has imposed crippling financial sanctions and called on member states to withdraw from the ICC and isolate it.

Must Read

What happens to Rodrigo Duterte’s case if ICC is dismantled because of Trump?

The ICC is the world’s sole permanent war crimes tribunal, set up to prosecute individuals accused of war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide when national jurisdictions fail to do so.

Duterte is only the second former national leader to appear before it for crimes allegedly committed while in power, after Laurent Gbagbo of Ivory Coast, who was acquitted in 2019.

Four serving national leaders face ICC arrest warrants: Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Russia’s President Vladimir Putin, Afghanistan’s Taliban leader Hibatullah Akhundzada and Myanmar military leader Min Aung Hlaing.

Duterte will be asked on Monday to enter a plea. Prosecutors will then present opening arguments. His lawyers have told judges he denies the charges.

“There was no state or organizational policy to murder,” they argued in a pre-trial brief. “This is not a crimes against humanity case and, as such, does not belong before this court.”

Death squads

Despite his lawyers arguing that Duterte was unfit to stand trial because of cognitive decline, judges ordered him to stand trial and attend hearings. Court sessions will be shortened to accommodate his age.

During the trial, which is expected to run well into 2027, more than 500 alleged victims will be represented in court.

Prosecutors have said Duterte created, funded and armed death squads responsible for thousands of extrajudicial killings between 2011 and 2019. Philippine law enforcement agencies acknowledged 6,248 deaths.

In language his lawyers dismissed as mere rhetoric, Duterte told supporters during his 2016 election campaign: “I will do just what I did as mayor. You drug pushers, hold-up men and do-nothings, you better go out. Because I’d kill you.”

In March 2025 Duterte was arrested and taken to The Hague, where he is being held in a detention unit for war crimes suspects within a Dutch prison. – Rappler.com

It said the ban violated the principle of proportionality by excessively restricting their freedom of expression. Experts say lawmakers should hear directly from foreign residents and clearly define any restrictions. “The decision confirms that foreigners’ political expression is also protected under freedom of expression, which is a fundamental human right,” said Kim Kwang-jae, an attorney at Shin & Kim who represented the petitioners. articles.title: Suicide deaths fall 16.3 percent in September
articles.summary: The number of suicide deaths fell 16.3 percent from a year earlier to 1,014 in September, while the figure for the first nine months of the year dropped 11.7 percent on-year to 9,591, data from the Office for Government Policy Coordination showed Friday. Of September's total, men accounted for 69 percent, or 701 deaths, while women accounted for 31 percent, or 313 deaths. Across all regions, the total number of suicide deaths through September dropped from the same period last year, except for the central administrative city of Sejong, which saw a 27.3 percent increase in such deaths from a year ago, the data showed. The southern island of Jeju saw the biggest drop of 24.6 percent in suicide deaths this year, followed by the central city of Daejeon at 21.4 percent, and the southeastern cities of Ulsan and Daegu at 20.9 percent and 16.4 percent, respectively. The Korea Customs Service said Friday that Guatemala officially opened its upgraded electronic customs system, known as UNI-PASS, at the headquarters of its tax authority, the Superintendency of Tax Administration, in Guatemala City on Thursday (local time). The ceremony was attended by Kim Ki-dong, director-general for information and data policy at the Korea Customs Service, Korean Ambassador to Guatemala Kim Deuk-hwan and Guatemalan tax chief Werner Ovalle, along with officials from both countries. The project, launched in 2022 as part of Korea’s official development assistance program, involved 6.9 billion won ($4.8 million) in support over five years. It upgraded Guatemala’s risk management and data analysis systems, introduced a cargo management platform and established a portal allowing customs documents to be transmitted directly. The project

articles.title: Sungkyunkwan University ranks 24th worldwide in THE Interdisciplinary Science Rankings
articles.summary: Sungkyunkwan University (SKKU) ranked 24th worldwide in the Times Higher Education (THE) Interdisciplinary Science Rankings 2027, highlighting its growing strength in interdisciplinary research. SKKU climbed 19 places from last year’s ranking of 43rd to become the top-ranked university in Korea. “This achievement reflects international recognition of our university members’ efforts to tackle societal challenges beyond disciplinary boundaries,” SKKU President Yoo Ji-beom said. “We will continue to advance as a global research-oriented university at the forefront of interdisciplinary research,” he added. A total of 1,058 universities worldwide were ranked in this year’s assessment, released by THE, a U.K.-based higher education ranking organization. Launched in 2024 by THE in partnership with Schmidt Science Fellows, the rankings assess universities’ contributions and commitment to interdisciplinary scientific research. articles.title: Korea's speed, Finland's lifelong learning could build human skills in AI age
articles.summary: As concerns mount over artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted cheating in examinations, educators and experts are calling for a fundamental rethink of how students are taught and assessed in the age of AI. The issue was a central topic at the Korea-Finland Innovation Forum 2026, held Wednesday at Korea University's SK Future Hall. Under the theme "Human Capabilities in the AI Age," academics, government officials and industry representatives explored how education must move beyond memorization to developing creativity and critical thinking. Welcoming participants, Finnish Ambassador to Korea Jyri Järviaho said AI would have a profound impact on future jobs and the skills required to perform them, making it essential for education systems to adapt to changing realities. "Our goal is to ensure that individuals and societies have the capabilities to thrive in the AI age by strengthening AI literacy, fostering trust in new technologies and encouraging the responsible adoption of AI," he said. articles.title: Korea boosts commuter bus accessibility for people with disabilities
articles.summary: More than half of Korea’s city buses now feature low-floor designs, marking a significant step toward making public transportation more accessible to an aging population and people with mobility challenges. The Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport said Friday that low-floor buses accounted for 51.8 percent of the nation’s city bus fleet in 2025, with 18,160 vehicles in operation. That represents an increase of 2,417 buses from the previous year, bringing the country past the 50 percent milestone. The progress comes as demand for accessible transportation continues to grow. According to the ministry’s 2025 transportation accessibility survey, 16.46 million people, or 32.2 percent of Korea’s population, were classified as having mobility challenges at the end of last year, up approximately 330,000 from 2024. The category covers a broad range of people, including those with disabilities, adults aged 65 and older, pregnant women, people accompanying children under 7 and children aged 12 or younger. articles.title: HUFS to build 1st inter-university dormitory among private universities
articles.summary: Hankuk University of Foreign Studies (HUFS) signed a memorandum of understanding with the Korea Advancing Schools Foundation on Monday to build an inter-university dormitory and improve its educational facilities. The agreement was signed by HUFS President Kang Kee-hoon and Lee Ha-woon, chairman of the foundation, at HUFS’ Seoul campus, the university said. The two institutions have agreed to build a privately funded Haengbok (Happy) Dormitory that will accommodate students from HUFS and nearby universities in Seoul, while improving the university’s educational environment and promoting sustainable development. The project is the first of its kind to be undertaken by a private university in Korea, HUFS said. Under the agreement, HUFS will provide the site behind the Humanities and Sciences Building on its Seoul campus free of charge to a special-purpose company (SPC) established by the foundation to build a dormitory that can accommodate about 400 students. The university will also work with the foundation to provide administrative and financial support for the project. The foundation

articles.title: CSAT perfect scorers shun spotlight amid AI cheating suspicions
articles.summary: At least three students are believed to have earned perfect scores on this year's College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), yet they are shunning the spotlight for fear of being suspected of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted cheating. The current tally of three is based on preliminary self-grading, with the number expected to rise when official results are released on Dec. 11. High schools and private academies have long been eager to publicize perfect scorers on Korea's high-stakes college entrance exam, with news of such achievements emerging as early as exam day last year. Their study habits, daily routines and university aspirations have often made headlines, while schools have celebrated their success as a source of pride. This year, however, even students who earned their scores legitimately are reluctant to come forward for fear of cheating allegations. The shift in sentiment follows an admission of AI-assisted cheating by the top scorer on the national tax accountant qualification exam, which has fueled widespread suspicion of high achievers across national exams. articles.title: Data reveals how medical tourists explore Korea beyond hospitals
articles.summary: Korea is looking to turn its booming medical tourism industry into a wider driver of regional tourism, using big data to understand where international patients travel, shop and spend beyond their hospital visits. The Korea Tourism Organization (KTO), in partnership with the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, hosted the third Korea Tourism Today Data Seminar at Coex in southern Seoul this week. Bringing together around 500 representatives from local governments, the tourism industry and academia, the event explored the current landscape and future growth potential of K-medical tourism through mobility and consumption data. The seminar presented an analysis of medical tourism spending across six major regions: Seoul, Busan, Daegu, Jeju, Gyeonggi Province and Incheon. Notably, medical tourism expenditure in Busan and Jeju surged 150.6 percent and 157.6 percent, respectively, in the first nine months of 2026 compared with the same period last year. articles.title: Exam misconduct cases rise 70% in this year's CSAT: ministry
articles.summary: The number of exam misconduct cases detected during this year's College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT) rose nearly 70 percent from a year earlier, despite tighter exam management and oversight, the education ministry said Friday. Notably, cases involving smart devices rose 3.6-fold, accounting for nearly a quarter of all violations detected during the Nov. 19 exam, the ministry said. According to a report submitted to the National Assembly, a total of 474 cases of CSAT-related exam misconduct had been reported as of Wednesday, up 69.9 percent from 279 a year earlier. By category, the most common violations involved writing answers after the end-of-exam bell and breaches of answer-sheet rules during the fourth-period social studies session, with 127 cases each. The former surged from 25 cases last year, while the latter increased by 53. They were followed by violations involving smart devices, which jumped to 112 from 31, possession of electronic devices at 51 from 53 and other forms of misconduct, including failure to follow proctors' instructions at 57, up 38 from the previous year. articles.title: Lee's approval rating rises for 2nd straight week: poll
articles.summary: President Lee Jae Myung's approval rating rose for the second consecutive week to 41 percent, a poll showed Friday. The survey, conducted by Gallup Korea from Tuesday through Thursday on 1,000 people aged 18 and older, showed that positive assessments of Lee's performance gained 1 percentage point from the previous week. Those who disapproved of Lee's handling of state affairs also rose 1 percentage point to 50 percent. Lee's approval rating has fluctuated between 39 and 41 percent for seven weeks since mid-October. Among those who positively assessed Lee's performance, 29 percent cited diplomacy, up from 24 percent the previous week, followed by economic and livelihood issues at 10 percent, and communication at 5 percent. Lee returned home last Thursday after attending the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summits, where he also held a series of bilateral talks. articles.title: Police raid justice ministry, prosecution over alleged records leak to lawmaker
articles.summary: Police on Friday raided the justice ministry and prosecution offices over allegations that investigative records were leaked to independent lawmaker Han Dong-hoon. The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency sent investigators to search the ministry, the Supreme Prosecutors Office and the Seoul Western District Prosecutors Office and secure evidence related to the allegations. The ruling Democratic Party of Korea filed a complaint against Han in September on suspicion of disclosing official secrets after he raised lobbying allegations against then Justice Minister nominee Kim Seung-won. Han at the time unveiled a prosecution report about Kim's lobbying allegations, drawing questions over how he obtained the document. Kim later withdrew his candidacy amid growing controversy over the scandal.

articles.title: North Korean troops cross inter-Korean border about 40 times over past 2 months: lawmaker
articles.summary: North Korean troops have crossed the heavily fortified inter-Korean border on roughly 40 occasions over the past two months, a South Korean lawmaker said Friday, following September's mine blast in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that injured three South Korean soldiers. The North violated the Military Demarcation Line (MDL) about 30 times in October and roughly 10 times this month, according to data submitted to Rep. Yu Yong-weon of the main opposition People Power Party. North Korean soldiers' border crossing has continued even after the Sept. 21 explosion of North Korea-planted mines south of the DMZ. Pyongyang has denied responsibility. Pyongyang has reinforced border fortification work by installing barbed-wire fences and land mines along the inter-Korean border. Such activities became evident after North Korean leader Kim Jong-un declared the relations between the two Koreas as those between "two hostile states". articles.title: 2 Korean naval submarines under repair after accidents
articles.summary: Two of the Korean Navy's attack submarines are undergoing repairs after sustaining damage in separate accidents, military officials said Friday. One 1,800-ton Son Won Il-class submarine suffered damage to its protective hull coating after getting entangled in discarded fishing nets during a nighttime mission in the Yellow Sea in September, according to Navy officials. No casualties were reported. With its navigational systems intact, the vessel was able to return to its home port under its own power, the Navy said, adding that it is currently undergoing maintenance and repairs for restoration. Another submarine of the same class, the Hong Beom Do vessel, caught fire in April while undergoing a scheduled overhaul at a shipyard in the southeastern city of Ulsan, about 300 kilometers southeast of Seoul. The Navy has been assessing the damage and carrying out repairs on the vessel, noting that no timeline has been set for when the work will be completed. articles.title: AI bruise-measuring tool wins top prize at public safety contest
articles.summary: A sticker that helps police use artificial intelligence (AI) to document injuries in suspected abuse cases won the top prize at a national invention contest for public servants, the Ministry of Intellectual Property said Thursday. Other winning designs included a chair that screens for drugs concealed on the body without a hands-on search and floating beacons that guide people off tidal flats as the tide comes in. The ministry announced the winners of the 2026 Public Safety Invention Challenge at an awards ceremony at the National Assembly. It co-hosted the ceremony with the Korea Customs Service, the Korean National Police Agency, the National Fire Agency, the Korea Forest Service, the Korea Coast Guard and Reps. Jang Chul-min and Jeon Eun-su. Now in its ninth year, the contest invites employees from the five agencies to develop inventions that address safety problems they encounter on the job. articles.title: KAI needs private ownership to compete in global market, defense consultant says
articles.summary: A veteran of the European defense industry says the Korea Aerospace Industries (KAI) should move into private hands so it can invest for the long term and warns that the KF-21 fighter jet may struggle to find buyers abroad without that stability. Kong worked on bids to sell the Rafale and Eurofighter to Korea and was involved in the country’s acquisition of Taurus missiles and Airbus aerial refueling aircraft. He said steady production by Korean suppliers helped manufacturers deliver tanks and howitzers to Poland quickly. articles.title: Why do celebrities keep driving drunk despite having so much to lose?
articles.summary: Click here for more articles by Kormedi.com. They can afford chauffeurs and have people willing to help them. An arrest for drunk driving can cost them their public image and force them to suspend their careers. Yet news of celebrities driving under the influence continues to surface, with some getting behind the wheel again even after being punished. Why do they keep making the same choice despite having so much to lose? The question has long been raised overseas, too. CNN's former entertainment program “Showbiz Tonight” once examined cases involving Lindsay Lohan, Nicole Richie and Paris Hilton, asking, “Why don't they hire a driver when they have the money and the means?” The program looked beyond the cost, pointing to attitudes shaped by special treatment, environments in which risky behavior goes unchecked and persistent drinking problems. Paris Hilton explained her drunk driving case in a 2007 interview on CNN's “Larry King Live.” She said she had had one drink and was on her way to a restaurant a few blocks away. She acknowledged that she should not have been driving.

articles.title: India-US trade agreement nearing completion: Indian commerce minister
articles.summary:
India said Friday it was close to finalising a long-awaited trade deal with the United States after Washington proposed higher tariffs on the country’s goods if negotiations fail.

“The US trade deal is close to culmination,” Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal told an industry conference, adding that differences were beginning to be resolved.

“The process and pathway, which was always something which held back finalising the deal, is now taking some shape,” he said.

Goyal’s comments came after US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer on Wednesday said Indian goods would face tariffs of 17 per cent if a trade deal is reached but rise to as much as 25pc if not.

The new tariffs face a period of public consultation process before taking effect next year.

The United States is India’s largest trading partner and the two have been negotiating a trade deal since reaching an interim accord in February.

New Delhi has sought access to the US market for key export sectors including textiles, pharmaceuticals and engineering goods, while Washington has pushed for greater access for American products and closer alignment on trade rules.

Since February, several rounds of talks have taken place but have been complicated by Washington launching a probe into unfair trade practices against multiple countries, including India.

Last month, New Delhi’s Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said trade deal talks between India and US had reached a “plateau”, after negotiations dragged on for months with the sides struggling to resolve sticking points.

On Wednesday, the US unveiled proposed tariffs on 14 economies, including India, after a months-long probe into alleged excess production. The duties, proposed at up to 20pc, came over allegations that the economies “are promoting production and capacity divorced from the realities of demand and market principles,” a senior US official said on condition of anonymity.

articles.title: Is Pakhtunkhwa stuck between a rock and a hard place?
articles.summary:
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has been simmering for months and the crisis has all the markers of a national one. It ticks most boxes: An emergency was declared; a provincial government was suspended. Governor’s rule was imposed. The army was deployed. Protests were managed. A constitutional court clipped the powers of a provincial court. A president withdrew protection against preventive detention for provincial lawmakers. A chief minister became a chief-minister-under-preventive-detention. A federal oversight committee was formed. A technocratic council replaced the provincial cabinet. The bureaucracy was shuffled. An independent secretariat was created to run the former Federally Administered Tribal Areas (plus four bonus districts).

These are the historic developments so far, even if their import remains unclear—including to those who made them history. This dispensation — at least governor’s rule and the attendant technocracy — is constitutionally valid for a maximum of six months (two months at a time, to be extended by a joint sitting of parliament) even if, as it would ominously appear, the stewards of this interregnum are settling in as if for a full term.

Almost in parallel, it has been hard to miss the background noise of a largely manufactured debate about the creation of new provinces. The cure to the woes we know and the woes we don’t, we are told, lies in smaller administrative units. If such territorial reorganisation were to dilute political strongholds at the provincial tier and centralise power in the name of decentralisation, that would be a happy accident and not an intended consequence.

Creating new provinces may at most involve some tinkering with the federation’s administrative plumbing and redrawing some cartographic lines. (For historical edification read about the One Unit here). Such an undertaking would be acceptable as long as the intention was to create more intimacy between (political, administrative, fiscal) power and the people. Such a relationship usually takes the shape of local government, but elections that would make that possible have been delayed.

The elephant in the room

Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s peculiar circumstances can be attributed to the elephant in the room: the relationship of its ruling party, the Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI), and the regime. One political party’s entrenchment in a province symbolises all that a central government would despise (as detailed in the 18th Amendment): a financially independent, autonomous government with an entire administrative machinery at its disposal and which is not shy of flaunting its democratic mandate.

The PTI’s hold on calling the shots in KP tightened dramatically over the last three elections: from 35 of 99 general seats in 2013, to 66 of 99 in 2018, to around 90 of 115 in 2024 (the last won by PTI-backed independents after the party lost its electoral symbol). It holds the popular mandate in the province without a doubt.

In the centre’s version of events, this mandate was used to flagrantly launch attacks; in PTI’s version, its government in KP was the last line of defence against excesses and power grabs. From either vantage point, though, surely, political strife does not provide sufficient grounds to upend democracy. It is another matter, however, if a government is unable to fight terrorism and cooperate with the centre on security concerns (which was radically equated with collusion with terrorists). It was this argument that set us down the road to relying on Articles 232 and 234 of the Constitution, the suspension of an elected government, and the decision to place the province under foster care.

An aside on the terrorism. To be fair, it would be impossible and unwise for anyone to make a case claiming the security situation in KP is under control. It is not. The numbers don’t lie. Between 2021 and 2025, according to PIPS, the annual figures have gone from 169 killed and 122 injured to 581 killed and 698 injured. And this does not even convey the intensification of the scale, frequency, and sophistication of these attacks.

If we were to believe former Awami National Party MNA Samar Haroon Bilour, though, the militants are now shaking in their boots. The MPA recently joined the ruling coalition and now serves as an Adviser to the Governor on Information. She has claimed that terrorism is down 80 per cent in the last five weeks alone. It is unclear if she counted the abduction of the former Additional Chief Secretary’s two children from home in Peshawar four days after the imposition of governor’s rule.

But why resort to such extreme measures now? And why KP and not also Balochistan, as both provinces faced 95 per cent of terrorist attacks combined in 2025? The ostensible reasons provided must include: a threat of war, the provincial government’s inability (or unwillingness) to discharge its duties, and the assertion that the federal government has a better track record of managing security challenges and terrorism threats. The latter would be a bold claim if a cursory look were cast over how previous policies have impacted KP and, in particular, erstwhile FATA.

The build-up

Just last week, the freshly posted Peshawar corps commander asked a gathering of elders in Miranshah to join him in offering a prayer. The congregation raised their palms as the general prayed for the safety, peace, and prosperity of the region. He spoke of his love for the land and respect for its people and concluded with a prayer for divine retribution against himself if he has been sent on a secret agenda to seize control of mineral resources. This video is from November 21, 2026. To understand why minerals are finding mention in congregational prayers, we’ll have to go back a little.

In the build-up to the emergency and governor’s rule, and especially afterwards, the internet was ablaze with rumours that this was a ploy to plunder KP’s mineral wealth. The province has built industries around limestone, marble, granite, soapstone, gypsum, and gemstones, but says only 30 per cent of its terrain is geologically mapped. There are claims of abundant deposits of antimony, copper, gold, tungsten, and rare earth elements.

Minerals have been a provincial domain. In addition to that, the 18th Amendment introduced joint federal–provincial ownership of oil and gas. While KP and Balochistan maintain that they have been unable to exercise any such ownership or benefit from it in any meaningful way, the centre’s recent push—via the Special Investment Facilitation Council—to stimulate investment in mineral extraction has set off alarm bells.

To be clear and fair on the timeline, the minerals debate preceded the imposition of an emergency in KP by over a year. Back in April 2025, a bill was unsuccessfully tabled in the assembly, setting off a storm when critics from both sides of the aisle accused it of facilitating federal control over the province’s mineral resources. In August 2026, the United States officially discussed “cooperation” over critical minerals with KP government representatives. Both these developments took place while the PTI still ruled KP and both fed public rumours that the centre had an eye on the resources.

The emergency and governor’s rule seemed to confirm everyone’s worst fears. Within the first week, the governor announced plans for how KP would extract and sell its mineral resources to seek investment. Earlier this month, the flagship Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum in Islamabad was presided over by the prime minister and Chief of Defence Forces. A day before that, the KP governor met foreign investors, and a day after that, he cancelled all gold-mining leases in the province, claiming that illegal mining was being used to finance terror groups and funnel profits to Afghanistan.

The advisory council, governor, and federal government should rest assured that every single move over the next few months will be closely scrutinised. The legitimacy of any decision with permanent political, administrative, or economic implications for KP will be put under the microscope, even if justified in the name of good governance. They would do well to remember that governance may be technocratic or bureaucratic, centralised or devolved, even good or bad, but one thing it is not is apolitical. Governance is an extension of the political process, a product of it, a manifestation of the public will. And as such, its sustainability rests on foundations of political legitimacy, even if it is sidestepped in the short term.

This choice presented to us between politically legitimate bad governance and politically illegitimate good governance is a false one for two reasons. First, it pushes the view that the bitter pill of autocracy has necessarily led to good governance, while the entire history of Pakistan is proof that it has not. And second, it limits our public debate by reducing our options to a facile and false dichotomy. Those cannot be our only options. To demand good governance stemming from political legitimacy must be the least we demand of ourselves as a nation.

Trauma unexpressed

Every meaningful sociopolitical analysis of the Peshawar Valley over the past few decades has been in agreement on how some fundamental dynamics of the region have changed. Drastic urbanisation and the expansion of the middle class have altered the political landscape entirely. The Peshawar Valley was already far more ‘integrated’ with the country compared to the rest of the province, but these dynamics accelerated that ‘mainstreaming’.

All the hot-button Pashtun nationalist topics, such as Kalabagh Dam and renaming the province, gradually lost steam. The valley that gave birth to the Khudai Khidmatgar now had the same political aspirations as anywhere in north Punjab. This persisted despite the post-2001 bloodshed. Even though the Awami National Party paid the highest price through its rank and file, it could not compete with the centrist, populist, nationalist version of Pakistani politics espoused by the PTI.

From the centre’s perspective, this was a success story. Today, it merits reassessment. Over the past decade, the relationship between KP as a whole—including the Peshawar Valley—and the centre has taken on a distinctly ethnolinguistic tone. The sense of marginalisation and ‘othering’ felt by people along the lines of that identity—indeed, because of that identity—is potent fuel for discontent.

Consider the two most prominent, and starkly contrasting political expressions emerging from KP in recent times: the Pashtun Tahaffuz Movement and the PTI. One has been banned and the other’s government has now been suspended. In their stead came an oversight committee led by Ishaq Dar and a governor declaring that KP’s policies will now come from Islamabad not Kabul.

Trauma unexpressed will always find a channel. It would be grave folly to assume that the absence of an immediate, widespread, and sustained outpouring of rage in reaction to the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule is proof that such rage does not exist. That feeling of being disenfranchised at such a fundamental level, especially for millions of young people struggling to keep their heads above water, cannot be mollified with announcements of grand packages. Broken legitimacy cannot be forced back through technocratic bandaging and suppression of dissent.

By the end of six months, if these lessons have not been learnt, and if there is an attempt to bend the system beyond breaking point, decades of ‘mainstreaming’ can be brought to nought. And if subjective disapproval of a government’s performance is accepted as sufficient grounds for doing away with democracy, then all elected governments in Pakistan—provincial and federal—will rue the day. That is to say, it comes down to a simple choice. You either believe there can be extenuating circumstances that justify the suspension of democracy, or you don’t. If you are prone to believing the former, the circumstances tend to—at some point, in some shape, under some doctrine of necessity—present themselves.

Header art by Mohsin Alam

articles.title: Erdogan completes Turkiye's ratification of Makkah defence pact
articles.summary:
President Tayyip Erdogan has formally approved the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, the country’s Official Gazette said on Friday, completing Turkiye’s ratification after parliament ratified it earlier this month.

Turkiye’s parliament ratified the agreement on November 5, paving the way for Ankara to support Riyadh amid attacks by Yemen’s Houthi militia against the kingdom. Under the agreement, an attack on one party constitutes an attack on all.

The approval comes as Pakistan hosts a two-day meeting of the tripartite alliance’s top decision-making body from Friday, with discussions also expected to feature the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi fighters.

The third session of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee (SPDC) is being held in Islamabad, where authorities have announced a public holiday and imposed special movement restrictions for the high-level gathering. A local holiday has also been announced in Rawalpindi.

The meeting is expected to focus on finalising standard operating procedures (SOPs), establishing an implementation mechanism and defining coordination between the three countries’ political, defence and military institutions, a Pakistani official said.

Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said on Thursday that the foreign and defence ministers of Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan would participate in the meeting, adding that the “continuous turmoil south of Saudi Arabia will obviously be one agenda point in the meeting”.

A ruling party lawmaker told Reuters last month that Turkiye would also submit a mandate to parliament seeking approval for the deployment of military personnel to Saudi Arabia under the agreement.

Ankara’s ratification clears another step towards the implementation of the pact, which could allow Turkiye to provide military support to Riyadh amid attacks by Houthis against the kingdom.

The alliance

The three countries signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement on Aug 7. The pact provides that an armed attack on any one member will be considered an attack on all, obliging the other two to extend assistance through available means, including military support.

The SPDC, which brings together the foreign and defence ministers and chiefs of defence staff of the three countries, is the alliance’s principal decision-making forum.

A permanent secretariat has been established in Riyadh to coordinate its work, with Pakistan’s retired Lt Gen Nauman Mahmood appointed as its first secretary general for a three-year term. A working committee comprising officials from member countries is also functioning.

Turkiye’s ratification of the agreement has completed the accession process for all three member states.

The alliance has yet to publicly define its doctrine, the composition of forces, command arrangements or procedures governing a collective military response.

An emergency SPDC meeting in Riyadh on Oct 5 had called for moving towards practical implementation of collective defence commitments, including arrangements for the rapid deployment of agreed forces and capabilities, subject to national laws.

Wider regional tensions

The alliance’s formation also comes against the backdrop of wider regional tensions involving Iran, the United States and Israel.

While the three members share an interest in strengthening regional deterrence, their differing strategic priorities make it important to define the alliance’s scope without allowing it to become an instrument for wider military confrontation.

Asif declined to comment on how the alliance would respond to a direct Iranian attack on Saudi Arabia, but identified Israel as a possible threat to other countries in the region.

“The possibility of some conflict, or aggression from the Israeli side exists, so we need to close our ranks, the countries of this region,” he said.

Managing relations with Iran will be particularly important for Pakistan, which has sought to preserve diplomatic engagement with Tehran while deepening defence cooperation with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye.

A meeting in Tehran involving representatives of the three countries and Iranian officials, held on Pakistan’s initiative, reflected efforts to keep channels of communication open between the two sides.

Pakistan brokered a June accord that led to a brief halt in fighting between the US and Iran and laid out a roadmap for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and negotiations on Tehran’s nuclear programme.

However, the truce collapsed, with Washington and Tehran accusing each other of violating the agreement, prompting months of shuttle diplomacy led principally by Qatar and Pakistan.

Asif said Pakistan had played “a very, very constructive role” between Washington and Tehran, but the outcome of ongoing mediation was “still fragile” and peace was “not yet embedded in a way people were expecting”.

Turkiye had earlier stressed the defensive character of the agreement and remained cautious about involvement in combat operations in Yemen.

articles.title: LHC seeks replies on plea by five Afghan medical students over MBBS registration
articles.summary:
LAHORE: The Lahore High Court (LHC) on Friday issued notices to the Pakistan Medical and Dental Council (PMDC) and other respondents on a petition filed by five Afghan medical students seeking registration to sit their first professional MBBS examination in January.

The petitioners — Forough Dihqanpur, Shahira Sharif, Zahra Nabawi, Faiza Noori and Shabana Rahimi — are enrolled in the first year of the MBBS programme at Sheikh Khalifa Bin Zayed Al Nahyan Medical and Dental College, Lahore, under the Allama Muhammad Iqbal Scholarship Programme run by the Higher Education Commission (HEC).

Advocate Asad Jamal, counsel for the petitioners, informed the court that they joined the college on April 6 after undergoing a multi-stage selection process conducted by the HEC. They were subsequently issued student cards and bona fide certificates, he added.

He argued that registration is a mandatory prerequisite for appearing in the first professional examination, scheduled to be held from Jan 4 to 11, 2027.

He pointed out that the college has asked the University of Health Sciences (UHS) to open its registration portal for the students, but the university has declined, saying the PMDC has not permitted such admissions for the 2025-26 session.
