The counsel further said that the PMDC subsequently approved the placement of 68 nominated Afghan students in public-sector colleges beyond the approved intake.

Relying on Regulations 6 and 7 of the PMDC’s 2025 admissions regulations, he argued that the affiliating university was required to verify and register admitted students and that UHS could not withhold a decision indefinitely.

He asked the court to declare the inaction unlawful and direct the respondents to complete the petitioners’ registration. He also sought provisional registration in the interim to enable them to sit the examination.

However, Justice Asim Hafeez issued notices to the respondents, directing them to submit their replies by Dec 1 to the main petition and the application for interim relief.

The petition named the PMDC, UHS, the Punjab government, the college, the federal government, the health ministry and the HEC as respondents.

In September, the LHC suspended the operation of PMDC directives ordering Afghan medical students to return to Afghanistan. The order came after 13 Afghan students, including seven women and six men, enrolled at different medical colleges in Lahore, challenged the directives.

The PMDC barred medical and dental colleges from admitting or placing Afghan students for the current academic session and said those already enrolled in such programmes were required to return to Afghanistan.

In October, the LHC extended its stay against the expulsion and deportation of Afghan medical students and granted the PMDC more time to submit its reply.

Separately, the Peshawar High Court (PHC) temporarily restrained the deportation of 86 Afghan students enrolled in public-sector medical colleges in the province and allowed them to continue their studies.

articles.title: Who Controls America’s AI Chokepoint?
articles.summary:
On November 23, Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, less than two weeks after his resignation amid a controversy stoked by national-security concerns. Huang admitted to having had multiple affairs, including with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Nonetheless, US President Donald Trump personally intervened with the company’s board to secure his return.

The US political establishment’s response was swift. Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton is calling the scandal “Supergate,” owing to the potent mix of national-security concerns, corruption, insider trading, and market manipulation. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries sees Huang’s reinstatement as “indefensible” and is promising a congressional investigation.

On the Republican side, former House Speaker Newt Gingrich has called for an investigation, and Senator Tom Cotton is pushing for stronger export controls on chips. Senator Kevin Cramer has warned that while Nvidia’s board has assumed the legal and reputational risks of reinstating Huang, the national-security risks fall on the American military and public.

The episode exposes a paradox at the heart of American technological hegemony. American AI dominance gives the US leverage over China, but the US economy’s dependence on Nvidia has created a second, domestic chokepoint.

Owing to Nvidia’s strategic importance, the US has a powerful incentive to protect the company’s leadership and commercial success, even though it also has a duty to regulate Nvidia and safeguard national security. Put another way, Nvidia gives the US leverage over China; but the geopolitical power that Nvidia makes possible gives it leverage over the US government.

Nvidia’s power rests on its chips and software, which are essential to AI. The US has the power to restrict foreign access to American technology, but such restrictions obviously affect Nvidia’s bottom line.

In April 2025, the US restricted exports of Nvidia’s H20 chips to China on national-security grounds, resulting in a $4.5 billion write-off in unsold chips and associated commitments. Three months later, the Trump administration reversed course, with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick arguing that keeping Chinese companies dependent on American technology served US strategic interests. The US was now defending some chip sales to China as a way to preserve American technological dominance, despite having restricted them on security grounds.

The H20 reversal was not the only decision to draw scrutiny. On November 19, the House Foreign Affairs Committee revealed that, by May 11, 2026, the Commerce Department had approved licenses for roughly 880,000 advanced Nvidia and AMD chips destined for Chinese companies, some of which were later flagged by the Defense Department for alleged military ties.

But even when the US prohibits sales, chips can reach China through third countries. US authorities are now investigating whether the Singapore-based compute provider Megaspeed illegally diverted Nvidia chips to China. This is the company at the center of the current scandal. Huang had an extramarital affair with one of its top executives, Alice Huang (no relation), who is alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence.

Some US lawmakers are also questioning whether Nvidia’s close contacts with US Commerce Department officials influenced its investigation into Megaspeed, which was added to the US export blacklist only on November 23. Taken together, these controversies raise questions about whether the US government can independently regulate a company it considers indispensable to American technological leadership.

Nvidia’s influence is not simply a matter of corporate lobbying or political access. American technological hegemony rests on far-reaching international networks of customers, developers, manufacturers, and commercial partners. These intangible assets are what generate profits for Nvidia and geopolitical leverage for the US. Yet restricting access arguably can encourage the development of alternatives. In an August 2026 securities filing, Nvidia claimed that its exclusion from much of China’s compute market had helped competitors expand their customer bases and networks of software developers.

Nvidia’s strongest argument against export controls is not simply that they cost the company money. It is that shutting Chinese customers out of American technology may strengthen Chinese competitors and eventually erode America’s leverage over China. Yet allowing those sales also gives China access to the computing power that US restrictions are meant to deny.

Preserving American technological hegemony requires distinguishing between the national interest and the commercial interests of the corporations on which American power depends. Export controls should be imposed when national-security concerns warrant them, without privileged political access influencing those decisions. Investigations into possible violations must remain free from corporate influence. And Congress should scrutinize these decisions even when doing so threatens the interests of firms that the US government considers indispensable.

This is the deeper paradox of America’s AI chokepoint. We have just witnessed how private corporate power can constrain and influence what should be independent national-security decisions. The two forms of power reinforce one another, but they do not necessarily serve the same interests. The more indispensable American technology becomes to the world, the more politically indispensable its corporate owners become to the US economy and government. American technological hegemony strengthens the private corporations on which it depends, even as they become harder for the US to govern.

This article was originally published on Project Syndicate and has been reproduced here with permission.

articles.title: Making waves: Pakistani woman breaking jet ski barriers
articles.summary:
Gliding across the waters of Kallar Kahar Lake, instructor Farhat Jabeen grips the handlebars of her jet ski, executing sharp turns and sending spray flying into the air.

Clinging on and nestled in front of her, a woman passenger looked thrilled as Jabeen deftly manoeuvred the jet ski.

This photograph taken on October 24, 2026 shows students wearing life jackets arriving for a boat ride across the waters of Kallar Kahar Lake in Pakistan’s Chakwal district. —AFP

“A woman should be brave,” Jabeen, 35, told AFP on the shores of the scenic lake, 125 kilometres (78 miles) from Islamabad.

The mother-of-four has spent the past two years taking women on jet ski tours, as well as riding with other instructors.

Jabeen’s arrival has been transformative for women travellers and thrill-seekers like Qamar-un-Nisa, who only gave her first name.

“Appointing a female instructor is a very admirable step,” said the 50-year-old school principal, who was visiting the lake with her students.

“Her skill was excellent. I really enjoyed it a lot,” she added after a ride with Jabeen.

Jabeen told AFP that she was “a little afraid” when she started the job.

“It was very difficult when I first came here for this job. Many objections were raised about me,” she said.

This photograph taken on October 24, 2026 shows visitors gather for jet ski and boat rides at the Kallar Kahar Lake in Pakistan’s Chakwal district. —AFP

“Some said ‘You’re a woman, how will you work among men?’” she added.

Under the guidance of a senior instructor, Jabeen spent a month mastering the jet ski’s controls and safety procedures.

She works up to 11 hours a day now, inspecting boat engines, cleaning equipment, and stitching damaged life jackets before embarking on dozens of rides.

‘Nothing to be afraid of’

Despite the busy schedule, Jabeen said she is enjoying the work.

“When I go home and meet my children in the evening, when I see them, all my tiredness goes away,” she added.

Jabeen’s appointment by regional tourism authorities as a jet ski guide has unlocked recreational access for women visitors, said instructor Tariq Mahmood.

This photograph taken on October 24, 2026 shows visitors riding a boat in the waters of Kallar Kahar Lake in Pakistan’s Chakwal district.—AFP

Ever since Jabeen joined, “it has become completely easy for us to send women to ride” with her, he told AFP.

Her arrival has removed barriers for women visitors, said Muhammad Abbas Ashraf, manager of Kallar Kahar’s Tourism Development Corporation.

“When we first introduced the jet skis, women who visited here faced difficulties, because we could not have them sit with us and ride,” he told AFP.

Jabeen encouraged women to be “brave” and not be afraid of seeking out employment.

“Women should step out of the house and do some kind of work,” she said.

“There is nothing to be afraid of,” she added.

Header image: Farhat Jabeen (rear) takes a visitor for a spin on a jet ski across the waters of Kallar Kahar Lake in Chakwal district.—AFP

articles.title: AJK rolls out Rs15bn 100-day action plan
articles.summary:
• Programme focuses on health, education, transport and tourism; long-term projects extend beyond timeframe
• 70 mobile hospital units, 75 electric buses and five Daanish Schools among key initiatives
• PM Gillani says govt exploring options to complete stalled Jagran-II hydropower project

MUZAFFARABAD: The PML-N-led Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) government on Thursday unveiled a Rs15 billion, 100-day action plan, pro­mising improvements in health­care, education, transport, tou­rism and civic infrastructure.

At a press briefing, five cabinet members outlined immediate initiatives as well as long-term projects extending bey­ond six months.

Health and Population Wel­fare Minister Dr Mustafa Bas­hir Abbasi said the package aimed to accelerate development and provide basic amenities at the grassroots level. Under the Sehat Karwan initiative, 70 mobile hospital units would serve remote areas, while the Essential Medicines Programme would ensure the availability of life-saving drugs, emergency care and dialysis facilities at major hospitals.

He said the government would also establish 20 model basic health units (BHUs) and 10 model rural health centres (RHCs), besides setting up operating theatres and nursery units at tehsil headquarters. District and divisional hospitals would be upgraded.

AJK prime minister Iftikhar Gillani speaks on the floor of the Legislative Assembly on Thursday. — Photo by author

Longer-term healthcare projects incl­uded catheterisation laboratories in Kotli, Rawal­akot and Bhimber, stroke centres in Muzaffarabad, Kotli and Mir­pur, and the Muhammad Nawaz Sharif Modern Cardiac Hospital in Bagh.

Education and jobs

Education Minister Sardar Umair Naeem said out-of-school children would be enrolled and provided free education under the Darsgah project. A cellular biometric attendance system, designed to work without internet connectivity, would also be introduced to curb absenteeism.

The plan included constructing five Daanish Schools across AJK and establishing a Daanish University in Muzaf­farabad. The government would also launch scholarship progra­mmes, distribute 5,000 laptops on merit in the first phase of the AJK Laptop Progra­mme and offer interest-free loans under the Naujawan Rozgar Scheme.

An Asaan Karobar initiative would introduce a one-window operation and regulatory reforms to facilitate investors.

Transport and civic facilities

Minister for Forests and Wildlife Waqar Ahmad Noor said 75 electric buses would be introduced in seven AJK cities under the Kashmir Express Service.

Road resurfacing in Poonch, Bhimber and Kotli was also planned. Rescue 1122 units were being established in Neelum and Bagh.

The Suthra Kashmir campaign would be launched across all 10 district headquarters, alongside urban beautification projects in Muzaffarabad, Mirpur and Rawalakot.

Longer-term civic projects included landfill sites across the three divisions, a slaughterhouse and fruit and vegetable market in Muzaffarabad, and an urban drainage and flood protection scheme in the capital.

Mr Noor said the AJK One Portal would bring e-stamping, e-tendering, e-procurement and e-payment services together on a single platform, complemented by a Prime Minister’s Complaint Cell.

Tourism schemes

Minister for Industries, Commerce and Tourism Chaudhry Abdul Rehman Arain said the Discover AJK and Clean Tourism Azad Kashmir initiatives would focus on eco-tourism, hiking and adventure trails. The government also planned to revamp 26 guest houses and 32 tuck shops under a public-private partnership and build highway rest areas along the Kohala-Muzaffarabad and Azad Pattan-Rawalakot roads.

Other initiatives included interest-free housing loans for homeless people under the Apna Ghar scheme, mass weddings for deserving women through the Dhee Rani programme, and extensive tree plantation along highways under the Sarsabz Shahrah drive.

Jagran-II project

Separately, Prime Minister Iftikhar Gillani told the AJK Legislative Assembly that his government was exploring options to complete the 48-megawatt Jagran-II hydropower project in Neelum Valley, where work has remained stalled due to multiple factors.

Responding to a call-attention notice by PPP lawmaker Mian Abdul Waheed, he said 93 per cent of the project had been completed, with only 7pc of the work remaining.

He attributed the delay to the Covid-19 pandemic, activities of the now-proscribed Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) and Operation Bunyanun Marsoos, during which the Chinese contractor suspended work and demobilised its workforce.

The company was now reluctant to return to the site, he said, adding that the government had held discussions with relevant institutions to find a way forward. Electrical equipment was already available at the site, while negotiations on outstanding matters were underway.

Mr Gillani said completion of the project remained among the government’s priorities and would boost electricity generation and revenue for AJK.

Published in Dawn, November 27th, 2026

articles.title: Cricket Australia widens 'Sandpapergate' forum to 2017-2018 Ashes
articles.summary:
Cricket Australia (CA) widened its independent “Sandpapergate” forum on Friday to include the preceding Ashes series against England, while pledging to make the findings and its response public.

The governing body has ruled out reopening its investigation into the explosive 2018 ball-tampering scandal in South Africa that blew up again this month.

Instead, it proposed a forum for players, coaches and staff on the tour to share their versions of events.

In a surprise development, the terms of reference released on Friday broadened to include “ball-management practices” during the 2017-2018 season, including the home Ashes series which Australia won 4-0.

The hosts’ consistent ability to get reverse swing in that series had England’s bowlers scratching their heads.

In the wake of the South Africa fallout, England great Alastair Cook, who was part of the Ashes side, was asked whether the team suspected Australia of ball-tampering.

“Yes a little bit, certainly in Perth when the outfield was wet with rain they got the ball-reversing,” he said.

The issue went no further.

Experienced senior counsel Fiona McLeod will lead the forum, which will be open for six weeks and is voluntary.

Players’ accounts, which can be written or verbal, will be confidential.

She will investigate the Ashes, all four Tests of the South Africa tour, the events of March 24, 2018, when Cameron Bancroft was caught with sandpaper, and the conduct of the 2018 Cricket Australia probe.

McLeod will provide a report detailing the principal themes and her recommendations.

But what players say will not be published, no new sanctions will come out of it and she is not charged with determining any individual responsibility.

“This is an opportunity to provide their accounts in a safe environment and to provide the CA board with relevant information including about the events of that tour and resultant investigation,” said Cricket Australia interim Chairman David Boon.

“We are acutely aware of the enormous toll the renewed focus on this tour eight years ago has had on those involved and their welfare remains our main priority.

“This forum is the best opportunity for people to speak and be heard, and for CA to listen and learn,” added Boon.

“Publishing the report in full is part of our commitment to transparency, and to be open with cricket fans about what we learn. It is also very important to understand that it will not seek to sanction or recriminate.”

Reignited

The issue was reignited this month by Usman Khawaja, who claimed in his autobiography that the whole team knew about the plot to alter the ball with sandpaper during the third Test in Cape Town.

He also claimed the practice was used in the second Test at Port Elizabeth.

A CA probe at the time concluded only skipper Steve Smith, his deputy David Warner and Bancroft were in the know. They were sent home in disgrace and banned for between nine and 12 months.

Khawaja’s version of events was backed by Warner and Bancroft, but strenuously denied by current captain Pat Cummins and fellow bowlers Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood.

The bowling group at the time — which also included Nathan Lyon — released a joint statement in 2021 denying any involvement.

CA last weekend said Cummins had their “unanimous support” to remain Test captain and rejected any suggestion his integrity had been compromised, while praising him for changing the culture of the team.

Australia are preparing for four Tests against New Zealand, starting in Perth on Dec 9.

articles.title: Death toll from Baloch Colony building collapse in Karachi rises to six
articles.summary:
KARACHI: Death toll from the collapse of an under-construction six-storey building near Karachi’s Baloch Colony area rose to six on Friday after rescue workers recovered two more bodies from the rubble.

On Wednesday, three people were killed and 14 others injured when an under-construction building — reportedly being constructed illegally on a residential plot — collapsed. Another body was recovered on Thursday, taking the death toll to four.

A Rescue 1122 spokesperson said the operation to recover bodies was underway.

“Rescue 1122 has located the bodies of more people trapped beneath the rubble,” the spokesperson added.

Sindh Local Government Secretary Waseem Shamshad, who also served as director general of the Sindh Building Control Authority (SBCA), was removed from both posts on Thursday on the directives of Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah following the incident.

The CM ordered sweeping action over the incident while chairing a high-level meeting, further issuing directives for the removal of East Deputy Commissioner Nasrullah Abbasi, as well as Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) East Zubair Sheikh over “negligence”, a statement issued by the CM Office said.

In addition to the removal of the three officials, CM Murad further issued directives for the suspension of 16 SBCA officials and the initiation of an inquiry against them.

He directed the police to “immediately” arrest the building’s owner, Salman Tahir, and the builder, Zeeshan.

Moreover, he instructed that the building’s architect and structural engineer be included in the incident’s investigation to determine whether the construction complied with approved plans, building regulations and safety standards.

14 ‘illegal’ buildings in KAEHS to be demolished

The KDA’s Additional Deputy DG Farhan Kaiser visited the site on Thursday and told the media that their first priority was to remove the debris. He said that under the directions of the Sindh CM and LG minister, “illegal buildings” were being sealed across the metropolis.

He said that so far, 14 buildings had been sealed in the KAEHS after the building collapse and would be demolished in a second phase of the operation.

Kaiser added that it was the responsibility of the residents to report illegal buildings in their respective areas, and vowed to take action against the builders and owners of these buildings.

Members of the Chief Minister Inspection Team (CMIT) Bilal Memon and Anwar Shar visited the scene and collected samples of the material used in the construction of the building for investigation purposes.

Rehabilitation secretary Rafiq Mustafa Shaikh, SBCA DG Abid Saleem, Rescue 1122 DG Brig. (retd) Wajid Sibghatullah Mahar and Rescue 1122 COO Dr. Abid Jalaluddin Shaikh also visited the site and supervised the rescue operation.

FIR registered

A first information report (FIR) of the incident was registered at the Tipu Sultan police station on Wednesday, on the complaint of an official of the Sindh Local Government Department.

The FIR, seen by Dawn, invoked Sections 302 (intentional murder), 119 (public servant concealing design to commit offence), 427 (mischief causing damage), 337-H(1) (hurt caused by rash or negligent act), 109 (abetment) and 34 (acts done by several persons in furtherance of common intention) of the Pakistan Penal Code.

The building’s four owners — including Salman Tahir whose arrest the Sindh CM has ordered — its builder, architect, structural engineer and its contractors have been nominated in the FIR.

According to the FIR, the complainant alleged that poor-quality material was being used in the construction of the building. He claimed that the suspects, in collusion with the officials of various government departments, had been involved in constructing additional structures and not complying with the building’s approved plan.

This was why the building collapsed around 1pm, the complainant alleged.

Police have arrested four of the suspects, including one of the owners, Saad Tahir, and three contractors, who were produced before the judicial magistrate (south) today.

The judge granted police five-day physical remand of the suspects.

articles.title: Woman hurt in acid attack in North Karachi
articles.summary:
KARACHI: A woman social worker was injured in an acid attack in North Karachi, officials said on Thursday.

Central SSP Dr Mohammed Imran Khan told Dawn that the woman, identified as Nazia Mohammed Ali, 38, was riding a motorcycle and passing by a public school in Sector 11-C 2 in North Karachi when a man attacked her with acid and fled.

She suffered burns and was taken to hospital for treatment.

As per initial investigation, the woman disclosed that she is a social worker and lives along with her family/husband in government quarters in Sector 11-A of North Karachi.

She named Tabish Ali as the person who threw acid on her, stating that a few days ago she had recorded a statement against his father in a court of law.

She believed that due to her statement in court, the man threw acid on her when she was going on her motorbike towards Nagan Chowrangi.

The senior officer said owing to wearing a helmet and a jacket, the victim managed to avoid serious wounds and received minor injuries on her back.

Later, the police carried out a raid and arrested suspect Tabish.

Published in Dawn, November 27th, 2026

articles.title: Greed, official negligence and the collapse
articles.summary:
KARACHI: For residents of Karachi Administration Cooperative Housing Society, the rubble of the six-storey collapsed building represents far more than a violation of the city’s building regulations. They believe the tragedy reflects a wider construction system in which the builder mafia, the indifference of relevant authorities and the misuse of official powers have put human lives at risk.

They added that the collapse had once again exposed how the rule of law and institutional accountability in the city had been reduced to little more than official claims.

According to them, after every tragedy, officials arrive at the scene, issue statements shifting responsibility onto one another and announce investigations. With the passage of time, however, public attention fades, while the question of who should be held responsible remains unanswered.

One resident, expressing anger over the incident, asked how a building approved for ground-plus-one construction could have reached six storeys. Such a structure, he pointed out, could not have been built overnight. Construction had continued in broad daylight for months, yet no relevant authority had considered it necessary to halt the work and take action in accordance with the law. Now, following the collapse, everyone was offering explanations to evade responsibility.

Another resident said that, following the incident, government officials, the Karachi mayor and ministers had maintained that the Sindh Building Control Authority (SBCA) had approved only ground-plus-one construction for the building, but that the owners or builders had added further floors in violation of the approved plan. According to the authorities, when the SBCA ordered construction to stop, the owners obtained a stay order from court.

Residents say structure approved for ground-plus-one construction could not have risen to six storeys without authorities’ knowledge

He asked whether the relevant authority had challenged the stay order before a higher court.

An elderly resident said the tragedy was the result of greed and profiteering, which had brought the city’s institutions to ruin. In his view, investigations, statements and mutual accusations would continue for a few days, with every institution trying to shift responsibility onto another and absolve itself. Ultimately, however, no one would be held accountable or identified as responsible.

Had the institutions genuinely been fulfilling their responsibilities, effective measures would have been taken following earlier incidents, including the building collapses in Lyari. Had the protection of citizens’ lives and property been a priority for the authorities, they would not now be facing renewed demands for accountability after yet another tragedy.

Residents appealed to the authorities to move beyond announcements and temporary crackdowns and take sustained, indiscriminate action against illegal construction across Karachi.

They said there was still time to prevent the city from reaching the brink of disaster, but this required past tragedies to be treated not as fleeting news events but as opportunities to put things right.

Bungalows replaced by flats

Speaking to Dawn, another resident said that over the past decade there had been a sharp rise in the conversion of bungalows approved for ground-plus-one construction into multiple portions and flats in the admin society.

In his view, this trend had not only placed considerable pressure on the area’s population and residential infrastructure but had also created new opportunities for profiteering through violations of building regulations and alleged collusion with the relevant authorities.

He explained that one common practice was for builders to approach owners of older bungalows and offer them up to twice the property’s prevailing market value. Attracted by the substantial sums on offer, owners would sell their homes, after which builders would demolish the properties or replace them with multi-storey residential buildings. In this way, several times more flats could be built and sold on a single plot than had previously been possible.

The resident, however, alleged that the lucrative business was also facilitated by the patronage and collusion of certain officials in the relevant institutions.

If the authorities discharged their duties in accordance with the law, he argued, no builder should be able to erect a building that exceeds the approved plan.

Another resident said that the land of the society was known to be marshy, making it essential to assess the nature of the soil, its load-bearing capacity and the strength of foundations before undertaking any new construction. Proper soil testing was therefore vital.

He questioned how the relevant authorities verified whether a building’s foundations and structural framework were actually being developed in accordance with the soil report and its technical recommendations, even when a soil test had been conducted. Completing paperwork, he said, was not enough without on-site monitoring of construction standards and technical requirements.

Published in Dawn, November 27th, 2026

articles.title: Big fat wedding in India draws 400,000 guests
articles.summary:
PATNA: Some 400,000 guests attended a wedding hosted by a politician in India’s poorest state, choking roads and sending spectators scrambling up electricity pylons for a glimpse of the lavish celebrations.

Anant Singh, a six-time lawmaker who faces dozens of criminal cases including murder charges, invited villagers, political allies and VIPs to his daughter’s wedding in the eastern state of Bihar on Wednesday.

The scale was staggering even by the standards of India’s famed extravagant weddings that last for days.

Guests were treated to 500,000 pieces of traditional sweets and a vegetarian feast prepared by an army of 500 chefs and cooks, Singh’s confidant Munna Singh said.

The event in Anant Singh’s native village of Nadawan drew such huge crowds that roads leading to the venue ground to a standstill. One politician, unable to force his way through the traffic chaos, abandoned his car and rode a tractor across farm fields to reach the venue, the Times of India reported.

Organisers built five helipads to ferry in VIP guests, with each helicopter touchdown whipping up clouds of dust that swept through crowds of curious onlookers.

Images published by the Press Trust of India news agency showed thousands jostling for a glimpse of the sprawling venue, while others perched precariously atop trees and electricity towers. Organisers were forced to postpone a horse race as part of the celebrations after some 100,000 people turned up to watch the spectacle involving 200 horses.

Elaborate flower arrangements featuring blooms imported from China and a fireworks display also enthralled guests. The bride arrived in a luxury BMW, while the groom travelled in a convoy of around 200 cars.

More than 10 million weddings take place in India every year, feeding an industry estimated to be worth $40-$50 billion, according to KPMG.

Published in Dawn, November 27th, 2026

articles.title: Constitutional liability
articles.summary:
EVERY out-of-school child is a living reminder to the state of its constitutional commitment, and these reminders have been increasing since the inception of Pakistan. Now these living reminders have crossed 25 million.

Seventy-nine years after independence, Pakistan is still struggling to fulfil one of the most fundamental responsibilities of a modern state, ensuring that every child receives an education. A nuclear state has produced generations without an education system capable of accommodating them.

Pakistan’s failure to educate its children is not a recent phenomenon, nor did the constitutional responsibility of the state begin with Article 25-A in 2010. The commitment dates back to the country’s early constitutional history. The 1956 Constitution explicitly recognised the state’s responsibility to eliminate illiteracy and provide free and compulsory primary education. The 1962 Constitution retained this commitment. The 1973 Constitution went further through Article 37(b), requiring the state to remove illiteracy and provide free and compulsory secondary education within the minimum possible period.

The insertion of Article 25-A through the 18th Constitutional Amendment in 2010 was therefore not the beginning of the state’s educational responsibility. It was an attempt to transform a longstanding constitutional aspiration into an enforceable fundamental right. Yet, decades of constitutional commitments have failed to produce universal educational access.

From the promise of compulsory primary education in 1956 to the guarantee of education for every child aged 5-16 in 2010, the state has repeatedly renewed its commitment without ensuring its fulfilment.

Every child denied education represents lost human capital.

The question is why, despite repeated constitutional commitments, successive governments have failed to ensure that every child has access to a school. It seems every government has also failed to realise that every child denied education represents lost human capital and another potential victim of intergenerational poverty.

A country cannot build a knowledge economy, strengthen democratic institutions, or achieve sustainable development while leaving millions of its children disconnected from education and the opportunities that accompany it. The children are not the liability. The liability is created by a system that allows millions of children to grow up without education, skills, opportunities, or meaningful participation in society.

Unesco data indicates that Pakistan has a substantially higher proportion of primary-school-age children out of school compared with India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, the Maldives, and Sri Lanka. While these countries have made considerable progress in expanding educational access, Pakistan continues to struggle with millions of children excluded from the education system.

This regional disparity suggests that the crisis is not merely a consequence of poverty or population growth, but also reflects persistent failures of educational planning, governance, investment and political commitment.

Bringing over 25m out-of-school children into the education system is not merely a matter of an enrolment campaign. It requires an enormous expansion of educational infrastructure, human resources and recurring public expenditure.

Assuming 40 students per classroom, Pakistan would need approximately 628,750 classrooms to accommodate these children. At an illustrative staffing ratio of 1.2 teachers per classroom, the country would require approximately 754,500 additional teachers. If these teachers were recruited at the initial BPS-14 pay of Rs27,060 per mon­th, the annual salary bill alone would be roughly Rs245 billion. This estim­ate covers basic salaries only, excludes allowances, pensi­o­­ns, and teacher tr­­a­ining. The capital cost of constructing schools with basic amenities, as well as recurring administrative expenditure, would certainly be a substantially higher fiscal commitment.

The scale of the challenge is enormous, so is the cost of inaction. Pakistan’s reported education expenditure of Rs962bn in FY2024-25 was already insufficient to meet the needs of its existing education system. The question is therefore not simply how much it would cost to educate the excluded children, but why a country that has constitutionally guaranteed education to every child has failed to develop a sustainable financing mechanism to fulfil that guarantee.

A constitutional right cannot remain confined to the pages of a constitution, nor can the state continue to measure its educational achievements through policies announced, schools inaugurated, or budgets allocated. The real measure of its commitment must be the child sitting in a classroom, learning to read, write, think, and participate in society.

The writer is a social development practitioner.

Published in Dawn, November 27th, 2026

articles.title: More credit, fewer women
articles.summary:
IMAGINE Sakina, up at the crack of dawn to go see her precious Billo, a fine cow her father had given her. This would be Sakina’s 30th day selling Billo’s milk to a nearby farm owner who wanted good milk for his young children. She was excited to get paid. She got ready to head out, feeling like a businesswoman.

Three years later, Sakina has four animals. She feeds them, looks after them and gets the milk ready for collection. She knows when a cow is giving less milk, when feed becomes heavier on the pocket and when it makes sense to buy another animal.

Her 40-plus customers know how rich the milk is. But ask them where it comes from and they’ll tell you it’s from Kareem bhai, the doodh wala. Kareem is Sakina’s husband. He delivers the milk and his name is also the one on the ledger that she has maintained all these years.

Sakina is sure she could manage 10 animals. She decides to start with two more cows and goes to a bank for a loan. That’s when the name in the ledger becomes a problem. She has years of milk sales to show the bank. She’s kept the records herself but they are in Kareem’s name. The bank decides against giving her a loan.

Pakistan’s agricultural lending ambitions must look beyond the size of the portfolio.

The State Bank of Pakistan’s Banking on Equality figures show that agricultural financing to women rose from Rs44 billion in 2021 to Rs105bn in 2025 in nominal terms. In those same years, the number of women agricultural borrowers fell from 436,000 to 377,000, a decline of about 14 per cent. The data doesn’t show why fewer women borrowed or who received the additional financing. Yet the amounts lent more than doubled while the number of women borrowers fell.

That matters for Banking on Equality 2026. The policy asks banks and development finance institutions to aim to double their financing portfolios for women and qualifying women-owned or women-led businesses across priority sectors by the end of 2028. A bank can grow its loan book by lending more to people it already knows. Reaching a woman like Sakina takes a closer look at who’s been running the business all these years.

Agriculture accounts for roughly 23pc of Pakistan’s GDP, and livestock makes up nearly two-thirds of the sector’s value added. The Labour Force Survey 2024-25 tells us that about six in 10 employed women work in agriculture, forestry or fishing. What’s harder to see is who gets paid for that work and who decides how the money is spent.

Take three women who look after cattle. One is paid a wage. Another tends the family’s animals and earns no income of her own. The third runs a dairy business like Sakina’s. To decide if a loan makes sense, a bank needs to understand how each woman earns her living and how much of that income she can use to repay it.

Sakina’s milk delivery records could give the bank a place to start. Then come the questions she already asks herself. How much does feed cost? What happens to her income when a cow stops producing milk? What does she already owe? Banking on Equality encourages banks to consider evidence like this when assessing women-owned and women-led businesses.

There’s one question the loan officer needs to ask a woman like Sakina directly. When the buyer pays for the milk, who can use that money? A buyer could put the supplier account in her name tomorrow and still hand the cash to Kareem. If the loan is in her name, the bank will expect her to pay it back. Can she decide where to sell the milk and set aside enough for the next instalment?

In Kenya, CGAP documented how Agrilife and New Kenya Cooperative Creameries used digital delivery records to help dairy suppliers get advances against milk they’d already delivered. A separate study of two Kenyan dairy cooperatives found that farmers short of cash or facing uninsured health expenses shifted sales towards buyers who paid on the spot.

Financing a cow means working out what it might produce in the future. And records kept in a farmer group’s name may tell a bank very little about what one woman sold. Could we use the records buyers already keep to show what women like Sakina actually sell and earn?

A provincial livestock department could bring milk buyers and banks together to work with women who already run dairy businesses and want to expand. Ask buyers to record what each woman delivers and what she’s paid. If she wants to be paid into an account, let her choose one she can operate herself. If the money is paid in cash or through several buyers, the department maintains a record. With her consent, the bank can use those records alongside its usual checks and see whether they change its decision.

After a year, we should know whether banks approved applications they would previously have declined and whether more women received payments directly. We can follow the loan cycles for longer too. Could the women keep up with repayments? After feed, veterinary bills and instalments, did they have more income left? Could they decide what to do with it?

SBP can do something now. Put the amount lent and the number of individual women who borrowed on the same page. Show how many took out a formal loan for the first time and where borrower numbers are falling.

Sakina knows the business and what it will take to grow it. She went to the bank to get support but came back without a loan or a clear way forward.

When the banks report back in 2028, we should look at how many women like Sakina got far enough to have someone sit down with them and assess their potential for growth. Sakina may still look at the instalment and decide to wait. But that should be her decision to make.

The writer leads the women’s economic and digital inclusion portfolio at Karandaaz Pakistan.

Published in Dawn, November 27th, 2026

articles.title: Makers step up rollout of electric bikes
articles.summary:
KARACHI: Amid the falling trend in petrol prices, a growing number of stakeholders have stepped up efforts to test their new electric bikes in the market.

But some assemblers are still enjoying robust sales of petrol-run bikes. For instance, Atlas Honda posted record sales of 173,152 units last month, jacking up the aggregate to 643,561 units in 4MFY27 from 505,269 units. It was followed by United Motorcycle, with sales rising to 82,474 from 56,519 in the same period.

Millat Tractors Ltd (MTL) is set to launch its EV two-wheelers on Nov 29. It has already designated its dealers and production is underway.

According to Topline Securities, MTL said at a corporate briefing that it plans to introduce five lithium-ion-powered models, including bikes and scooters.

Millat Industrial, a subsidiary of MTL, will manufacture the electric two-wheelers, with an annual production capacity of 250,000 units.

ICMAP urges focus on domestic EV industry instead of subsidising purchase

Initially, five or six variants of both bike and scooty will be launched.

Air Link Communication Limited had launched its AirV EV bikes on Nov 4 with an annual production capacity of 100,000 at Sundar Green Special Economic Zone.

The management plans to scale up output gradually and has set a target of importing 10,000-15,000 units and will place further orders based on market response.

Topline Securities, while revealing this information from Air Link’s corporate briefing, said the prices of its bikes would range between Rs200,000 and Rs500,000. The firm does not intend to sell the product on credit.

Subsidy on purchase of bikes

The Punjab government has decided to provide a subsidy of Rs50,000 for the purchase of electric bikes, while the Pakistan Accelerated Vehicle Electrification programme (PAVE) has also offered a subsidy of Rs80,000.

Mohammad Sabir Shaikh, an expert on bikes, said assemblers are testing their luck in the electric market. The current prices of EV bikes range between Rs170,000 and Rs700,000.

The sale of EV bikes has hit over 300,000 over the past 12 months, with Punjab leading other regions in the number of units sold. The Karachi market is showing a moderate growth, Sabir Shaikh added.

Urgency of transition

According to an analysis by the Institute of Cost and Management Accountants of Pakistan (ICMAP), titled “Can PAVE shift Pakistan from EV adoption to EV industry”, the urgency of this transition is underscored by volatile fuel prices.

The analysis observes that the country’s electric vehicle transition should move beyond subsidising vehicle purchases towards building a domestic EV industry, or risk replacing dependence on imported petroleum with dependence on imported electric vehicles, batteries and related technologies.

Under the New Energy Vehicle (NEV) Policy 2025-30, it is envisaged that Pakistan Accelerated Vehicle Electri­fication Programme (PAVE) will accelerate electric mobility through subsidies, financing and vehicle distribution.

The programme’s first two phases envisage the distribution of approximately 116,000 electric bikes. Despite the latest decline, the price has remained almost 20 per cent higher than at the beginning of March, illustrating the country’s vulnerability to international petroleum market volatility, import costs and foreign-exchange pressures.

The ICMAP advises that PAVE should be positioned not merely as a vehicle subsidy scheme, but as a strategic economic instrument linking energy security, household affordability and industrial competitiveness.

However, the analysis highlights the gap between generating demand and translating it into vehicles on the road. During the initial phase, banks received 44,689 applications by May 31, but they processed only 9,889, or merely 22pc, of these.

Approval was granted in just 4,075 cases, representing just 9pc of the total number of applications, while 34,800, or 78pc, remained unprocessed.

Financing provided at that stage amounted to Rs143 million, while 5,409 vehicles were reported as distributed, the analysis said.

Published in Dawn, November 27th, 2026

articles.title: Amid talk of new provinces, Sindh CM announces consultations on local govt empowerment
articles.summary:
• Forms body to meet opposition; says next local govt elections to be held on time

KARACHI: Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah on Thursday announced a comprehensive consultation process for a new local government law and formed a two-member ministerial committee to hold talks with all stakeholders and submit its report within three months.

The announcement comes against the backdrop of talk of creating new provinces and administrative units across the country, including in Sindh — a demand that the Pakistan Peoples Party has been vociferously opposing.

Addressing a press conference at the CM House, the chief minister said that the aim was to strengthen local bodies, give them greater autonomy and improve their financial and administrative capacity.

Flanked by provincial ministers Sharjeel Memon, Nasir Shah, Saeed Ghani and Ziaul Hassan Lanjar and Karachi Mayor Murtaza Wahab, the chief minister added that the committee would consult political parties, civil society and other relevant stakeholders.

The committee comprising ministers Syed Nasir Hussain Shah and Ziaul Hassan Lanjar would start work next week, contact all stakeholders and present its recommendations following comprehensive consultations within three months, he added.

“The proposed legislation will be made through amendments to the existing local government law, while the next local government elections will be held on time,” he added.

The chief minister said that the province had held elections even in difficult political and security conditions.

“We want to make local bodies more empowered. How they will be empowered will be decided through consultation with all stakeholders,” he said, adding that the government also wanted to strengthen the finances of local councils through the Provincial Finance Commission.

Answering a question about a proposed referendum for the creation of new provinces, the chief minister said that no one had spoken to him on the matter, nor had he been asked to initiate any such process.

“The Sindh Assembly has already rejected proposals to create new provinces within Sindh’s boundaries by a two-thirds majority,” he added.

Published in Dawn, November 27th, 2026

articles.title: PHC orders Rs10m compensation for man imprisoned for a decade without trial
articles.summary:
PESHAWAR: A single-member Peshawar High Court bench has ordered the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government to pay Rs10 million in compensation to a petitioner who remained imprisoned in the Karachi Central Prison for a decade without trial due to the failure of the relevant officials to arrange his transfer here.

Chief Justice SM Attique Shah declared that the petitioner’s continued detention in Karachi Central Prison from May 24, 2016, until his transfer to Kurram tribal district in May 2026, without being produced before the competent court, was unlawful.

He held that the omissions of the relevant public functionaries had violated the detainee’s fundamental rights under Articles 4, 9, 10-A and 14 of the Constitution.

“The petitioner (Ameen Hussain) is awarded compensation of Rs10 million. Fifty per cent of this amount shall be paid by the government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa through the chief secretary within 60 days of the receipt of this judgement,” the bench declared in a detailed 21-page order in the case.

Directs govt, negligent officers to pay the amount; orders action against those responsible

It added that the remaining amount would be borne personally, in equal shares, by the officers held responsible in the inquiry report, namely the then Upper Kurram assistant political agent (2017-2018) and assistant commissioner(s) (2017-2019) and the Kurram district police officers (2019-2026), while the chief secretary and the inspector general of police would identify those officers by name from the official records within 15 days of the receipt of the verdict’s copy.

“Each officer shall deposit his share with the additional registrar (judicial), by crossed cheque in the name of the petitioner, within 60 days of the receipt of this judgement. In case of failure, the share shall be recovered from his salary or other dues in accordance with law,” it declared.

The court added that the liability would be independent of disciplinary proceedings against the officers and that the compensation would not be paid or indemnified from public funds.

The petitioner had been imprisoned in Karachi Central Prison in a narcotics case and completed his sentence on May 24, 2016. However, he was not released because he was wanted in a case registered in Kurram district (formerly Kurram Agency), under Section 302 of the Pakistan Penal Code read with Section 11 of the Frontier Crimes Regulation, 1901, relating to the murder of his father.

From 2016 onwards, the senior superintendent of Karachi Central Prison and the Sindh home department repeatedly wrote to authorities in Kurram and Kohat districts and the KP home and tribal affairs department to take custody of the prisoner and arrange his transfer from the prison. However, no action was taken.

The petitioner remained in Karachi for a decade without being tried or produced before any court in Kurram, rendering him unable even to apply for bail. He was eventually transferred on the high court’s orders in May 2026 before being granted bail.

“The petitioner remained in custody in Karachi from 24.05.2016 until his transfer in May 2026, about ten years, without trial and without access to the court that could hear his bail. No amount of money can make up for ten years of a man’s life. Lost liberty cannot be restored, and the time spent in a prison cell cannot be lived again,” the bench observed.

“This court’s orders can’t give the petitioner back a single day of those years. What this court can do is make sure that the compensation is not so small that it fails to reflect what was taken from him.”

The bench directed the chief secretary to initiate proceedings against the then assistant political agent of Upper Kurram, the assistant commissioners who served in the district during 2017-2019 and any other officer or official of the political or district administration found responsible. It ordered that the proceedings be conducted under the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Government Servants (Efficiency & Discipline) Rules, 2011.

The court also directed the provincial inspector general of police to identify the police officers and officials of Kurram who had failed to act on requests from the district public prosecutor during 2019-2026, including the official or officials in whose custody the original case file had been placed.

“He shall proceed against them under the law and rules applicable to police officers,” it declared.

The bench directed the Kurram deputy commissioner and DPO to trace the original case file and determine responsibility for its misplacement.

“The disciplinary proceedings shall not, however, be held in abeyance on that account,” it noted.

The bench ruled that all proceedings initiated under its directions must be conducted strictly in accordance with the law, after giving the officers concerned a proper opportunity to be heard and defend themselves. The proceedings must be concluded within two months of receipt of the judgement.

It also directed the additional chief secretary (home) to place the reforms recommended by the inquiry officer in the case before the competent forum for consideration and a decision, and to include details of the steps taken in the compliance report.

“The chief secretary and the inspector general of police shall submit a consolidated compliance report to this court through the additional registrar (judicial) within two months of the receipt of this judgement positively, for perusal of the Bench in Chamber.”

The bench declared that the report should include proof of payment of compensation, the names of the officers who paid their shares and progress on the disciplinary proceedings.

It also discussed the relevant constitutional provisions and superior court judgements.

Published in Dawn, November 27th, 2026

articles.title: UN says violence against women rising, support services shrinking
articles.summary:
WASHINGTON: The United Nations on Wednesday launched its annual 16 Days of Activism campaign against gender-based violence, urging governments and societies to speak out against abuse, believe survivors and demand justice.

“Speak Out. Believe Survivors. De­­m­­and Justice,” read the message iss­ued by the UN to mark the first day of the global campaign, which runs until Dec 10, Human Rights Day. The campaign warned that too many survivors of violence and online harassment still face silence, disbelief and victim-blaming, allowing perpetrators to escape accountability.

“Every unanswered call for help, every dismissed report, and every unpunished act of violence” strengthens the web of impunity, the UN message said. It urged people to challenge attitudes that excuse violence, listen to survivors without judgment and respect their choices. Governments were asked to strengthen and enforce laws, fund support services and hold perpetrators and institutions accountable.

The campaign comes amid mounting concerns over violence against women in the digital and physical worlds, particularly in countries where social restrictions and inadequate protection systems discourage victims from seeking help.

A UN report on Pakistan, released on the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on Nov 25, warned that online harassment was increasingly spilling into the physical world, contributing to femicide, suicide, physical violence and loss of employment.

The findings also showed how deeply entrenched social attitudes discourage women from challenging harassment. A survey in Pakistan found that 54pc of women believed women should leave their jobs if they faced harassment, while 83pc acknowledged that men often got away with harassing women.

The report said online abuse was not merely driving women and girls away from digital spaces but was also affecting their participation in professional and public life. It raised concerns about the response of companies, noting that most lacked clear policies to prevent and address online gender-based violence, while existing policies were often poorly implemented.

UN findings on attitudes in South Asia, including India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, pointed to a wider climate in which victims of harassment could face pressure to withdraw from public and professional life rather than expect perpetrators to be held accountable. The report also highlighted the global scale of violence. In the Arab states, 60pc of women internet users reported experiencing online violence.

Worldwide, an estimated 50,000 women and girls were killed by intimate partners or family members in 2024 — an average of 137 every day, or one every 10 minutes — according to figures released by the UN Office on Drugs and Crime and UN Women.

The UN has urged women facing on­­­­line abuse to cut off contact with pe­­­r­­­p­­etrators and report online harassment, while calling on governments and technology companies to strengthen protections and accountability. The campaign’s launch also coincided with a renewed warning from UN Women about the deteriorating situation of women and girls in Afghanistan, where the risks of violence are increasing even as essential support services are disappearing because of funding cuts. In a statement marking the start of the campaign, UN Women Afghanistan urged governments and donors to increase support for Afghan women’s organisations, describing them as an essential lifeline for women and girls facing mounting social, economic and humanitarian pressures.

“Just as the risks of violence agai­nst women and girls are growing, the services they depend on are disappearing because of aid cuts,” said Su­­s­­an Ferguson, UN Women’s Special Representative in Afghanistan.

The UN said women’s organisations were particularly important in reaching survivors and providing services in circumstances where restrictions and economic hardship had sharply reduced their options.

Published in Dawn, November 27th, 2026

articles.title: 26th, 27th Amendments sparked judicial conflict: ex-IHC judge
articles.summary:
• Kayani calls for parliamentary intervention to resolve judicial conflict
• Urges authorities not to issue notices to media under Peca

ISLAMABAD: Former Islam­abad High Court (IHC) judge reti­red Justice Mohsin Akhtar Kayani has said that the 26th and 27th Constitutional Amendments have triggered a conflict between two superior courts, warning that the disregard for established judicial precedents and the creation of new ones have further complicated the constitutional and legal framework.

Speaking at a seminar titled ‘Personal Safety and Justice in a Digital World’, organised by the Institute of Regional Studies in Islamabad, Justice Kayani said that the issues arising from the Nadia Sarwar case before the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) could only be addressed through parliament.

He said the current state of the Constitution was evident to everyone, yet people remained silent despite being aware of what was happening.

“The 26th and 27th amendments have given rise to a conflict between two superior courts,” he said, adding that established judicial precedents were being disregarded and new, problematic precedents were being set.

He said parliament was the appropriate forum for resolving conflicts between the superior courts, emphasising that legislation was its prerogative, while the interpretation of the Constitution was the responsibility of the courts.

He urged lawmakers to debate legal matters in parliament before introducing legislation to ensure that parliamentarians fully understood the laws being enacted and their implications.

The former judge also questioned the growing use of laws regulating online expression, particularly the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (Peca), saying that journalists, members of parliament and lawyers were among those affected by the legislation.

He urged the authorities not to issue notices to media organisations under Section 26-A merely for publishing news reports.

“For God’s sake, do not issue notices to the media under Section 26-A. It should not be the case that the moment the media reports a story, a notice is im-mediately issued against them,”

he said, stressing the need to protect journalists.

He questioned the effectiveness of establishing new agencies to enforce such laws, remarking that authorities often created new agencies only to appoint the same officers under different uniforms.

He also pointed out that several terms associated with online harassment remained poorly understood, adding that those for whom the legislation was intended had neither been properly consulted nor adequately informed about its provisions.

Published in Dawn, November 27th, 2026

articles.title: Journalist Shahid Maitla granted bail
articles.summary:
QUETTA: A district and sessions court has granted bail to senior journalist Shahid Maitla and ordered his release against surety bonds worth Rs3 million.

District and Sessions Judge Quetta Ghulam Qadir Shah Bukhari anno­unced the decision on a post-arrest bail petition filed by the journalist.

A case was registered against Shahid Maitla following a complaint submitted by former caretaker prime minister Anwaarul Haq Kakar to the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency. The NCCIA subsequently arrested Mr Maitla in Islamabad and transferred him to Quetta. He was later sent to jail under court orders.

Following his arrest, Mr Maitla had filed a post-arrest bail application before Judicial Magistrate Syed Akhtar Shah. However, the magistrate rejected his bail plea.

Subsequently, Mr Maitla , through his counsel Rahib Buleedi, approached the sessions court, which has granted him post-arrest bail.

Published in Dawn, November 27th, 2026

articles.title: AJK govt removes Rawalakot mayor over allegations of 'anti-state activities'
articles.summary:
MUZAFFARABAD: The Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) government on Thursday removed Rawalakot Mayor Abdul Naeem Khan from office and terminated his membership of the municipal corporation over his alleged “involvement in anti-state activities”.

A notification issued by the Local Government and Rural Development Department said the action was taken under Section 23(2) of the Local Government Act, 1990.

According to a separate notification by the AJK Home Department, dated Nov 15, Khan’s name was among those placed on the Fourth Schedule under Section 16 of the AJK Anti-Terrorism Act.

The notification, listing at least 28 names, cited a decision of a cabinet meeting held on June 5, adding that the AJK president approved placing “activists” of the proscribed Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) on the Fourth Schedule.

Khan, who reportedly belongs to the Jammu Kashmir Peoples Party (JKPP), was elected mayor in 2023.

Before his election, he had headed a faction of the Rawalakot traders’ body with JAAC leader Umar Nazir Kashmiri serving as his deputy. After Khan became the mayor, Kashmiri was made the president of the traders’ forum.

The region has witnessed violence-marred protests over the past few months, particularly in June and July, with reports of sporadic unrest in recent weeks. At the root of the tensions was JAAC’s demand to abolish the 12 refugee seats in the AJK Legislative Assembly.

Rawalakot of Poonch district witnessed multiple protests in June and July, with clashes between demonstrators and law enforcement personnel on at least two occasions.

On June 5, following the announcement of the JAAC’s June 9 strike, the then-PPP-led AJK government declared the committee a proscribed organisation and placed it under the First Schedule of the local ATA.

The federal government had accused militant elements “pu­r­­s­u­ing a foreign age­nda and backed by Indian funding” of fomenting the unrest in AJK.

On Wednesday, the AJK Legislative Assembly offered to reopen negotiations with JAAC, subject to the disbandment of armed groups, surrender of those allegedly involved in serious crimes and an unequivocal commitment to pursue demands through constitutional and democratic means.

Registration of 14 private schools in Poonch cancelled

Separately, the AJK Elementary and Secondary Education Department has approved the cancellation of registration of 14 private educational institutions across Poonch district, including Rawalakot, Hajira, Jandali and Thorar.

An order issued by the department on Thursday said the decision had been approved by the chairman of the AJK Private Educational Institutions Regulatory Authority (Peira) under Rule 8(3) of the Private Educational Institutions (Registration, Regulation and Promotion) Rules, 2015.

The action was taken on the basis of reports alleging that the institutions had been involved in activities contrary to the integrity and solidarity of the state, the order said.

Of the 14 institutions, seven are located in Rawalakot and its adjoining areas, three in Hajira, and two each in Thorar and Jandali.

Copies of the order have been forwarded to relevant departmental authorities, the Poonch divisional commissioner, the chairman of the Federal Board, the chairman of the AJK Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education, Mirpur, and education officials in Poonch division.

Previously, the registration of 10 private schools was cancelled on similar grounds.

articles.title: JUI-F chief Maulana Fazl among nine party leaders barred from Sargodha district for 30 days
articles.summary:
LAHORE: Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman is among nine party leaders barred from entering, residing or remaining in Sargodha district for 30 days, according to a notification issued by the deputy commissioner.

The development came as the party was scheduled to hold a rally in Sargodha on Nov 26 (Thursday).

The order, a copy of which is available with Dawn, states that the restriction was imposed under Section 7(1) of the West Pakistan Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, 1960, read with the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order (Amendment) Ordinance, 2008, and would remain in force for 30 days from Nov 25.

Besides Maulana Fazlur Rehman, whose district is listed as Dera Ismail Khan, the notification names eight other party leaders: Maulana Naseer Ahmad Abrar, Maulana Amjad Khan and Prof Ghazanfar Aziz, all from Lahore; Maulana Safi Ullah from Bhakkar; Maulana Muhammad Noor Khan Hans from Multan; Maulana Muhammad Zakria Shah from Faisalabad; Maulana Muhammad Yahya Abbasi from Muzaffargarh; and Maulana Jamal Abdul Nasir from Dera Ghazi Khan.

According to the notification, the deputy commissioner reviewed a report submitted by the Sargodha district police officer and expressed concerns that the individuals had a history of delivering provocative and objectionable speeches that could threaten public order.

It described them as “firebrand speakers” whose speeches were allegedly provocative and inflammatory, adding that they were likely to assemble crowds unlawfully and incite public sentiment against the state and its institutions.

The order further stated that their presence could create a law and order situation and pose a potential threat to peace and security.

Meanwhile, several senior JUI-F leaders were detained in Sargodha and served notices for allegedly violating Section 144, police said. Several local JUI-F leaders were also detained under the Maintenance of Public Order (MPO) Ordinance in Khushab district.

Separately, the JUI-F chief, in a video message, said that despite the road restrictions and blockade, he was leaving for Sargodha.

He demanded that the government immediately remove all restrictions, release detained party leaders and workers and ensure that constitutional rights and civil liberties are protected.

JUI-F Punjab spokesperson, Hafiz Ghazanfar Aziz, said the government was continuing its “high-handed tactics” against the party.

Aziz claimed that a large number of party workers had been stranded on the road and that arrests were being made across Punjab, with cases registered against JUI-F activists.

Fazl should engage in dialogue: Tarar

Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said that based on Fazl’s statements and attitude in recent days, it “seemed that he wants there to be a confrontation”, adding that the government did not want so.

Asked about the actions against JUI-F on Geo News programme ‘Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Sath’, Tarar said, “Traffic jams keep happening in the country; it is no big matter. I would not give too much importance to this issue, it is not an important issue.”

The minister said one should not go to the extent of concocting a “pro-Afghanistan, anti-Pakistan narrative”.

He said the JUI-F chief should engage in negotiations through a “democratic and political process”.

Noting bitterness and increased use of inappropriate remarks, Tarar said one should “retain space [for talks] in politics and not enter a dead end”.

The minister said it was unfitting for a senior politician to create an “anti-Pakistan narrative”, accusing Fazl of “promoting unrest in the country”.

He affirmed that the government had remained engaged with the JUI-F chief and accorded him respect, including on the matter of governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

“I personally believe that matters should be resolved through mutual understanding and by sitting together and talking,” Tarar emphasised.

Asked about notices issued to Fazl’s family by the accountability watchdog, the information minister maintained that the institutions function independently and there is no “ill intention” behind the actions.

Fazl-govt rift

On Tuesday, JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman claimed he had been put under an hours-long “state siege” to restrict his movement.

The JUI-F chief was scheduled to participate in a multiparty conference hosted by the Lahore High Court Bar Association on Tuesday. However, he could not leave his residence in a private housing society on Multan Road due to the deployment of a heavy police contingent.

The development came after tensions persisted between JUI-F and the Centre. Fazl had criticised the Centre for imposing governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and making the then-PTI provincial government non-functional. The JUI-F chief also accused the Centre of reneging on its commitments despite his efforts to mediate between the PML-N and PTI governments.

Tensions escalated when Fazl accused the Centre of depriving the provinces of their rights, resulting in the veteran politician and key federal ministers exchanging harsh remarks.

In recent weeks, PPP Chairman Bilawal-Bhutto Zardari — a key ally of the ruling PML-N — has voiced his support for Fazl and condemned the “government’s actions” against him.

Last week, police and Federal Constabulary (FC) personnel deployed to protect Fazl and other members of his family were withdrawn from the residences they guarded in Islamabad and Dera Ismail Khan.

A JUI-F spokesman had confirmed the withdrawal, alleging that the Maulana’s Islamabad residence had been cordoned off by capital police and that security personnel had harassed visitors. He also claimed that the party’s Central Secretariat in Islamabad had been besieged by police.

An Islamabad police official, however, said only one police guard had been withdrawn.

The JUI-F chief’s son has also come under scrutiny from the anti-graft watchdog, with the National Accountability Bureau (NAB) summoning former federal communications minister Asad Mahmood over alleged irregularities in 4,252 appointments at Pakistan Post during his 2022-23 tenure. Mahmood skipped two consecutive summonses issued for Nov 10 and 14, according to a NAB source.

The JUI-F staged protests in parts of Sindh and Balochistan on Nov 7 against a “coordinated character assassination campaign” targeting Fazl.

Party leaders and workers condemned the alleged drone surveillance of his residence and the circulation of footage on social media, demanding an impartial investigation and action against those responsible.

articles.title: Govt reduces petrol price by Re1 per litre, diesel by Rs2 per litre
articles.summary:
The government reduced the price of petrol by Re1 per litre and that of diesel by Rs2 per litre, according to a notification by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra).

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs313 per litre and high-speed diesel (HSD) at Rs346 per litre on Nov 27 (Friday).

The prices of HSD and petrol have gone below the July 18 rate of Rs354.35 and Rs316.15 per litre, respectively, as of price reductions made to both on Wednesday.

The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel.

Under an arrangement announced on Nov 2, for 30 days, oil refineries will contribute to the petroleum levy by bearing a cumulative impact of Rs15 billion, according to the government. This allows a Rs14.71 reduction in the petrol price at the consumer end.

On Sept 17, the government rolled out the Prime Minister’s Fuel Relief Scheme across the country to ease the public’s burden amid rising fuel prices due to the Middle East situation.

The subsidy scheme applies to owners of motorcycles, rickshaws and vehicles of up to 800cc.

Rise in fuel prices

The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28.

The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March.

Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm, and fuel allocations for official vehicles have been cut by 50pc for three months.

Since July 17, the government has been revising fuel prices on a near-daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US.

The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give Ogra the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends.

Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the conflict. The federal government had also announced targeted relief measures in April to provide subsidised fuel.

Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes.

Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators.

Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

articles.title: Achakzai's proposal of national govt only solution to political, constitutional crisis: TTAP
articles.summary:
ISLAMABAD: The Tehreek-i-Tahafuz-i-Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP) on Thursday maintained that forming a national government is the only solution to the country’s ongoing political and constitutional crisis.

Earlier this week, TTAP Chairman and National Assembly Opposition Leader Mahmood Khan Achakzai had called for the formation of a national government and comprehensive constitutional and political reforms to steer the country out of the mounting crises.

However, the main opposition party, the PTI, has distanced itself from Achakzai’s proposal. A joint meeting of its parliamentary groups discussed the matter, and a majority of the members opposed the idea, according to one participant.

Speaking to Dawn on Thursday, TTAP spokesperson Akhunzada Hussain Ahmed Yousafzai argued that a national government would pave the way for the release of PTI founder and former prime minister Imran Khan, who has been in prison since Aug 5, 2023.

However, Yousafzai made it clear that the proposed arrangement could not be imposed or negotiated behind closed doors.

TTAP spokesperson Akhunzada Hussain Ahmed Yousafzai. — Photo via X/File

He stressed that all political forces, particularly PTI and its founder, must be part of consultations before any decision on the formation of a national government.

However, he warned that excluding any political force would undermine the democratic legitimacy of a possible national government.

“The political uncertainty cannot be overcome through political victimisation or unilateral decisions, but requires serious and meaningful dialogue among all political parties, democratic stakeholders and the establishment,” the TTAP spokesperson stated.

“The proposal for a national government is neither directed against any political party nor intended to provide political advantage to any particular group,” he affirmed, describing it as an effort to restore public confidence in democratic institutions and end political polarisation.

Under the proposed framework, the first priority would be restoration of a democratic environment in which “fundamental rights, constitutional freedoms, freedom of expression and political activities” are protected, Yousafzai said.

He added that such an arrangement would allow all the parties to participate in peaceful political activities without discrimination.

The TTAP spokesperson also called for making the Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) independent under a mutually agreed, credible and non-partisan chief election commissioner who enjoyed the confidence of all major political parties.

Yousafzai said the proposed national government should ensure free, fair and transparent general elections across the country in accordance with the Constitution so that the people’s actual mandate was reflected in the composition of the elected government.

He also called for a multi-party conference to be convened before the formation of the proposed government.

The meeting, he said, should focus exclusively on reaching a consensus over the mechanism, framework and necessary arrangements for holding credible elections and establishing a genuinely representative government.
