articles.title: Trump says war in Ukraine might not have happened had Russia remained in G8
articles.summary:
US President Donald Trump has said that if Russia had remained a member of the Group of Eight (G8), there might be no war in Ukraine today.

Source: Trump speaking to journalists on Thanksgiving, as reported by European Pravda

Details: Commenting on the possible attendance of Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin at the G20 leaders' summit in Florida in December, Trump recalled that Russia had been expelled from the G8 (now the G7).

Trump suggested that had this not happened, there might not be a war in Ukraine today.

"When he was a member of the G8, if he stayed a member, President Obama wanted him out. And if he stayed a member, you might not have this war right now. He was very insulted when that happened, and now it's a G7," Trump said.

"I believe if they didn't do that, I really believe strongly, if they didn't do that, we would not have that war going on right now. The First Lady wouldn't have to go over and try and get a ceasefire to get people out," Trump added, referring to Melania Trump's humanitarian mission in Oleshky.

He said he would not have voted to exclude Russia from the group had he been president at the time.

Trump also said he would like to see Putin at the G20 summit in Florida, even though "some people wouldn't like that".

"We have a meeting and we're talking about Russia, Ukraine. I said, 'Wouldn't it be nice to have Russia in the room?'" Trump explained.

Background:

Russia was expelled from the Group of Eight in 2014 over its annexation of Crimea.

In April 2026, it emerged that the US was planning to invite Putin to the G20 leaders' summit, scheduled to take place in Miami on 14-15 December. Washington later sent an invitation to the Russian leader.

Trump suggested that he might invite his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy to the G20 summit.

Kaja Kallas, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, believes that Putin's possible attendance at the G20 summit in Miami in December could risk legitimising Russia's return to international forums while the war in Ukraine is still ongoing.

articles.title: Ukraine always coordinates attacks on Russian ships in foreign waters with other countries – Zelenskyy
articles.summary:
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that Ukraine always coordinates its attacks on Russian ships with countries in whose waters or near whose infrastructure Ukrainian forces operate.

Source: Zelenskyy in an interview with the BBC

Details: Zelenskyy said Ukrainian diplomats work with their counterparts from other countries when Ukraine operates in certain waters, including international waters, or near another country's infrastructure. He stressed that Ukrainian forces "never attack" without coordinating with the country's partners.

Zelenskyy was responding to a question about whether he was concerned that strikes such as the attack on the Russian corvette Merkury off the coast of Libya could take the war beyond Ukraine's borders.

The journalist also pointed out that even Italy had criticised the Ukrainian attack in this case, accusing Ukraine of violating Libya's sovereignty. She asked Zelenskyy whether he considered striking a ship in another country's port rather than in international waters a mistake.

Zelenskyy defended Ukraine's actions, calling the Merkury an "absolutely fair goal". He explained that Ukrainian forces know whether a vessel is under sanctions or, in the worst-case scenario, whether it is also carrying Russian weapons under the Russian flag.

He added that Ukraine's Armed Forces, Security Service and intelligence agencies are aware of these circumstances and are doing their job. Zelenskyy stressed that Ukraine is clear and open about its actions and cannot allow Russian ships to attack the country or transport weapons.

Background:

Zelenskyy confirmed that Ukrainian naval drones had sunk the Russian corvette Merkury, which had a Ka-27 helicopter on board, and also struck the dry cargo ship MV Angara, which Russia was using to transport weapons, near the Libyan port of Benghazi.

Two Libyan officials previously told the Associated Press that the Russian corvette Merkury had suffered serious damage as a result of a strike on a naval base in Benghazi, and a fire had broken out at the base. Citing an initial investigation, AP wrote that the ship may have been hit by Ukrainian naval drones.

Musa Al-Koni, a member of Libya's Presidential Council, condemned Ukraine's attack on the port of Benghazi, describing it as tantamount to a declaration of war against Libya.

articles.title: Ending support for Ukraine would put Europe's security at risk – Macron
articles.summary:
French President Emmanuel Macron has said that the war in Ukraine is an existential issue for European security and that ending support for Kyiv would put Europe's security at risk in the short or medium term.

Source: Macron at a press conference in Brussels on 26 November

Details: Speaking to journalists at an emergency EU summit, Macron commented on discussions about aid to Ukraine amid criticism from French politicians, including presidential candidate Marine Le Pen, as well as judoka Teddy Riner.

Macron noted that France has imposed sanctions on Russia and supported Ukraine since February 2022. He said France has not allocated the largest share of its national budget compared with other countries because of its more limited financial resources, but has made up for this by supplying weapons, training troops and pursuing political initiatives, including through the Coalition of the Willing.

He stressed that EU aid has become crucial because of the "US withdrawal since the beginning of 2025". He added that France supports the European Commission's proposal to create a new funding system for Ukraine for 2027.

"Ukrainians are fighting for their country's sovereignty and territorial integrity, but they are also on the front of European security. We need to look at the map and revisit history. So yes, this war is an existential issue for European security," Macron said.

He stressed that inaction or ending support for Ukraine would quickly have consequences for the entire continent.

He added that if support for Kyiv were withdrawn, many European countries would feel the threat in the short rather than the medium term. He pointed to Russia's daily acts of aggression against European countries.

"If we abandoned Ukraine, we would put our security at risk in the short or medium term. And when I look at the situation many countries in our Europe are facing, it is clear that we are talking about the short rather than the medium term. You only have to look at Russia's daily aggression against us all," the French president said.

Macron urged people not to create "doubt and confusion" about support for Ukraine, as major countries and the European Union as a whole remain united in their support for Kyiv.

"The Ukrainians' fight is also our fight. It is a fight for Europe's security because Vladimir Putin's targets are the European Union and NATO," the French president stressed.

articles.title: It's like calling Hitler a friend: Zelenskyy outraged by Trump's friendly embrace of Putin
articles.summary:
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has criticised US President Donald Trump's friendly greeting of Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin during the recent trilateral summit in China, calling the Russian leader an aggressor and a murderer and comparing him to Hitler.

Source: Zelenskyy in an interview with the BBC

Quote: "Of course, it's up to the president of the United States, but… it's strange. He [Putin] is an aggressor and a killer. He can't be a friend. Just cannot be. It is the same if somebody says about Hitler during World War II that he's a good friend. No, he's not a friend."

Details: Zelenskyy was responding to the interviewer's question about how he felt about the warm greeting between Trump and Putin in China and the US president's posts featuring the Kremlin leader on his Truth Social platform.

Zelenskyy added that he believes many people found this deeply strange and that it was particularly painful for families who had lost their sons and daughters and were pinning their hopes on the US president.

He stressed that Ukraine is also relying on its relationship with the US and on its allies. However, he questioned how Ukrainians were supposed to view a killer whom the US described as a good friend, reiterating that Putin could not be considered a friend.

Background:

During a bilateral meeting at the summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen on 19 November, Trump greeted Putin with a hug and the words: "He's my friend."

Trump later posted a photo of himself with Putin on his Truth Social platform, captioned "my friend".

articles.title: Drones strike Russian plant that produces components for Iskander missile fuel – photos, videos
articles.summary:
Drones struck the Yefremov Synthetic Rubber Plant in Yefremov, Russia's Tula Oblast, on the night of 26-27 November. The plant makes materials used to produce solid rocket propellant for short-range and ballistic missiles, including Iskanders.

Source: Ukrainian monitoring Telegram channels Exilenova+, Dnipro Osint, Exile+ and Supernova+; Russian media outlet Astra; Tula Oblast Governor Dmitry Milyaev

The Yefremov Synthetic Rubber Plant
Photo: Dnipro Osint Telegram channel

Quote from Exile+: "The Yefremov Synthetic Rubber Plant, which is involved in the production of solid rocket propellant for Iskander missiles, has been struck. The facility is one of Russia's leading producers of synthetic rubber and is strategically important to its military-industrial complex."

Details: The attack caused a large fire near the facility. Numerous explosions and seats of fire were reported near the plant's main production units, DK-5 and DK-7. The impact of the strike and the extent of the damage are still being assessed.

Photo: Astra

An OSINT analysis by Astra indicates that the Yefremov combined heat and power plant, which supplies electricity to the factory, was also damaged.

Photo: Astra

Milyaev confirmed the drone attack on the region but reported only four drones shot down and broken windows in three houses. He also claimed that no infrastructure had been damaged.

The Yefremov plant specialises in synthetic rubber, polymers and polyisobutylene additives.

Ukraine's General Staff says the plant produces components for plastic explosives and materials used in solid rocket propellant, including for Iskander ballistic missiles.

articles.title: Russia hits infrastructure facility in Zaporizhzhia, causing fire
articles.summary:
Russian forces struck an infrastructure facility in Zaporizhzhia on the evening of 26 November, causing a fire in an industrial building.

Source: Mykhailo Semikin, acting Head of Zaporizhzhia Oblast Military Administration

Quote: "The enemy has attacked Zaporizhzhia. An infrastructure facility has been hit."

Details: The attack caused a fire in an industrial building.

Background: Russian forces also attacked the Dniprovskyi district in Zaporizhzhia that evening, killing one person.

articles.title: Former Ukrainian commander-in-chief Syrskyi helps Norway strengthen air defences on border with Russia
articles.summary:
Oleksandr Syrskyi, former commander-in-chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, has visited northern Norway to help the Norwegian military strengthen its air defences along the border with Russia.

Source: Syrskyi on Telegram

Details: Syrskyi and Norwegian Army Commander General Eirik Kristoffersen visited the Jarfjord border outpost and an observation post in Grense Jakobselv this week. The generals spoke to Norwegian conscripts and inspected the area around the Varangerfjord, where Norway's maritime border with Russia extends into the Barents Sea.

The generals returned to Oslo after the visit. Syrskyi said Kristoffersen wanted to inspect the area first and then use simulations to explore possible scenarios, assess deterrence capabilities and discuss how to respond in the event of a threat.

Quote from Syrskyi: "I am grateful to Norway for its assistance to Ukraine, particularly its support in strengthening our air defences. I am now helping our Norwegian partners strengthen their air defences. I am doing this out of gratitude and for the sake of our shared security."

Support Ukrainska Pravda on Patreon to help us keep reporting!

articles.title: Russian forces advance near Petropavlivka in Kharkiv Oblast – DeepState
articles.summary:
DeepState, a Ukrainian group of military analysts, has reported that Russian forces have advanced near the village of Petropavlivka in Kharkiv Oblast.

Source: DeepState

Quote: "The enemy has advanced near Petropavlivka."

Details: According to DeepState's map, Petropavlivka is now in the grey zone.

Background: DeepState reported on 23 November that Ukraine's defence forces had pushed Russian troops back near Ustynivka in Kharkiv Oblast. On the same day, the analysts reported that the Russians had advanced near Verkhnia Tersa in Zaporizhzhia Oblast.

articles.title: Zelenskyy on threat of large-scale attack: Ukraine will repair damage and respond to every Russian strike
articles.summary:
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that Ukraine will respond to every Russian strike and urged Ukrainians to pay attention to missile threat warnings over the coming days.

Source: Zelenskyy in his evening address on 26 November

Quote: "Unfortunately, we have information that the Russians are preparing another massive strike. Please pay close attention to missile alerts over the coming days.

And let those in Russia know – we will restore what is ours, and we will respond to every Russian strike."

Background:

Earlier that day, following a conference call, Zelenskyy said that the Russians were completing preparations for a large-scale strike. According to intelligence reports, possible targets include energy and logistics facilities, as well as infrastructure providing essential services to cities and local communities.

Zelenskyy also said he expects a report from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on talks with partners about the supply of air defence equipment. He said the main task is to obtain interceptor missiles for Patriot and NASAMS air defence systems.

articles.summary:
Firefighters are extinguishing a fire at a business's premises in Khmelnytskyi district following a Russian attack, with no reports of casualties.

Source: Serhii Tiurin, Head of Khmelnytskyi Oblast State Administration, on Facebook

Quote: "As a result of a Russian attack, a fire broke out on the premises of a business in Khmelnytskyi district."

articles.title: EU summit: decision on Ukraine postponed until December, €45bn loan and new mechanism discussed
articles.summary:
European Union leaders at an extraordinary summit in Brussels on 26–27 November are discussing funding for Ukraine in 2027 and under the EU's next long-term budget.

Source: European Pravda, citing sources

Details: According to European Pravda, a final agreement on these issues is not expected at this summit, and the decision will be postponed until December.

A final agreement on the EU's next long-term budget for 2028–2032 as a whole is also not expected at the current summit. Based on the outcome of consultations, a new compromise proposal may be prepared to serve as the basis for negotiations at the December leaders' summit.

During the European Council plenary session on 26 November, EU leaders discussed the bloc's next long-term budget and funding for Ukraine, after which European Council President António Costa began consultations with leaders in groups.

A nearly two-hour discussion with the "Frugal Seven" (Germany, the Netherlands, Austria, Denmark, Sweden, Finland and Belgium), which advocates limiting increases in national contributions to the EU budget, has already concluded. A meeting is currently underway with the "Friends of Cohesion" – 17 EU member states seeking to protect the volume of funding from the EU budget.

Regarding a new €45 billion loan for Ukraine for 2027, three EU states – Hungary, Slovakia and Czechia – still need to be convinced to join it.

One European Pravda source said that while there are differing views on how to approach the matter, everyone knows it must be resolved by the end of the year, as it covers Ukraine's needs for 2027 that must be met.

The EU expects that separating the military and budgetary components of the loan will help bring all 27 member states on board. This does not involve two separate loans but rather an option for individual states to finance non-military spending within a single loan.

According to European Pravda's sources, a decision on the new loan for Ukraine could be taken at the next European Council meeting in Brussels on 17-18 December. Consultations with EU member states will continue until then.

As for funding Ukraine under the EU's next long-term budget for 2028–2034, António Costa is proposing to create a separate mechanism for paying interest on loans to Ukraine – in addition to the €100 billion Ukraine Reserve proposed by the European Commission.

Another European Pravda source explained that this was initially planned to be covered within the €100 billion, but Costa now wants to place it on top of that amount, which requires a special mechanism.

Background:

According to European Commission calculations, the cost of servicing loans for Ukraine (taking into account the newly proposed €45 billion loan) over 2028–2034 could range from €45 billion to €55 billion.

On 18 November, the European Commission proposed providing Ukraine with an additional €45 billion loan in 2027 – on top of the €45 billion already planned for next year under a previously agreed €90 billion loan.

On Thursday, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev announced that his country will join the non-military part of the new loan for Ukraine, which will amount to €20 billion.

articles.title: Russian strike on Komyshuvakha: Slidstvo.Info uncovers details about perpetrators
articles.summary:
Journalists from Slidstvo.Info have established that Russian serviceman Yaroslav Borodin, who commanded the tactical aviation group involved in the attack, was involved in the airstrike on a school in Komyshuvakha, Zaporizhzhia Oblast, which killed 72 people, and have also uncovered details about other Russian military personnel involved in the strike.

Source: Slidstvo.Info investigation

Details: The journalists found out that 36-year-old Yaroslav Borodin has been taking part in the war against Ukraine since 2023. At the time of the strike on Komyshuvakha, he commanded Tactical Aviation Group No. 5 of the Special Combat Group of the Reserve Aviation Group of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces.

Five days after the attack on the school in Komyshuvakha, Defence Intelligence of Ukraine published a list of Russian military personnel involved in the airstrike.

Slidstvo.Info journalists found their photographs, social media pages and other personal data. The Kiborg project team helped search for information in closed databases.

According to Defence Intelligence, the strike on Komyshuvakha was planned by 42-year-old Colonel Fyodor Zubakov, head of the fire damage group at the headquarters of Russia's Dnepr Group of Forces.

Among the Russian pilots identified by Defence Intelligence is 31-year-old Captain Sergei Yeliseyev. According to the journalists' sources, he has served in the Russian forces since 2015 and has been fighting against Ukraine since March 2022.

Another is Senior Lieutenant Rodion Plotnikov. According to Slidstvo.Info's data, he has served in the Russian forces since August 2016. His name appears in tax records of the Chelyabinsk branch of the Air Force Academy. In applications on financial services, Plotnikov himself stated that he works as a navigator and is linked to a military town at the Chelyabinsk Higher Military Aviation Red Banner School of Navigators.

Lieutenant Vadim Perekhrest also closed his social media pages. In photos, Perekhrest is mostly wearing glasses or pictured from behind. However, Slidstvo.Info found the contacts of his wife, Irina. On the banned social network VKontakte in May 2022, she posted a photo of them together. She later published several wedding photos and, in May 2025, a photo with their daughter.

Another pilot is Senior Lieutenant Nikita Ignatyev. "According to our data, he has been taking part in the war against Ukraine since September 2022. We found photos of Ignatyev on the pages of his wife, Tatyana. She published their wedding photos and later a photoshoot before the birth of their son. Ignatyev himself does not post photos on social media," the journalists write.

"Two more servicemen remain on the Defence Intelligence list whom we also identified. One is 37-year-old Captain Dmitry Zverev. He has served in the Russian forces since May 2012, is married and is raising a son and a daughter," Slidstvo.Info writes.

Another is Senior Lieutenant Maksim Sokolenko. He is 27 years old and has served in the Russian forces since August 2015. He married in 2023, and his son was born in the summer of 2026.

In response to a request from Slidstvo.Info, the Security Service of Ukraine (SSU) reported that investigators from the SSU Directorate in Zaporizhzhia Oblast are investigating the Russian military's airstrikes on the premises of the Dzherelo school of the Komyshuvakha Settlement Council on 2 November 2026. The Russians used FAB-500 and FAB-3000 bombs.

Zaporizhzhia Oblast Prosecutor's Office reported that all versions are being examined as part of the pre-trial investigation. However, the main one is the deliberate targeting of civilians and civilian infrastructure.

"No one has yet been served with a notice of suspicion in these criminal proceedings," the journalists write.

articles.title: Ukrainian who set himself on fire in Warsaw is in intensive care in critical condition
articles.summary:
The Ukrainian Embassy in Poland has reported that Polish police have confirmed the Ukrainian citizenship of the man who set himself on fire near the Presidential Palace in Warsaw on the evening of 25 November. Due to severe burns, he is in intensive care in a critical condition.

Source: European Pravda, citing a statement by the Ukrainian diplomatic mission on Facebook

Details: According to the statement, the embassy received official confirmation from Polish police that the man who committed self-immolation in central Warsaw on 25 November is a Ukrainian citizen.

The man is currently in an intensive care unit in a critical condition with severe burns, the statement adds.

Polish police are establishing the circumstances of the incident, including possible motives, and are checking whether third parties may have been involved or influenced the man's actions.

Quote: "The embassy's consuls are keeping the case under special control, providing the necessary consular assistance and maintaining contact with the victim's relatives, Polish medics and law enforcement."

Details: The diplomats called for respect for the privacy of the victim and his family.

Background:

On the evening of 25 November, a man set himself on fire on the square between the Presidential Palace and the Ministry of Culture and National Heritage building in Warsaw.

The Ukrainian Ministry of Foreign Affairs reported that the victim is, with a high degree of probability, a citizen of Ukraine, and that the Polish side is currently carrying out procedures to definitively confirm his identity.

Media outlets also reported that the man demanded that Ukrainians in Poland be treated the same as Poles.

articles.title: Russia wants to build a new security framework to end the war. This is why it won’t work
articles.summary:
When negotiators from Russia, the United States and Ukraine met in Abu Dhabi recently for peace talks on ending the Ukraine war, the Russians pushed a long-held demand for a new security architecture for Europe. Washington has appeared open to this, with US President Donald Trump touting a “big, beautiful agreement” that “might involve all of Europe”.

While little was revealed about what such a framework would look like specifically, a recent speech by Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov provides some clues.

Sergei Lavrov’s speech at the Minsk International Conference on Eurasian Security.

At a security conference in Minsk, Belarus, earlier this month, Lavrov proposed a new security architecture for the entire Eurasian continent.

Reiterating the claim Russia has long made to justify its war in Ukraine, Lavrov said NATO had repeatedly pledged not to expand eastward to contain Russia, but did so anyway. And, he said, the West is now pursuing a new “NATO-style military-political bloc in Asia”.

In response, Lavrov said Russia wanted to build a new security framework that would encompass all of Europe and Asia – echoing the Soviet Union’s communist alliances during the Cold War.

A new arrangement like this would be “committed to the principles of indivisible security, openness and equality”, Lavrov said, adding European nations were welcome to join. Russia does not “desire nor plan any war whatsoever with Europe”, he stressed. But he added:

If Europe, as it threatens, is itself preparing for war and initiates one, we are ready.

A security proposal based on “sovereignty” and “equality” may sound appealing to some states across the region. However, there are several reasons to be sceptical.

What Europe wants

The prevailing view in Europe is that Russia is the continent’s principal security threat. So, the idea of European states joining Russia in a new arrangement of any sort is unlikely to gain broad acceptance.

And despite Russian President Vladimir Putin’s claims he is not against “having a dialogue with Europe, Moscow has made clear it does not want European representatives in the Ukraine peace talks. So it stands to reason Europe wouldn’t have a voice in a future security agreement either.

That said, the political view towards Russia in Europe is evolving. As economic pressures continue to mount, support for right-wing, populist parties is growing, including one of Ukraine’s staunchest supporters, Germany.

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party opposes financial and military support for Ukraine, arguing the war is not in Germany’s national interests.

In fact, its platform in one recent eastern state election where it finished first called for a revival of Russian language teaching, an end to sanctions and closer energy ties with Russia.

This highlights the diversity of views in some countries on both the war and Europe’s broader strategic priorities.

Some have raised the possibility of a more robust Organization for Security and Co-operation (the only European security group that Russia belongs to), or a revived NATO-Russia Council. However, this seems far-fetched in the absence of trust between the two sides.

Many in Europe believe Russia’s true aims for a new security framework are to carve up the continent into Cold War-era spheres of influence and expand its influence beyond its borders.

Read more:
Russia wanted a new world order. This wasn’t the one it had in mind

What China wants

Second, it remains unclear how China, the region’s other major power, and its own security ambitions fit within Russia’s vision.

Chinese foreign policy has long emphasised a principle of not interfering in the domestic affairs of other states. This has proven attractive to many authoritarian countries. At the same time, China has successfully advanced major global economic initiatives, notably the Belt and Road Initiative. And Beijing often promotes its own vision of the international order.

As such, Russia’s proposed security framework would need to accommodate another major power with its own interests and priorities.

Despite their growing cooperation in recent years, China and Russia are also competing for influence in a pivotal Eurasian region – Central Asia. While Russia has traditionally been the dominant power in the region, China has quietly advanced to the point where it can now compete with, if not surpass, Russia’s influence.

What the rest of Asia wants

Lastly, Eurasia is already home to a complex landscape of international organisations, blocs and multilateral security agreements. Beyond the European Union, these include the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, the BRICS (the group originally comprised of Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa), and the Gulf Cooperation Council, among others.

Each of these groupings has its own distinct strategic interests and priorities. So, it remains unclear how a new Russia-led security framework would interact with these groups, or potentially compete with them.

Indeed, there seems to be a growing preference, especially in Asia, for smaller alliances between countries with similar ideological world views, such as the new security pact between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey.

At the same time, other nations, particularly those in Southeast Asia, have held fast to their non-aligned status, preferring to seek partnerships with an array of countries that suit a variety of interests.

Read more:
What Australia could learn from its Southeast Asian neighbours about power and the changing global order

What comes next?

We may be witnessing the gradual erosion of the post-second world war international order. Now, the big question is what comes next.

While Russia’s aims seem reminiscent of Soviet influence during the Cold War, this is a new world, and there are too many hurdles for its vision of a new security framework to become a reality.

New international orders do not emerge overnight. Rather, they evolve through the cumulative decisions of states pursuing their own interests, forming new alignments, alliances and partnerships along the way.

Dilnoza Ubaydullaeva receives funding from the Japan Foundation Program.

articles.title: Elon Musk has approval to launch 1 million satellites. An astronomer explains how this would impact the sky
articles.summary:
A long-exposure image of the Orion Nebula with a total exposure time of 208 minutes showing satellite trails in mid-December 2019. A. H. Abolfath/Wikimedia

This week, on the eve the Thanksgiving holiday, the United States Federal Communications Commission approved SpaceX’s plan to launch one million “Starmind” artificial intelligence (AI) data centre satellites. This decision reflects the convergence of a satellite boom, an AI bubble and the Trump administration’s disregard for environmental regulation.

If Starmind proceeds in full, the number of operational satellites will be multiplied by a factor of 50. Space and our night skies will become vastly busier places.

SpaceX’s pitch is to take the impact of data centres away from Earth, using a million solar-powered satellites to do AI data crunching in space and beam the results to Earth.

But what is the impact of one million satellites, both in space and on Earth? Why has the Federal Communications Commission made this decision? And will a million satellites actually end up in orbit?

Ups and downs

We are currently in a satellite boom, and constellations of hundreds or thousands of satellites are a key feature.

The Starlink internet satellites (another SpaceX project) is the best known example of such a constellation. Orbital rocket launches have increased to almost one per day, while the number of operational satellites is creeping towards 20,000.

But Starmind represents something else. A million satellites.

To get so many satellites into orbit would be a vast undertaking. If the satellites have a lifetime of five years (similar to Starlink satellites), then roughly 500 satellites would need to be launched every day.

This also implies that roughly 500 satellites would eventually need to be disposed of every day. For satellites less than 2,000 kilometres above Earth, disposal usually means reentry and burning up in the atmosphere. And this has consequences.

When satellites burn up in the atmosphere, their materials react with and are deposited into the upper atmosphere. We now have satellites depositing far more aluminium, titanium, copper and lead into the atmosphere than the natural quantities from meteors.

Aluminium is of particular concern, as alumina can lead to the destruction of ozone in the upper atmosphere. This could increase ultraviolet light on Earth and the risk of skin cancers.

It’s getting busy

Increasing the number of satellites by a factor of 50 is going to change our view of the sky.

If you look up during the early evening, you will see the stars your ancestors saw. But within a minute or two you will see a satellite. A point of light silently moving from horizon to horizon.

Satellites are already common enough, and Starmind would make matters worse.

Our view of the night skies could fundamentally change.

Each satellite would be 75 metres wide and in the early evening they will be brighter than any star. And with a million satellites in orbit, there will be hundreds of Starmind satellites above the horizon irrespective of where you are.

The orbital clutter comes with real risks.

Satellites travel at speeds of roughly seven kilometres per second, and collisions produce clouds of debris that can produce further collisions. A nightmare scenario is the Kessler Syndrome – a runaway cascade of debris producing collisions that render low Earth orbit unusable.

Of course, SpaceX is aware of the risks of orbital collisions, and it already mitigates this risk with Starlink by manoeuvring satellites away from potential collisions. However, such manoeuvres require operational satellites and it is inevitable some satellites will fail.

Those uncontrolled satellites will pose a real danger.

Regulator or promoter?

The Federal Communications Commission has been a key regulator for American satellites. This has included regulating the radio frequencies that satellites use for communications to and from Earth, the disposal of satellites at the end of their useful lives and environmental impacts.

However, under the Trump administration, the commission is taking a looser approach to regulating satellites. This includes no consideration of environmental impacts, which is reflected in the commission’s decision on Starmind. It says the commission “will not require further environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act […] for SpaceX’s Starmind system”.

There are also some statements from the commission on Starmind that are, quite frankly, bizarre. For example, it claims Starmind “promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization – one that can harness the full power of the sun”.

This is sci-fi silliness. A Kardashev II civilisation would need many trillions of square kilometres of technology in orbit around the Sun. Starmind is not a stepping stone to a vast “Dyson sphere” – a hypothetical megastrucutre that would surround the Sun and capture its energy.

But can it work?

One reason data centres are so unpopular on Earth is their use of precious resources, including water for cooling hot computer processors. But cooling in space is harder still. When stuck in a vacuum, one can only radiate heat away. And if you are familiar with vacuum flasks, you will know this can be a slow process.

Of course, it is possible to regulate heat in space, and satellites do it all the time. But they typically aren’t pouring out heat like data centres do.

Google recently launched an AI demonstrator satellite into orbit and tasked it with undertaking AI calculations. But it had to have downtime between calculations to dispose of excess heat.

And apart from the physics there’s the finance.

Right now we are in an AI boom, with the inflow of investment being vastly higher than revenues. And the cost of deploying AI in orbit will be vastly higher than equivalent AI on Earth.

If the AI boom is a bubble, then the burst can bring Starmind back to Earth.

Michael J. I. Brown does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Got a frozen shoulder? It could be down to your blood sugar and genes
articles.summary:
Frozen shoulder can make everyday movements difficult – and it’s more common in people with diabetes. PeopleImages/Shutterstock

Frozen shoulder can develop seemingly out of nowhere. One day your shoulder feels uncomfortable. A few months later, even putting on a coat or reaching into a cupboard can be difficult. Research on blood sugar offers a clue to why some people are more likely to develop it, particularly those living with diabetes.

Pain is often the first symptom, particularly at night. Over time, the shoulder grows stiffer. The flexible tissue that wraps around the joint, called the shoulder capsule, thickens and tightens, making it harder to move the arm.

That stiffness is a clue when a doctor or physiotherapist examines the shoulder. Even when someone else tries to move your arm for you, the movement is restricted. This is often most noticeable when they turn the arm outwards. The condition often improves, although recovery can take months or years.

Frozen shoulder is estimated to affect 2% to 5% of people and is most common between the ages of 40 and 60. It’s more common in women and people with diabetes are at higher risk. It can also develop after an injury or operation that stops you moving the arm as usual. Often there’s no clear trigger.

In type 1 diabetes, the body makes little or no insulin, the hormone that helps control blood sugar. In type 2 diabetes, the body makes too little insulin or has trouble using it. In a 2014 study, nearly a third of participants reported a history of frozen shoulder. They had lived with type 1 diabetes for an average of 31 years. A 2021 study using genetic data also found evidence that type 1 diabetes increases the risk of frozen shoulder.

High blood sugar

A 2024 study using data from nearly 380,000 UK Biobank participants investigated whether raised blood sugar might help explain that link. Some inherited differences in DNA are linked to higher blood sugar. Because those differences are present from birth, they give researchers a kind of natural experiment. They can use them to estimate the effects of having higher blood sugar over many years, something a single blood test can’t capture. The study found evidence that persistently higher blood sugar makes frozen shoulder more likely.

One possible explanation is that sugar gradually changes the structure of the tissue around the joint. Sugars can react with collagen, a protein that gives the tissue much of its strength. The substances formed in that reaction can join collagen fibres together, making the tissue less flexible. In one small study of tissue taken during shoulder surgery, researchers found stronger signs of these compounds in samples from people with frozen shoulder than in samples from people with other shoulder problems. It’s a clue to how the tissue might stiffen. To find out whether these substances help cause frozen shoulder, researchers would need to know whether they build up before the shoulder stiffens.

Long-term high blood sugar has been linked to both frozen shoulder and Dupuytren’s disease, a hand condition that can make it difficult to straighten the fingers.
gdragan/Shutterstock

A 2021 study found five stretches of DNA linked to frozen shoulder. The strongest link was near a gene called WNT7B, which helps cells send signals to one another. Intriguingly, the same stretch of DNA has also been linked to Dupuytren’s disease, a condition in which tissue in the palm thickens and can pull the fingers inwards, making them hard to straighten. This suggests the two conditions may share some of the processes that cause tissue to thicken and tighten. The blood-sugar study found another link. Years of higher blood sugar appeared to make Dupuytren’s disease more likely, too.

For people with diabetes, persistent shoulder stiffness is worth bringing up at a routine appointment, especially if it’s starting to interfere with sleep or everyday tasks. For clinicians, it deserves attention alongside more familiar problems diabetes can cause in the eyes and kidneys. Whether improving blood sugar control can help prevent frozen shoulder or speed up recovery once it has developed is still an open question.

articles.title: Expert reaction: what the Timms review into Pip disability benefits gets right – and where it falls short
articles.summary:
Zamrznuti tonovi/Shutterstock

Personal independence payments (Pip) are UK-wide benefits that are meant to help people with long-term health issues cope with the extra costs associated with their conditions. But it’s controversial – from the application process to who qualifies.

Sir Stephen Timms, the disability minister, has published a long-awaited report into Pip, recommending a raft of changes to the system.

Here’s what experts made of his findings.

‘Constant dread’ during the application process

Stephanie Allan, Research Associate in Mental Health & Wellbeing, University of Glasgow

Humanising the benefits system, as Timms claims his review will, is crucial. As part of our research, participants told us that applying and being assessed for disability benefits such as Pip has caused psychological distress, particularly for those applying due to conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder or schizophrenia.

We’ve been told assessments can feel like “being on trial”, with constant dread of unexpected letters coming through the door, and can even cause re-traumatisation.

The review’s call to reduce unnecessary reviews and improve communication between assessors and applicants may address these issues – as may its suggestion of training assessors in trauma-informed practice. This means they should offer consistency and transparency in explaining how decisions are made and not minimising people’s difficulties.

Some people living with serious mental health problems face profound challenges and struggle to do things many people take for granted. The report proposes fast-tracked paths for peopel who have “serious, well-evidenced conditions whose impact on their daily life is clear”. But it’s ambiguous which conditions this will cover, and this could also cause worry for potential Pip recipients.

While the Timms review acknowledges the impact of stigma, our work emphasises how negative media reporting and politicians’ speeches about disability benefits can cause distress, especially if it frames claimants as burdens. It can also influence how people respond, and make them even more afraid to participate in society.

People with fluctuating mental health problems have told us that fears of being falsely reported for fraud by neighbours and community members can make them avoid activities such as volunteering, exercise, or even taking part in clinical research that could improve mental health for them or others in future.

Training on trauma-informed care is arguably not enough on its own. Without stronger legal safeguards – such as independent oversight when things go wrong – the power imbalance between claimants and those in charge remains intact.

Furthermore, reforming the claiming process by itself will not make people feel safe if political rhetoric and media narratives continue to frame disabled people as a burden.

Every day is different when you’re disabled

Steve Atkin-Teillet, Lecturer in Law, Nottingham Law School

The nature of some conditions means that symptoms can fluctuate from day to day. The review found that in order to capture the varying nature of a claimant’s needs, the Pip application form should be changed so that it’s simpler for claimants to report what they experience.

This should be underpinned by better training for Pip assessors on the rules surrounding variances and fluctuations in what someone is able to do. This should not only include a requirement to assess whether someone can perform an activity, but also whether they can do so reliably.

Stephen Timms’ report claims it will ‘humanise the benefits system’
House of Commons/Flickr, CC BY

Right now, a claimant should only be considered capable of a task if they can do it safely, repeatedly and in a reasonable amount of time. In 2024, I recommended that the new Pip form include these three elements under each activity the claimant describes, as well as on the government’s Pip advice page.

At present, people claiming Pip can be assessed by any type of medical professional. Someone applying for mental health reasons could be given a physiotherapist as their assessor. This is a concern, as claimants sometimes feel their assessor was not competent or well placed to understand their condition.

The Timms review proposes a specific Pip assessor role – but this doesn’t fully address concerns over competency. As it stands, it’s unclear how someone in this new role would be trained to assess a full range of potential disabilities and conditions.

More understanding of neurodiversity since Pip launched

Mindy Ptolomey, Lecturer in Disability Studies, University of Leeds

The review has highlighted that when Pip was designed and implemented – back in 2012 under David Cameron’s coalition government – it did not consider the barriers neurodivergent people face in everyday life. Neither did it take into account their needs in terms of the application process. As pointed out in the interim report of the review, long paper forms with no online version, rigid deadlines, and having to use the phone can all create barriers for neurodivergent people.

Read more:
The Milburn report sets out a plan to improve the lives of young people who are Neet – experts respond

The review’s recognition of neurodivergent people’s needs is especially important as the diagnosis of ADHD and autism has increased in recent years. In the UK, new adult autism diagnoses increased more than tenfold from 2010 to 2023, and monthly referrals for ADHD diagnosis more than tripled between 2019 and 2024.

A government review published last month highlights that there is no evidence of widespread over-diagnosis. These increases are instead due to a range of factors like historical under-recognition and greater awareness.

It’s encouraging to see a continued commitment to involving disabled people during the design and implementation stages of any reforms. Disabled people were part of the review’s steering group and their views were included in a range of ways. However, more can be done to make sure the people who face the greatest barriers are included in shaping reforms. Involving neurodivergent people is important for ensuring the core purposes of Pip are delivered supporting disabled people’s independence, participation and autonomy.

Pip can make an important contribution to meeting the additional costs of being disabled, for those in and out of work. The review recommends linking the amount people will receive through Pip more closely to the additional costs they face due to disability or health conditions.

However, questions remain about how these costs will be identified and calculated. Previous data shows that it is difficult for disabled people to understand the additional costs of being disabled, especially when you’ve had a condition all your life, which is the case for neurodivergent people.

Mental health conditions could face cuts

Sarah Ledden, Research Associate in Population Mental Health, King’s College London

One key element of the proposed reforms is to only provide Pip to those who incur additional costs due to a long-term health condition or disability. The challenge here will be creating appropriate mechanisms to assess these costs, without repeating current difficulties the system has in evaluating fluctuating and ‘harder-to-see’ conditions.

The Department for Work and Pensions recently released a research report which aimed to understand the disability-related needs that create additional living costs among Pip recipients. It indicated that people with mental health conditions were less likely to have additional costs for equipment and travel needs, though they did more often have paid treatment needs (such as counselling).

However, these people experience employment and income gaps, earning 32% less than people with no such conditions, and higher levels of financial hardship. This indicates that there are often financial challenges for people with mental health conditions, but many of these costs may be hidden or cumulative.

If the transition to a new benefit is managed poorly, with proposed impact assessments not designed to capture these types of costs, it risks people with mental health conditions being left behind. The Timms review has recommendations around understanding inequalities in experiences and outcomes of different groups, which will be vital in ensuring the system works.

The DWP’s evidence published with the review reported that only 1 in 5 Pip claimants reported having a single condition. Most people reported multiple conditions. Only 4.4% of total Pip claims are those solely claiming for depression and anxiety, with these more often reported alongside other conditions.

The rise in these cases is based on the “primary condition” reported on Pip claims, although this is in line with evidence that these conditions are rising in the general population.

Previous research from our team on Pip receipt among people who accessed specialist mental healthcare found that receiving Pip is related to greater clinical need (including diagnosis type and longer time receiving care). If the government aims to reduce welfare spending by assessing mental health Pip claims using stricter criteria, this may not have as big an impact as they expect.

Stephanie Allan currently receives funding from the Chief Scientist Office at the University of Glasgow.

Mindy Ptolomey has previously received funding from the Economic Social Research Council and the British Academy.

articles.title: Indonesia’s huge peat fires burn underground – so we still don’t know just how much carbon they have released
articles.summary:
A recent peatland forest fire in South Kalimantan, Indonesia, one of thousands across the country this year. Amazing Aerial / shutterstock

At the peak of Indonesia’s 2026 wildfire season, we were in Palangka Raya, a city of 300,000 people surrounded by dense peatland rainforest. Smoke covered the city in a thick yellow haze. Between mid-September and mid-October, we recorded air pollution levels equivalent to smoking about 14 cigarettes per day. On the worst days, that rose to around 30.

Our colleague Sanz Rio Griffio Limin is from the region and works at Cimtrop, a peatland research centre at the local university. “This year the fires are the worst in my lifetime,” he told us. “I am 41, and I have never seen this kind of smoke and fires.”

Unlike most wildfires, peatland fires burn beneath the ground as well as above it. These underground fires can smoulder for weeks or months and are notoriously difficult to extinguish.

Peat has accumulated carbon from dead plants over thousands of years. When it burns, that carbon is released into the atmosphere. The deeper the fire burns, the more carbon it releases.

Indonesia has wildfires every year, but they’re significantly more intense in El Niño years like this one, when there is less rain and the ground dries out further.

The country last experienced wildfires on this scale in 2015, another El Niño year. In September and October that year, Indonesia’s peat fires were releasing carbon dioxide faster than the entire European Union.

But estimates of emissions from these fires remain uncertain because we have surprisingly few direct measurements of how deeply the peat burns. That’s why one of us (Maria) travelled to Palangka Raya to join an international team of researchers measuring how much peat these fires consume and how much carbon they emit, alongside colleagues at Cimtrop, where our co-author Kitso is based.

Measuring the hidden fires

Burning peat has a particularly intense smell, which penetrated even through our face masks and other protective gear. That smell, and the wall of heat and smoke, would hit us the moment we arrived and stepped out of an air-conditioned car.

We had to be constantly vigilant for unseen underground fires and the risk of falling into a peat fire pit. Surface fires would sometimes spontaneously ignite within a few feet of our team.

Researchers at a recently burned site measuring soil moisture and density, water table depth and peat burn depth.
PEAKFire

The scale of the burning was extraordinary. Reaching some sites meant driving for up to 45 minutes along narrow clay tracks through an almost post-apocalyptic landscape. At the sites, fires had consumed peat underground, burning away tree roots and causing them to collapse.

Previous research suggests the water level needs to remain within about 40 centimetres of the peat surface to reduce fire risk. This year, we measured water tables between 2 and 4 metres below the surface – leaving huge layers of dry peat available to burn.

Across ten sites, we used drones and ground surveys to measure how deeply the peat had burned and estimate how much had been consumed by fire. We also collected soil samples and recorded greenhouse gas emissions from burned and unburned peat. At active fires, we measured gases released by smouldering peat, including carbon dioxide and methane, and invisible but toxic air pollution particles.

Why it matters

The impacts of Indonesian peat fires extend far beyond areas that burn. Smoke is transported across borders, affecting millions of people across south-east Asia, disrupting daily life and causing widespread health problems. In years like 2015 or 2026, Indonesia’s peat fires are also one of the largest sources of carbon emitted into the atmosphere, anywhere in the world.

This fire burned the top 40cm or so of peat. In a fire like this, burning peat will emit far more carbon than surface vegetation.
Kitso Kusin

However, estimates remain uncertain because we still don’t fully understand how burn depth and emissions vary under different peat conditions. Measurements from our fieldwork this year will help improve these estimates and strengthen smoke forecasting systems in Indonesia and surrounding countries.

We also helped local researchers deploy an additional 25 low-cost air pollution particle sensors to track smoke exposure across urban and rural areas close to peatland environments during future fire seasons.

The peat fires and haze crisis in Indonesia are largely a human-made disaster caused by peatlands being drained and degraded, making them more vulnerable to fires during droughts. Restoration can reduce this risk by raising the water table and rewetting the peat, for example, through wells or by blocking drainage canals.

These measures can reduce the number of fires. However, restoration cannot fully restore the fire resistance of intact peatlands. Protecting remaining intact peatlands while restoring those that have already been drained and degraded is our best opportunity to reduce future fire risk, protect communities from hazardous smoke and preserve globally important carbon stores.

Ailish Graham receives funding from UK Research and Innovation.
This work was funded by a NERC Urgency Grant, it brought together a team from CIMTROP, University of Palangka Raya, London School of Economics, Liverpool John Moores University and University of Leeds.

Kitso Kusin works for the organization (university).
