articles.title: Grand Theft Auto 6: how gaming technology is helping everyone from scientists to filmmakers
articles.summary:
In Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6), released on November 19, players can explore the streets of Vice City and the surrounding fictional US state of Leonida. The game’s detailed environments reflect years of work to make digital experiences feel as close as possible to real life.

Aside from what hopefully amounts to great gameplay, this sort of realism is likely to be surprisingly useful in other fields. A US-German team of researchers has already used images from GTA 5 to help AI systems recognise roads, cars and buildings for technologies like self-driving cars. Because the game already contained data on the objects within it, the team were able to use this to label 25,000 images for training their AI system in just 49 hours. It would have taken several years to hand-label the same number of real photographs.

Many ways of benefiting from gaming technology relate to their engines, which are the software platforms used to build and run a game. GTA uses a proprietary engine developed by its maker Rockstar Games, but other prominent engines include Unity and Unreal Engine. These are helping everyone from engineers to designers to researchers to understand, test and interact with the real world in new ways.

One example comes from a project I worked on with colleagues exploring the diving tradition associated with Mostar’s old bridge in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Using Unity, we created a reconstruction that allowed users to explore the site in virtual reality, hear from a local diver and even experience a simulated dive from the bridge. The aim was to help people who weren’t familiar with Mostar to engage with this tradition and understand its significance.

That sense of being in a place also depends on what we hear. The way a voice echoes
around a church can convey something about its size and atmosphere. With colleagues, I have explored how to recreate the acoustics of historic buildings alongside their appearance.

This includes a case study of Panagia Angeloktisti, a Byzantine church in Cyprus. Our team used filtering techniques employed in game audio to recreate how sound behaves within a virtual space like this church. The sound appeared to be affected by the environment in which it was generated, like in a real building.

Virtual diving off the old bridge in Mostar.

Yet creating a convincing digital simulation is only part of the challenge. Understanding how people interact with these experiences is just as important as building them.

During the Mostar project, we carried out user testing to see if participants used the virtual environment in the way we had expected. The results led us to change an aspect of the interface that helped users to move around in the virtual setting.
It was a small adjustment, but it showed why researchers cannot assume people will interpret digital experiences as intended. Testing with real users remains essential.

The same principle applies in engineering and robotics. In a project with the UK-based visualisation engineer Marius Matulis, we trained an AI system to operate a virtual robot arm inside Unity, enabling the AI system to move objects around. We then linked the robot arm’s movements to a physical, 3D-printed arm. The goal was to see whether skills learned by the AI in a digital environment could transfer to the physical world.

This approach is known as “sim-to-real” transfer. Researchers can repeat tasks and try different approaches in simulation before testing them on a real machine. Similar techniques have been used, for instance, to train drones to navigate unfamiliar environments, including forests and damaged buildings.

That said, the physical world rarely behaves exactly like a simulation. Sensors make errors, movements can be delayed and conditions change. Researchers call this the “reality gap”. Closing it means checking how a machine performs in the real world and improving the simulation where it falls short.

Creative decisions

Game technology is also transforming the creative industries. One example is Disney’s The Mandalorian. The production used Unreal Engine to generate digital environments displayed on massive LED screens surrounding actors and physical sets. These included indoor and outdoor settings that might otherwise have entailed building expensive sets or extensive travel for location filming.

Filmmakers could see and work with these digital worlds during filming. This changed how scenes were lit, framed and planned, bringing technical and creative teams together earlier in the production process.

The virtual production of The Mandalorian season one (Inudstrial Light & Magic).

What connects these examples is the power of interactive simulation. Whether preserving cultural heritage, training robots or producing films, game technologies create environments where ideas can be explored, tested and refined, then put to work in the real world.

At Manchester Metropolitan University’s school of digital arts (SODA), this is exactly the kind of work we’re immersed in. As GTA 6 draws attention to what is possible in digital entertainment, these projects show why game technology matters elsewhere too. Its value lies in what we can do with the worlds we build, and how they help us understand and shape the world we live in.

Carlo Harvey's research has received funding from UKRI, AHRC, EPSRC, Innovate UK, the National Lottery Heritage Fund and Epic Games, and equipment support from Nvidia. He co-leads FUSE-M at Manchester Metropolitan University, which has been allocated funding through the Greater Manchester Combined Authority's Good Growth Fund.

articles.title: Nicotine-free vaping may still harm blood vessels – small MRI study
articles.summary:
Alones/Shutterstock.com

A nicotine-free vape sounds like a safer choice. Yet new research found that just one session of vaping, with no nicotine in it, can affect how blood vessels work.

The study, which was presented at the annual meeting of the Radiological Society of North America, identified changes in blood flow and oxygen levels following just one episode of vaping, regardless of whether the e-cigarette contained nicotine. The findings raise an important question. Have we been focusing too much on nicotine and not enough on what else we are inhaling?

E-cigarettes, commonly known as vapes, are battery-powered devices that heat a liquid to produce an aerosol vapour. Unlike conventional cigarettes, they do not burn tobacco, meaning users are exposed to fewer harmful chemicals.

The cloud that people inhale and exhale, however, is not simply water vapour. Most vaping liquids contain a mixture of propylene glycol, vegetable glycerine and flavouring chemicals. Although some of these ingredients are used in food production, eating a substance is not the same as inhaling it.

When heated, these liquids can produce potentially harmful chemicals, including formaldehyde and acrolein. Research has also identified tiny particles of metals, including nickel, chromium and lead, in vaping aerosols. Some originate from the metal coil used to heat the liquid. Simply removing the nicotine does not remove these substances.

What happens in blood vessels?

Blood vessels are more than a network of pipes transporting blood around the body. They are living structures that constantly adjust to the changing demands of our organs.

The inner lining of our blood vessels, known as the endothelium, produces a chemical called nitric oxide. This allows blood vessels to relax and widen, increasing blood flow when our tissues need more oxygen.

When we exercise, for example, blood vessels widen to deliver more oxygen to our working muscles. When this process becomes impaired, it is known as endothelial dysfunction, which is a very early feature of cardiovascular disease.

In the latest study, researchers recruited 41 otherwise healthy adults, aged between 20 and 50, who had smoked, vaped or used both products daily for more than a year. A further 17 people who had never smoked or vaped acted as a comparison (control) group.

Using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), researchers examined participants before and after three separate activities: smoking a cigarette, vaping with nicotine and vaping without nicotine. They measured several aspects of cardiovascular health, including how effectively blood vessels responded to changing oxygen demands and the stiffness of the aorta, the largest artery in the body.

Following all three activities, researchers found a reduction in the amount of oxygen remaining in blood returning from the leg. This could suggest that vaping temporarily interferes with the ability to transfer oxygen in the lungs into the bloodstream, although changes in blood flow and oxygen use by tissues could also explain the findings.

Surprisingly, vaping affected more of the measurements investigated than smoking did. This does not mean that vaping is more harmful than smoking. But it does challenge the assumption that nicotine-free vaping is harmless.

Vape liquids contain propylene glycol, vegetable glycerine and flavouring chemicals.
Rawpixel/Shutterstock.com

These findings chime with earlier research. In a study published in 2019, 31 healthy non-smokers were exposed to nicotine-free vaping aerosol. After a single session, the ability of an artery in the leg to widen in response to increased blood flow was reduced by 34%.

A 2022 study also found that regular e-cigarette users and cigarette smokers had poorer blood vessel function than non-users.

More recently, research published in 2025 found that smoking and vaping can affect how well the blood vessels supplying the heart regulate blood flow. This means the vessels may be less able to increase the blood supply to the heart when it needs more oxygen, such as during exercise.

One possible explanation is oxidative stress, which occurs when the body produces more reactive molecules than it can get rid of. These molecules can reduce levels of nitric oxide and cause inflammation, which can damage blood vessels and contribute to heart disease.

However, not all studies agree. A clinical trial published in 2018 found changes in blood vessel function following vaping with nicotine, but not without it. Differences in vaping devices, ingredients and research methods may partly explain these conflicting findings.

The latest study involved relatively few people and looked only at short-term effects. It is still unclear whether repeated exposure causes lasting harm or increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes.

It is important not to overlook the benefits of vaping for people trying to stop smoking.

A large, well-conducted review found that nicotine-containing e-cigarettes were more effective at helping people quit smoking than nicotine replacement products such as patches and gum.

The NHS advises that vaping is less harmful than smoking but is not risk-free.

Nicotine-free vaping may remove the addictive ingredient, but it does not remove all the potential health risks. Being nicotine-free is not the same as being harm-free. And that is a distinction that should not be overlooked.

David C. Gaze does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Black Friday: consumer behaviour expert on what’s really behind our need to chase bargains
articles.summary:
vetre/Shutterstock

Black Friday is a highly successful US export. The retail strategy designed to kickstart festive shopping has become a global phenomenon.

But are the hype and the pressure (and the occasional fight over electrical hardware) worth it? After all, most products on offer during Black Friday are available at the same price (or even less) at other times of the year.

So why do so many people still join in? Here are some of the marketing tricks and psychological drivers that help to explain the appeal of Black Friday.

Marketing push

Offers that exist for a limited time period are among the oldest retail marketing tricks in the book. And there is plenty of research which shows that they reliably increase a shopper’s intention to buy.

If we think a deal will disappear after Black Friday, the fear of missing out on a bargain can push us towards buying that air fryer or scented candle. Or we might buy it to avoid the potential feelings of regret that may come if we don’t.

Price tags also have a big effect. Psychologists have shown that when making value judgments, the first number we see disproportionately shapes how we evaluate subsequent numbers.

So when a price tag reads: “"Was £100! Now £60!”, the £100 figure is the one we latch on to. This makes £60 feel like a £40 saving rather than a £60 expense, even if the item was never really worth £100 in the first place.

Consumer pull

While many people will be aware of these kinds of retail marketing tricks, they will still willingly participate in Black Friday. This may be partly due to its timing, but also to the psychological rewards that shopping could offer.

In the northern hemisphere at least, Black Friday coincides with the “winter blues”, potentially offering a source of excitement as the days get colder and darker. We may also shop to improve our mood with a little “retail therapy”.

One explanation for the effectiveness of retail therapy is that negative emotions often come from situations we cannot change. Making choices about what we want and then buying those things might help us to restore a feeling of personal control.

Another reason is that buying generally might bring more positive than negative emotions. But studies have also shown that the temporary uplift from purchasing does not last as long as we often think it will.

Landing a bargain can also make us feel good about ourselves. Being a “smart shopper” has been linked to a personal sense of achievement and pride when we secure a good deal. Buying things at a (genuine) discount can also demonstrate competence and good financial management to others.

But that is not the only social appeal of Black Friday. Even the most independently minded consumer can be influenced by what other people do. And engaging in an activity at the same time as others, even among strangers, can temporarily enhance feelings of social connection.

What are we really buying?

Despite the thrill of a bargain, or joining in with a commercial social event, what feels rewarding in the moment may not necessarily contribute to our longer-term wellbeing.

Research in consumption has shown that spending money on things that fit our personality or that help us with personal goals might be a good idea. For example, an extrovert or someone looking to develop new connections will probably benefit more from spending money on social activities than buying a discounted item.

Read more:
Eight ways to resist spending too much on Black Friday bargains

But why we buy is as important as what we buy. In a recent study, my colleagues and I found that spending money in response to social pressure, to gain status or to seek others’ approval was linked to low wellbeing. So even experiences do not always bring more happiness.

Our expectations can also mislead us. In another study I worked on, my colleagues and I found that people thought that buying new clothes would make them feel better about themselves than buying second-hand clothes. But it turned out that buying old and new clothes had pretty much the same effect.

Stuff for sale.
Elena Rostunova/Shutterstock

More broadly, research shows that focusing on economic gains and consumption brings a lower sense of wellbeing and is detrimental to our personal relationships.

In contrast, choosing to live more simply or buying less is consistently linked with greater wellbeing. People who become less focused on material goals tend to become happier over time.

So perhaps Black Friday should not simply be about how much money we are saving or how much temporary joy our purchases might bring us. Maybe it’s a time to reflect on what we gain from spending more money on more stuff, and whether there might be more sustainable and lasting alternatives.

Olaya Moldes Andrés had received funding from the British Academy and the Academy of Marketing.

articles.title: Myanmar genocide ruling presents China with a dilemma
articles.summary:
The recent ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority in 2017 challenges China both economically and politically.

China is a close strategic partner of Myanmar. It has substantial economic interests in Rakhine, the state on Myanmar’s western coast where the atrocities against the Rohingya occurred.

Oil and gas pipelines connect the coast to China, starting around Maday Island and Kyaukphyu, farther south than the areas central to the genocide case.

China also has a close, longstanding diplomatic relationship with Myanmar, which it has maintained since the military seized power there in a 2021 coup.

Myanmar’s president, Min Aung Hlaing, paid a state visit to China in 2026 during which both countries pledged to deepen political and security cooperation. A withdrawal from these relationships would carry costs for Beijing.

The ICJ’s recent judgment does not order China to end diplomatic ties with Myanmar. Its binding force applies only to the parties in the case.

But the ruling, which marks the first time a state has been held responsible for committing a genocide, changes the legal context around China’s engagement with Myanmar.

China is now confronted with a difficult dilemma: how far can Beijing defend its partner and its own strategic interests while maintaining its stated support for international justice?

A diplomatic dilemma

The ICJ ruling orders Myanmar to cease any ongoing violations against the Rohingya, prevent similar violations from occurring in the future and to prosecute those involved in committing the genocide. It also orders Myanmar to allow the return of displaced Rohingya and the reunification of families.

In a statement released on November 19, the same day the ICJ issued its judgment, the UN Refugee Agency said more than 1.3 million Rohingya refugees remain displaced. Most of these people are currently living in Bangladesh, while over 200,000 remain internally displaced in Myanmar’s Rakhine state.

In its response to the ruling, China acknowledged the importance of international judicial institutions. However, it expressed concern that the ICJ had acted beyond its jurisdiction and flagged “overreach in interpretation”. Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun denounced this approach as “not conducive to the settlement of disputes”.

This response is in line with China’s stated foreign policy principle of non-interference in other countries’ internal affairs. The principle of non-interference is itself part of international law, to protect state sovereignty and political independence.

But so is the prohibition of genocide. China is party to the 1948 Genocide Convention, which requires states to prevent and punish it. The ICJ ruling makes it harder for Beijing to justify diplomatic restraint over Myanmar solely on the grounds of sovereignty.

China could urge Myanmar’s military leadership to investigate the crimes committed against the Rohingya by its own forces. But such pressure would almost certainly strain cooperation between the two countries on border security and investment. Myanmar has rejected the ICJ’s ruling, calling it “unfair”.

The Gambia, which filed the complaint with the court in 2019, can seek action from the UN security council if Myanmar fails to comply with the ICJ ruling. As a permanent member of the UN security council, China can veto substantive council resolutions – and it has done so in Myanmar’s favour before.

China, alongside Russia, vetoed a draft security council resolution in 2007 that criticised Myanmar’s human rights record. It could block future UN sanctions on Myanmar as well. But a veto would deepen diplomatic divisions between China and governments seeking to enforce the judgment.

Fourteen countries, including the UK and Canada, have called for Myanmar’s full compliance with the ruling. In any case, blocking attempts from the international community to enforce the ICJ’s orders would leave Myanmar’s legal obligations to redress the genocide intact.

Rohingya citizens fleeing Myanmar for Bangladesh in 2017.
Photo Gallarys / Shutterstock

In its response to the ruling, Beijing pledged to play “a constructive role” in facilitating the return of Rohingya refugees to Rakhine state. This suggests Beijing may look to present mediation as helping Myanmar meet its international obligations to redress the genocide.

But safe refugee return will require cooperation beyond Myanmar’s military leadership. The Arakan Army, one of Myanmar’s many ethnic armed groups, controls much of the territory where Rohingya refugees would return.

Beijing would need commitments from the Myanmar military and Arakan Army to protect returning families. These parties are currently engaged in intense fighting across Rakhine state. And even if the safety of refugees is guaranteed, their return alone would leave the court’s requirements for investigations and compensation unmet.

China has influence over Myanmar. Its response to the ICJ’s ruling will show whether it is willing to use this to support accountability when a strategic partner has been found responsible for genocide.

Xu Peng does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: GTA 6: four surprising ways playing video games could benefit your health
articles.summary:
Playing video games can offer opportunities to socialise, relieve stress and develop cognitive skills. Miljan Zivkovic/Shutterstock

After 13 years of anticipation, Grand Theft Auto 6 has finally arrived, with fans around the world celebrating the latest instalment of one of gaming’s most successful franchises.

The excitement surrounding its release has also brought renewed attention to a familiar debate: what effect does playing video games have on us?

Gaming has long been associated with concerns about addiction and social isolation. But depending on what we play and how we engage with it, gaming can offer benefits for our cognitive abilities, social lives and physical and mental wellbeing.

1. Developing cognitive skills

Playing an action game such as Grand Theft Auto can be mentally demanding. Navigating a busy virtual city while driving, monitoring your surroundings and responding to unexpected events requires considerable attention and an ability to process information quickly.

A 2022 study of 163 adults compared regular action video game players, whose preferred games included Grand Theft Auto and Assassin’s Creed, with people who rarely or never played video games.

The gamers performed better on tests of mental rotation, the ability to imagine how an object would look if turned in a different direction. They were also more accurate at keeping track of multiple moving objects.

However, the researchers could not establish whether gaming had developed these abilities or whether people with stronger spatial and attentional skills were naturally drawn to action games.

A review of experimental studies found that playing action games could improve our ability to focus on relevant information while ignoring distractions, as well as our understanding of spatial relationships. These skills are useful in everyday activities such as navigating unfamiliar places.

However, researchers continue to debate how far the skills developed through gaming translate into broader improvements in our thinking and learning.

2. Building social connections

Despite the perception that gaming is an isolating activity, many modern games are designed around interaction with other people. Online multiplayer games allow players to communicate, collaborate and maintain friendships across geographical distances.

A study of 2,213 gamers and 287 non-gamers in Germany found that social gamers were generally as well connected as non-gamers, and that spending more time playing socially increased the likelihood of forming friendships online. These connections became particularly valuable during the COVID pandemic, when people had fewer opportunities to meet in person.

Some games also encourage players to work together towards a shared goal. In massively multiplayer online games, where large numbers of people play in the same virtual world, team members may need to plan their approach and share information.

For instance, research into team communication in the game World of Tanks found that higher-ranked teams tended to communicate more before battles, although this does not establish that gaming improves teamwork outside the game.

Of course, online gaming communities can expose players to harassment or abusive behaviour. The social experience depends on the game, its community and the people involved.

3. Promoting wellbeing and relieving stress

Gaming can be something to look forward to after a long day at work, offering a chance to relax and put everyday responsibilities aside.

Completing a difficult level or overcoming an obstacle can also satisfy our psychological need for competence: the feeling that we are capable of achieving something. Even an unsuccessful attempt gives players an opportunity to adjust their approach and try again.

Games often described as “cosy” are particularly appealing to people who prefer a slower pace, achievable goals and a relaxed atmosphere. My personal favourite is the Animal Crossing series, in which players live alongside animal characters and take on tasks such as gardening and crafting.

In interviews with 27 families, researchers found that Animal Crossing: New Horizons helped some parents and children cope with pandemic-related stress. The National Videogame Museum’s Animal Crossing Diaries collects players’ experiences of the game during the pandemic.

Some games are designed specifically for health or education rather than entertainment alone. Known as “serious games”, they can be used as part of mental health interventions. A review of therapeutic games for young people found promising effects on anxiety and depression, although more rigorous research is needed.

4. Encouraging physical activity

Not all gaming involves sitting still. “Exergames” incorporate physical movement into play, through activities such as dancing or sports simulations.

These games can make exercise more appealing to people who find conventional workouts less engaging. Research on virtual-reality exercise suggests that adding game elements can increase enjoyment during high-intensity interval training.

My favourite example of a game that encourages physical activity is Pokémon Go. It encourages players to walk around their neighbourhoods to collect digital creatures and visit locations, using augmented reality to add virtual objects to a view of the real world.

A study using fitness trackers found that the most engaged Pokémon Go players increased their activity by an average of nearly 1,500 steps a day over a month. Whether that increase lasts in the longer term is less clear.

Finding the right balance

None of these benefits is guaranteed. Gaming can become harmful when it interferes with sleep, work, education or relationships.

The World Health Organization recognises gaming disorder as a condition involving impaired control over gaming and continued play despite significant negative consequences. Simply spending a lot of time playing does not amount to a diagnosis.

Read more:
From novels to GTA 6: the long history of fears about addictive entertainment

Why people play also matters. A review of research linked playing primarily to escape distressing experiences with problematic gaming, although those studies could not establish cause and effect.

Meanwhile, a large Oxford study found little evidence that the amount of time spent playing, on its own, substantially affected wellbeing.

While it is too early to establish the specific cognitive benefits of playing Grand Theft Auto 6, research into similar games suggests that navigating its virtual world could have some benefits.

Rather than judging all video games as good or bad, it is more useful to consider what people get from the games they enjoy and how gaming fits into the rest of their lives.

George Farmer does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Alzheimer’s drug targets tau protein in promising clinical trial
articles.summary:
pikselstock/Shutterstock.com

An experimental Alzheimer’s drug that reduces the production of a protein called tau has slowed the decline in memory and thinking skills by up to 54% in a clinical trial.

The drug, called diranersen, works differently from approved Alzheimer’s treatments. These focus on clearing amyloid, one of two proteins that build up abnormally in the brain. Diranersen targets the other protein – tau.

Amyloid forms sticky plaques between brain cells, while tau clumps together inside them, forming tangled structures. Both proteins damage brain cells, disrupting the signals they use to communicate and the processes that keep them alive.

Tau has an important job in a healthy brain. It helps stabilise tiny structures called microtubules, which act like railway tracks, transporting nutrients and other materials around brain cells.

In Alzheimer’s, tau changes structure, detaches from these tracks and clumps together inside brain cells, forming tangles. These tangles interfere with the cell’s internal transport system, contributing to its eventual death. The amount of tau accumulating in the brain is closely linked to how quickly people’s thinking skills decline.

Two drugs, lecanemab and donanemab, have been approved by most regulators (including in the US, Europe and the UK) for treating people with early-stage Alzheimer’s, although they are not available on the NHS.

Both help to remove amyloid plaques from the brain and modestly slow the decline in memory and thinking skills. Neither targets tau, and both can cause significant side-effects, including brain bleeds.

Tau tangles explained.

Researchers have found it harder to develop drugs that target tau. Several experimental treatments have used antibodies designed to recognise and destroy abnormal tau. However, these drugs have struggled to improve patients’ symptoms. The problem is that tau builds up inside brain cells, where antibodies find it difficult to reach.

Diranersen takes a different approach. Instead of trying to remove tangles that have already formed, it reduces how much tau brain cells produce in the first place.

The trial

The drug was tested in a phase 2 clinical trial, involving 416 people with early Alzheimer’s disease. Phase 2 is the stage when researchers investigate whether a drug appears to work and which dose is most effective.

The most promising results – which are yet to be peer-reviewed – came from the group given the lowest dose (60mg twice a year as an injection in the spine). After 96 weeks, 60 people taking this lower dose had 38% less decline compared with 115 participants originally assigned to placebo on a scale measuring memory, thinking skills and ability to carry out everyday activities.

On a separate test of cognitive performance, their decline was 54% slower. A third measure, assessing everyday activities, showed 30% less decline.

Most side-effects were mild. The most common were pain and headaches linked to the spinal injections, and short spells of confusion that typically cleared up within a week. The researchers found no new safety problems over the two years of follow-up.

Diranersen is a gene-silencing drug. It belongs to a class of medicines called antisense oligonucleotides, which are designed to switch off specific genetic instructions.

The drug attaches to messenger RNA – the molecule that carries the instructions for making tau – and causes it to break down. Without these instructions, brain cells make less of the protein.

Reducing tau raises an important question: could lowering a protein that brain cells need to function also cause harm? Studies in mice have suggested that substantially reducing tau does not significantly disrupt these processes, and the trial found no serious short-term side-effects. But nobody knows whether lowering tau in people is safe over many years.

How strong is the evidence?

There are important reasons to be cautious about the two-year results. They come from an extension of the original trial in which participants and researchers knew who was receiving the drug. After a year and a half, participants who had initially received a placebo were switched to diranersen. This meant researchers could no longer compare the drug with a placebo group over the full two years.

The original 18-month trial also failed to meet its main objective, which was to show that different doses produced a clear difference in clinical decline. Although some other measures showed improvements, missing this main target makes it harder to know how much confidence to place in the longer-term findings.

What is needed next is a much larger phase 3 trial, comparing the drug with a placebo in many more people. Regulators would want to see the results of such a trial before considering it for approval.

For years, Alzheimer’s research has concentrated on amyloid. Targeting tau offers another possible way to tackle the disease. Combining drugs that act on both proteins might eventually prove more effective than either approach alone. But both possibilities still need to be tested in larger trials.

Rahul Sidhu does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Creatine is popular with bodybuilders – could it help older adults stay independent?
articles.summary:
Creatine may give older adults a small extra gain in strength when combined with resistance training. Chay_Tee/Shutterstock

Climbing stairs or getting out of a chair can become harder with age, partly because muscle mass and strength tend to decline.

Resistance training, such as lifting weights or exercising with resistance bands, can help maintain muscle strength in later life. Research suggests that creatine, a supplement more commonly associated with bodybuilders and athletes, may help older adults gain a little more strength from this type of exercise. Whether that makes everyday tasks easier or helps people stay independent for longer is less clear.

Creatine is a naturally occurring compound that the body makes from amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. It’s also found in foods such as meat and fish. Most of the body’s creatine is stored in muscle, where it helps replenish the energy needed for short bursts of intense activity, such as lifting weights.

Taking creatine increases the amount available in muscles. That may let people complete a few more repetitions before their muscles tire. Over time, that extra work could help explain some of the gains in strength.

Muscle strength in later life

A 2026 review of 11 randomised trials found that adults aged 60 and over who added creatine to a resistance training programme gained slightly more strength than those who did the training without creatine. The review found no clear improvement in muscle mass or in how well people performed physical tasks.

Participants were generally healthy and were 67 on average, so the findings tell us less about people in their 80s and beyond. It’s also unclear whether the same benefits apply to people with sarcopenia, a condition in which low muscle strength is accompanied by reduced muscle mass or quality.

An earlier review found that people who took creatine gained about 1.3kg more lean tissue, on average, than those who took a placebo while following the same training programme. Measures of lean tissue include water. Creatine can make muscles hold more water, especially in the first few days, so it’s difficult to tell how much of that increase was new muscle.

When people take creatine without doing resistance training, some small studies suggest their muscles take longer to tire. The evidence for gains in strength is clearer for people who also train.

Everyday movement and falls

One way researchers test whether strength gains carry over into daily life is with the sit-to-stand test, also known as the chair-rise test. Researchers count how many times someone can stand up in 30 seconds or time how long it takes them to stand up five times, usually without using their arms for support.

A 2026 review pooled results from five trials of the chair-rise test. Middle-aged and older adults who added creatine to their training performed better than those who trained and took a placebo. The evidence for walking and balance was limited and inconsistent.

In the sit-to-stand test, researchers assess leg strength by asking people to rise from a chair repeatedly.
agusyonok/Shutterstock

In a two-year trial involving 237 postmenopausal women, whose average age was 59, both groups were asked to do resistance training and walk regularly. On average, the women taking creatine walked 80 metres about 1.5 seconds faster than they had at the start of the trial, while the placebo group’s time barely changed. There was no clear difference in reported falls through the end of the third year. The trial was designed to study bone health, so it gives limited information about whether creatine affects the risk of falling.

Research involving frailer older adults is also limited. In two trials involving people who were frail or at risk of frailty, participants got stronger with resistance training. Adding creatine produced no clear extra benefit. There is still too little evidence to say whether creatine helps older people avoid falls or remain independent for longer.

The brain also uses creatine to help maintain its energy supply. This has led researchers to investigate whether taking creatine might help preserve memory in later life.

A review focused on older adults found just two studies that tested supplements. They reached different conclusions. The other studies estimated how much creatine people got from food, so they could only identify links between intake and performance on cognitive tests. There is too little evidence to say whether taking creatine can slow cognitive decline or prevent dementia.

What to know about taking creatine

Creatine monohydrate is the most widely studied form. Some trials have used 3 to 5g a day, while others have used higher doses. The amount that might improve everyday physical function is still uncertain.

Creatine is generally well tolerated at the doses studied. Some people report stomach discomfort, and the extra water in muscle can lead to weight gain. Studies in people with healthy kidneys have generally found no evidence of reduced kidney function. There is less evidence on safety for people with kidney disease.

Creatine can raise blood levels of creatinine, a natural waste product, which is produced when the body breaks down creatine. Because blood tests use creatinine to estimate how well the kidneys are working, taking the supplement can make those results harder to interpret. Research on interactions with prescription medicines is limited. If you have kidney disease or take several prescription medicines, check with a GP or pharmacist before starting.

For older adults who want to stay strong, regular strength exercises are the place to start. NHS guidance for adults aged 65 and over recommends exercise to build strength and improve balance and flexibility on at least two days a week. For people who already do resistance training, creatine may offer a small extra gain in muscle strength.

Alexandra Cremona receives funding from the University of Limerick, Ireland.

articles.title: Solving the Neet crisis may come with a price tag the government can’t afford
articles.summary:
T.Vyc/Shutterstock

The UK’s one million 16 to 24-year-olds who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) are again at the centre of political and media debate, thanks to Alan Milburn’s latest review. The review’s diagnosis is correct: the challenge is not only young people’s skills and readiness for work, but also a shortage of jobs for them. So will the proposals solve the crisis?

Milburn – a former Labour minister – essentially suggests a fresh take on Labour’s New Deal for Young People (NDYP) from the 1990s. This mandated that people aged 18 to 24 who were long-term unemployed had to take up options to get them back into work. These options included a subsidised job, full-time education or training. If they did not participate, they faced benefit sanctions.

Back then, there was also a period of support. Taken together, these resemble the guarantee proposed in Milburn’s report. This has a period of early support; a menu of options (college, training, apprenticeship, work placement, civic service and help to start a business). There is also a paid job as part of the jobs guarantee, as well as an expectation that young people engage with the support.

Some of our earliest research focused on the NDYP, and we have continued to evaluate how the programme and the training provided improved employment prospects for young people.

So does evidence support the review’s suggestion that reforms will help an additional 440,000 young people into work by 2036? Unfortunately not.

It is true that by October 2001, more than three years after it started, 244,000 young people had left NDYP for sustained and unsubsidised jobs. But a large number would have found work anyway and the additional contribution of NDYP in its first two years was estimated at between 8,000 and 20,000.

A comparison from think tank the Resolution Foundation of costs per job suggests Milburn’s reforms need to be about three times as effective as previous employment schemes. Given the New Deal’s modest net effects, the gap may be wider still.

What’s more, nearly half (44%) of young people who are Neet are not claiming out-of-work benefits, so any expectation to engage, backed by the potential for benefit sanctions, will have less weight.

Whole-system change is unlikely

Milburn is correct to say that tackling the UK’s longstanding Neet challenge requires change across the “whole system”. But achieving that requires substantial funding. As such, the review is pitched to secure this money against competition from social care, housing, defence and the criminal justice system. Milburn projects a substantial return on investment, but as with any review, he is making the case to the Treasury.

It is a risky strategy to go for whole-system change in a world where so many other policy areas demand the same. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has accepted Milburn’s core principles, but stopped short of committing to all its recommendations. Any new money will be dependent on a white paper in the new year and the 2027 Spending Review, where it will compete with many other pressures.

The review has a package of hiring incentives worth around £1.1 billion a year at its peak. But it is counting on these subsidies to do most of the work of creating opportunities at a time of crisis in entry-level jobs.

Milburn proposes that further education and apprenticeship expansion should have “first call” on substantial new investment. We strongly agree, but this needs to go much further. Further education is best placed to link the whole system, but long-term deterioration in the sector’s financial position is likely to continue without substantial additional support.

Colleges need sufficient funding to make sure what they’re offering is attractive to young people.
KOTOIMAGES/Shutterstock

Colleges are where many of the young people at risk of becoming Neet find their path from age 16. Schools are funded for pupils before the age they may become Neet. Colleges are funded only if they enrol a young person and keep them learning – stopping them becoming Neet. Colleges have stronger incentives to seek out those at risk, but must be funded to provide an experience that re-engages young people.

One way round the shortage of jobs is to train more young people for work where employers already cannot find enough staff – electricians, carpenters and bricklayers, for example, as well as engineers and technicians. The commitment to apprenticeships is encouraging, but other promises in this area have not been met.

When it comes to AI, some takeaways from the latest research are that office jobs in routine professions (such as legal services, market research, trading and finance operations) are most exposed, while construction, installation, maintenance, repair and skilled trades are less exposed. Further education is where these skills are built.

Technology is also lowering the cost of experimenting with self-employment. The Milburn report drew on our work for the Youth Futures Foundation (an organisation to help marginalised young people to find work) and highlighted it as a route for young people who need flexibility because of health, disability or caring responsibilities. The offer – up to £500 to explore an idea, a £3,000 grant and “specialist support” – is welcome, but the review does not say what that support is, nor who judges which ideas are viable.

The ambition of Alan Milburn’s report is much needed, but the whole-system change it proposes is unlikely to be funded. It is vital to be imaginative in taking forward aspects of the review that embrace the risks and disruptions that are coming to the labour market. That means putting further education at the centre, building the skills that AI struggles to replace, backing self-employment and evaluating the reforms rigorously as they roll out.

Peter Urwin has received funding from the Economic and Social Research Council and the Nuffield Foundation to research the experiences of young people at risk of Neet.

Richard Dorsett has received funding from the Youth Futures Foundation, the Nuffield Foundation, the Cabinet Office, Youth Endowment Foundation and Department for Work and Pensions.

articles.title: Why are people listening to train journeys to fall asleep?
articles.summary:
Designer B_D/Shutterstock

It’s a dark and rainy evening and you’re settled into a comfy seat in a warm, quiet and dimly lit train carriage. You lean your head against the soft back of the chair and hear the rain fall against the window while you watch the hills rolling by. If there is something about this experience that sounds relaxing to you, then you’re not alone.

Sleep stories on meditation apps revive one of humanity’s oldest practices, bedtime storytelling, and repackage it for the digital age. Since their introduction on the meditation app Calm, they have been listened to more than 1 billion times. At a time when many adults struggle to fall or stay asleep, their popularity suggests a growing interest in stories that offer something different from conventional narratives.

One of the most popular forms of sleep story is the train genre, which features scenic rail journeys through a variety of real and fictional landscapes around the world. You could travel through Johannesburg in Africa, Darjeeling in Asia and Switzerland in Europe or even take a magical ride on the North Pole’s Christmas Express.

Some of the most famous stories set on trains feature action, murder and mystery, often requiring a bit of detective work from the reader. Think Murder on the Orient Express by Agatha Christie (1934) or Strangers on a Train by Patricia Highsmith (1950). The train-themed sleep stories in Calm’s library are very different. These audio narratives contain no conflict, suspense or adversary. They are designed to be engaging – but not so engaging that listeners will still be awake to hear the ending.

The train journey is particularly well suited to this purpose. Its steady movement along a predetermined route transforms falling asleep into a journey in which the listener can relinquish control and simply be carried towards their destination.

A study of train sleep stories I worked on with Paula Ghintuialǎ, an expert in how style in language and screen media shapes interpretation, explores the recurring linguistic features and storytelling choices that make these narratives unique, and which encourage sleep. Understanding how these unusual stories work offers an opportunity to rethink the linguistic and narrative strategies through which stories both hold, and deliberately release, our attention.

Sleep is a journey

Each story is structured around the same metaphor: sleep as a journey. The listener becomes the traveller, relaxation becomes movement along the route and sleep becomes the destination. Importantly, the journey is smooth and stress-free. Trains run on time, the seat is comfortable and spacious, and fellow passengers are few and quiet.

Every story also has a narrator who becomes your travelling companion. First, they give instructions for relaxing. You are told to “take in a few long deep breaths”, to “close your eyes” and to “let the weight of your body sink comfortably into your bed”. Similar to guided meditation practices, you are addressed through direct second-person (“you”) to help focus your attention on your immediate physical or physiological experience.

Gradually, you become a character inside the story. The narrator continues their instructions asking you to “imagine” or “picture” yourself, to shift your focus to another time and place.

Through these invitations, listeners are encouraged to inhabit the perspective of a fictionalised character who embarks on a journey. Instead of thinking about tomorrow’s meeting or an unfinished email, you’re crossing the Scottish Highlands or travelling through the Alps. These characters are generic and simply described, in order to make this embodiment a more effortless experience.

Along for the ride

Another key feature of these stories is that you don’t have to exert a lot of energy, nor do any active decision-making. Your actions take place within the confines of the train and are performed in the simple present – “you enter”, “you walk through”, “you come to”. This creates a perpetual “now”, similar to the language of mindfulness and guided imagery. These actions are also often low-energy, and paired with moments of reflection or reception. For instance, you are told that you “look”, “watch” or “see” and “notice”, “think” or “remember”.

In contrast, verbs describing the train’s movements are dynamic and incomplete (“running”, “passing”, “rolling”, “crossing”). Taken together, these patterns suggest continuous movement along a pre-set path, and establish a sense of ongoing, ambient motion. In other words, the train does the travelling for you. The route has already been decided, so all you have to do is be carried along it.

Finally, at the end of the journey, you’re described as disembarking the train, reaching a hotel room and settling into a bed. In these closing moments, the narration reconnects the fictional journey with the listener’s physical position. You might be told, for instance, that you climb into the wide bed, savouring the clean, pressed linen. The train, meanwhile, continues without you. You are asked to imagine it receding into the distance, while the end point of your own metaphorical journey – the destination of sleep – has been reached.
