articles.title: Flu and other winter viruses can hit older adults harder – here’s what you need to know
articles.summary:
Flu and other respiratory infections can be more serious in older adults, especially those with long-term heart or lung conditions. fizkes/Shutterstock

“Put a coat on or you’ll catch a cold.” It is a familiar warning, but it leaves out the most important character in the story, the virus.

Colds are caused by viruses, so cold air alone cannot give you one. In winter, though, viruses can spread more easily indoors, and cold, dry air may make some of the body’s early defences less effective.

For older people, there is a further concern. Infections such as flu and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), a common virus that can cause a runny nose or a cough, are more likely to lead to serious illness in this age group.

In colder weather, people often spend more time together indoors with the windows shut. In rooms where little fresh air comes in, tiny particles carrying viruses can build up in the air, making it easier for an infection to pass from one person to another.

If you’re unwell with a respiratory infection, put off visiting anyone at higher risk until you feel better. When you do get together indoors, open a window for a few minutes to help clear the air.

Some of the body’s first defences are inside the nose and airways, the passages that carry air to the lungs. Mucus, the sticky fluid that coats these passages, traps particles, including viruses, and tiny, hair-like structures sweep the mucus along so the body can get rid of it. These hair-like structures act like a tiny conveyor belt, helping clear viruses before they can establish an infection. A 2024 review of research on indoor air found that dry conditions can slow this process.

If a virus does infect a cell, another defence comes into play. Infected cells can send out chemical signals that warn neighbouring cells and help them protect themselves. This can limit how far the virus spreads.

A 2024 study found that some cold viruses multiplied more easily in cells from the nose when they were kept at lower temperatures. The cells also produced a weaker early immune response to the virus. But the study was done in laboratory conditions, so it doesn’t tell us whether being out in the cold makes someone more likely to catch a cold.

Serious illness in older people

The immune system, which helps the body fight infections, changes with age. Some of its cells become less effective, and the body can make fewer of the protective proteins called antibodies that help stop a virus from infecting cells. At the same time, the body’s reaction to infection can become harder to regulate. If it goes on too long, it can damage the tissues it is trying to protect.

Long-term heart or lung conditions can make an infection harder to cope with. Cold air can also narrow the airways, making breathing harder, and cold weather can raise blood pressure, putting extra strain on the heart. Flu can lead to pneumonia or make an existing heart or lung condition worse.

Vaccines give the immune system a head start by helping it recognise a virus and respond more quickly. Vaccines against flu, COVID and RSV can reduce the risk of serious illness.

Because flu viruses change and protection fades, the NHS offers a flu vaccine every year to people aged 65 and over and others at higher risk. In England, eligibility for COVID vaccination and RSV vaccination depends on factors such as age and health.

Most colds get better on their own. If you are 65 or over and have flu symptoms, the NHS advises asking your GP surgery for an urgent appointment or contacting NHS 111.

If you are in a group at highest risk of serious illness from COVID and develop symptoms, take a rapid COVID test as soon as possible, even if the symptoms are mild. If the test is positive, contact your GP surgery, NHS 111 or your hospital specialist promptly. Medicines for COVID need to be started early.

When checking on an older relative or neighbour, pay attention to whether they seem like their usual self. Older people can have flu without a high temperature. In someone who is already frail, going off their food or behaving differently can be a sign of illness.

New confusion or unusual drowsiness can be signs of serious illness. If someone is more short of breath than usual, seek urgent advice from their GP surgery or NHS 111. If they become suddenly confused, are difficult to wake or are struggling to breathe, call 999 immediately.

Fran Ludwig does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Climate summits need radical reform – here’s how to transform global negotiations
articles.summary:
DENIS ESAULOV 1987/Shutterstock

The recent failure of the UN climate summit, Cop31, went beyond already gloomy
expectations. Yet this political and diplomatic catastrophe may become a historical opportunity for global climate governance to tackle its structural problems.

It is a miracle that Cop climate summits have survived and grown for 31 years, with all decisions needing unanimous consensus from all 195 nations or parties. Cops have produced some positive results such as the 2015 Paris climate agreement to cut greenhouse gases. But now it’s time for radical reform. A reform that must not only abolish unanimity, but also make the Cop capable of engaging a strong enough coalition of interests to advance the climate change agenda.

Where could that start? What kind of alliance does such a reform need? A recent conference on the global governance of climate change provides some answers.

Ending unanimity

Cop has probably been killed by a contradiction. The first Cop in 1995 – chaired by Angela Merkel, then Germany’s young environment minister – was regulated by a UN law. This was the Framework Convention on Climate Change, which envisaged that decisions had to be taken by consensus or, if that wasn’t possible, by two-thirds of the parties (each state of the world is a “party”). This law, known as draft rule 42, was never accepted or rejected, leaving Cop trapped in the unanimity trap.

In 2010, this was enough for Bolivia alone to object to risk derailing the entire negotiation. It is a trap because countries have naturally different interests. Most developing countries are highly exposed to climate change and do not contribute much to the problem; some others not only benefit from oil production but also from global warming itself (notably Russia, as Arctic trade routes open up due to ice melting).

Most other traditional UN institutions do not operate under such strict consensus: the General Assembly (the main policymaking body of the UN), Unesco (the UN’s Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation) and the World Health Organization all vote with a qualified two-thirds majority on important matters.

So unanimity must be abolished. But that is not enough. Cop also manages to be both inefficient and not inclusive enough of the actors that matter a lot in achieving the goals of a climate change agenda. The parties include the tiny country of San Marino yet there’s no representation from megacities like Mumbai or Seattle – cities which may be exposed to climate disaster and host some of the solutions.

A new annual conference called Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels was a significant attempt to move beyond the Cop gridlock. In 2026, 57 countries joined the first meeting in Santa Marta, Colombia after realising at Cop30 last year in Brazil, that, by “consensus”, Cop cannot even agree on the need for a roadmap to end dependence on fossil fuels. And yet even shrinking the number of parties to a quarter of Cop’s total was not enough to get beyond the acknowledgement of such a necessity: the final document did not indicate any timeline nor commit countries to specific targets.

The Cop climate negotiation process hinges on all decisions needing unanimous consensus from all 195 nations or parties.
metamorworks/Shutterstock

It is too early to say that the Santa Marta process won’t work. But I would argue that it was a mistake not to invite certain nations, namely India and China and the US (although representatives from California did attend).

It was also risky to start the conference with a declaration (issued by Colombia’s
then president, Gustavo Petro about the inadequacy of capitalism to stop climate change. Capitalism may be a form of governing economy as primitive as fossil fuels, but to start from such a principle unnecessarily alienates leaders of other countries and business.

Coalition of the willing

Another way to bring together countries and political sides that may have different visions of the world yet share common energy interests is to invite all countries that may respond positively to two simple questions: “Are you interested in developing within two years and sharing your plan to reduce in your country (or city or region) the percentage of energy consumption coming from fossil fuels? If so, are you willing to support each other in building the necessary supply chains and financial facilities to improve that target?”

This may inspire politically diverse local and national governments and business leaders to gradually join what would become a concrete problem-solving exercise. Common ground could hopefully be found in their shared interest to reduce energy dependency and mitigate climate risks.

Read more:
What does climate adaptation actually mean? An expert explains

Once most of the net importers of fossil fuels are aligned, the net exporters (including some members of Opec, the oil producers’ cartel) may also commit. This is the sort of coalition of the willing that we need: an alliance capable of increasing its scope and delivering results.

As director of the thinktank Vision, I recently convened the fifth conference on global governance of climate change, held in Venice, Italy, in October 2026, titled Beyond Cop. Over three days, international delegates produced a strong proposal on how to reform Cop. The proposal was authored by professors and students including Kalypso Nikolaidis, chair in global affairs, and Helena Marchall, a masters student, both at the School of Transnational Governance of the European University Institute.

The conference proposes looking beyond ideologies, pre-defined agendas, cognitive biases and siloed thinking that make it difficult for politicians, business and academics to solve complex questions. One suggested change is to make Venice a permanent hub for a new global governance of climate adaptation (the practical steps to prepare for the consequences of a changing climate). This would help drive action and avoid the risk of focusing primarily on mitigation (cutting greenhouse gas emissions to achieve net zero).

We need courage, vision and pragmatism. These are the ingredients to respond to existential threats.

Francesco Grillo is Director of the think tank Vision.

articles.title: Jensen Huang, Nvidia and the risks that come with ‘boomerang bosses’
articles.summary:
Jensen Huang’s swift return as boss of Nvidia surprised – and pleased – many people. Donald Trump was happy about it, as were many who invest in the future of AI.

There are plenty of high-profile business leaders who have returned to a company after stepping down, with good results. Michael Dell did it at Dell computers, Steve Jobs did it at Apple and Sam Altman did it at OpenAI.

But there are also many cases where a returning CEO has actually harmed the performance of the firm. So will Jensen Huang prove to be a successful or a harmful “boomerang boss”?

As its co-founder and CEO, Huang was behind Nvidia’s extraordinary success. But the company also had one crucial weakness – its dependency on Huang.

The idea of “key person risk” is the vulnerability from depending heavily on one person whose absence could severely disrupt how a business works. This aspect of Nvidia was dramatically exposed when it was revealed in late October that Huang had had an extra-marital affair with an executive with alleged links to Chinese government secret services.

After another affair with an employee came to light a few days later, swiftly followed by claims about another, Huang stepped down. This led to a massive drop in the firm’s share price, which triggered wider falls in technology-focused markets around the world. Huang’s affairs had become a matter of global economic stability but also geopolitical importance, amid debates about how his departure might affect America’s narrow lead over China in the AI race.

The financial markets clearly approve of the Nvidia board’s announcement that Huang will step back into his role as CEO. The share price has shot back up, helping to lift many companies in the sector. But research on boomerang CEOs paints a more nuanced picture.

Often these bosses are invited to return on the basis that they had been successful in the past so are likely to be successful in the future. However, one study of over 6,000 CEOs found that boomerang bosses tend to perform significantly worse than others.

The main reason was that they often revert back to their old strategic playbook when the rest of the world has moved on. This means they are using outdated ideas.

Yet the dataset for this study included many founders who returned years after they had left. Huang was only out of the Nvidia saddle for 11 days, so his strategic playbook is likely to be as up to date as ever. A more recent working paper looking at boomerang CEOs who had only been away for a short time found that the firms in question showed improved operating performance, investment and growth.

However, other research suggests boomerang CEOs tend to receive slighly higher performance evaluations than other new hires mainly because they have a better understanding of the hidden social structure of the organisation and how to navigate it. Another study found that they tended to perform on average about the same as other managers, but were also more likely to leave.

Nvidia ups and downs.
Saulo Ferreira Angelo/Shutterstock

Back for good?

Beyond the world of business there are cases of boomerang leaders in politics and sport. In politics, returning leaders – including Winston Churchill, Silvio Berlusconi and Donald Trump – are a persistent but relatively minor feature of many political systems.

In the world of sport there are a of cases of coaches being fired and then returning to Premier League football teams. One piece of analysis found that of 11 Premier League coaches who returned, only three saw their results improve.

Read more:
Nvidia’s Jensen Huang is getting his CEO job back, but history shows companies perform better when corporate boards take executive misbehavior seriously

Perhaps this all suggests that Huang’s return to Nvidia may not be a cause for immediate performance concerns. His strategic knowledge and networks are still very valuable.

What is likely to be a longer term worry is issues of reputation and governance at the world’s most important chip-maker. Addressing these is likely to require revisiting the structure and oversight practices of the company – which the new old boss may or may not feel like doing.

Andre Spicer does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Ghost Town: a dream-like film about a Japanese community haunted by the 2011 tsunami
articles.summary:
In the aftermath of the 2011 earthquake that triggered a devastating 40-metre tsunami along Japan’s Pacific coast, taxi drivers in the Iwate port town of Kamaishi started reporting strange happenings.

Several drivers described picking up passengers who vanished during their journeys. The taxi community began to refer to them as “ghost fares”. The phenomenon soon attracted attention of news outlets, and even academics. Now these ghost fares are the subject of an equally strange film called Ghost Town, directed by British documentary maker Katherine Round.

The wall of water precipitated by the 9.0 magnitude earthquake on March 11 meant that casualties were almost entirely from coastal areas, mainly Fukushima, Miyagi and Iwate. Almost 20,000 people were killed and another 2,500 were reported missing.

I first came across these stories of ghost fares while working on my PhD, which focused on cultural engagement with dying and death. In a 2014 article Richard Lloyd Parry, the Tokyo-based Asia editor of The Times, wrote:

A cab driver in the city of Sendai picked up a sad-faced man who asked to be taken to an address that no longer existed. Halfway through the journey, he looked into his mirror to see that the rear seat was empty. He drove on anyway, stopped in front of the levelled foundations of a destroyed house, and politely opened the door to allow the invisible passenger out at his former home.

An in-between space

Round came across the phenomenon following a devastating loss of her own. Known for her deeply humane documentaries that follow the lives of ordinary people, she flew to Japan, where she rigged the cabs of four Kaimishi taxi drivers with cameras, and invited local residents to take a ride. Round describes her film as “an enquiry into memory, myth, life and death”.

The film follows four drivers – Konno, Iwasaki, Goto and Koike – mostly at night, as they weave their way through the streets “picking up occasional passengers and conversing with a visitor to the town about their lives”.

Rather than a documentary with an obvious narrative arc, Ghost Town is, as the director describes, a film that explores “a liminal space between documentary and dream”.

Audiences feel as if they, like the passengers of the taxis, are between one place and another, witnessing what passes by. With large stretches of silence and frequent changes of location between taxis, the audience is taken on a journey over the course of one night, moving ghost-like between different spaces and places and overhearing a range of conversations.

Journalist and filmmaker Shiori Ito – whose Black Box Diaries unleashed Japan’s Me Too movement – was part of the team, working with the people of Kamaishi to help create an inclusive process that locals could feel involved in. Once filming was underway, Ito also became a part of the film itself, taking on the role of one of the taxi passengers giving an outsider’s perspective.

The film has a moving, hypnotic quietness, but it’s never actually quiet. When the driver and passenger aren’t talking, the vehicle itself seems to take over: the hum of its electric engine becomes more pronounced as it glides through deserted streets; the radio seems to get louder; and the repetitive ticking of indicators becomes rhythmic and mesmerising. Outside there is a melancholy stillness to the darkness, punctuated by the pooled light from streetlamps.

For Round, the taxi became a “mobile confession booth”, with drivers and passengers sharing spontaneous stories about their experiences and memories, their lives, fears, hopes and regrets. While we know the drivers are real, we never quite know for sure if the person making the journey is real or an actor. The truth is never explained.

In this way the ambiguity plays on the idea of the ghost fares. These passengers could just as easily be imagined or, in effect, the ghost passengers that Kamaishi taxi drivers maintained they picked up after the tsunami.

Like Iranian director Jafar Panah’s film Taxi Tehran (2015), the technique of using cameras inside a car allows for a unique perspective on a location, seeing it pass by through windows as drivers and passengers look out, ask questions and share thoughts.

In Kamaishi, one driver mentions a “a phone box filled with spirits” trying to get through. It reminded me of another Japanese phenomenon, the “wind phone”: a disconnected phone box that gives the living a place to speak with the dead and express their grief.

In an episode of The Death Studies Podcast disaster recovery expert Lucy Easthope talks about how surprisingly similar disasters are around the world: big, life changing, and traumatic, they offer “brutal teachings”. There is a world before the disaster, and a world after the disaster.

The Kamaishi shown in Ghost Town has been reconstructed with modern buildings and roads, but seems deserted and haunted, its communities broken, interrupted and forever changed by the tsunami.

Regular sirens and preparation drills feature in Round’s film, reminding audiences of the risk natural disasters continue to pose. One particularly striking scene shows a taxi driver enjoying a break with his sudoku, at his favourite spot overlooking the water. Even though it was an enormous column of water barrelling in from the ocean that destroyed these coastal towns, the presence of water in Ghost Town is calming and benign.

Ghost Town functions as a retelling, a document, a memory and a reminder of the many individual lives that are affected by disasters. And of the losses they produce, and the people and legacies they leave behind.

Bethan Michael-Fox does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: You Can See Everything – a mind-bending odyssey that will leave you questioning what you see
articles.summary:
In their self-aware documentary You Can See Everything, filmmakers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim attempt to paint a portrait of convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes. The documentary initially follows the former founder and her partner, Billy Evans, in the last 34 days before Holmes’s incarceration for defrauding investors in her failed blood testing company Theranos.

Fielder and Oppenheim have been granted seemingly unfettered access to the couple’s home life. The pair claim that they are doing this because they want people to see the “real Liz”. What the filmmakers hope to get out of it, other than unprecedented access to a figure that has seized the cultural imagination, is less clear.

I have watched You Can See Everything three times, and found it every bit as genius as everybody says. The three-hour documentary is unique in its creation of layers of hyper-reality through its cinematography, editing, sound and use of reenactments.

While it feels groundbreaking, the documentary does reflect a logical combination and evolution of the styles of directors Fielder and Oppenheim.

Read more:
How Aristotle helps us unpack the art of deception in Nathan Fielder’s You Can See Everything

One in front and one behind

Fielder’s previous project The Rehearsal (2022-) will prepare any viewer for the twists and turns of You Can See Everything – and perhaps even help predict some of them.

In The Rehearsal, Fielder builds elaborate simulations of “real” places in order to rehearse difficult conversations or play out potential life choices. As the stories progress, the lines between what’s real and what’s fabricated blur.

The Rehearsal began with Fielder off camera as more of a behind-the-scenes orchestrator. But as the series progress, he became a more active participant in these “rehearsals”. For instance, in one episode he helps a woman rehearse what raising a child with someone would be like. After her initial co-parenting partner drops out, Fielder steps in and quickly becomes the centre of the experiment, allowing his obsessions and anxieties to dominate the rehearsal.

The hyper-reality in You Can See Everything operates according to similar principles. As in The Rehearsal, when Fielder steps out from behind the camera, viewers start to question everything – including Fielder himself.

In contrast, Oppenheim is never in front of the camera (except for one particularly pertinent reenactment of how the project began in the second half of the film). Unlike Fielder, he never appears in his feature documentaries. Oppenheim’s directorial style is remarkable, conjuring up haunting, peculiar portrayals of people and places through saturated colours, fantastical cinematography and dreamy soundscapes.

Lance Oppenheim’s 2024 documentary Spermworld.

Oppenheim’s way of telling stories with a dreamlike quality, without explaining why his subjects behave the way they do, lends itself particularly well to painting this purposefully incomplete picture of Holmes and Evans. Through his lens, the couple are imperfect beneficiaries – or victims, as they might like to add – of America’s obsession with investment in newness and in charismatic (particularly white, middle and upper class) individuals.

In the first half, this idea is captured through tight scenes of Holmes, Evans and Fielder within the confined spaces of the couple’s rented beach cottage in San Diego. Such shots, paired with a restrained use of music, establish an atmosphere that always feels hesitant and obscure.

Read more:
Elizabeth Holmes went from a startup darling to powerful seductress – these gendered portrayals profited investors

This might be unprecedented access, but no matter how strongly Holmes insists that Fielder and Oppenheim can see everything, you feel that they – and you – really can’t.

How do you show what you can’t see?

In the second half of the film, Holmes has started her 11-year prison sentence and the storytelling becomes less straightforward.

How do you film a documentary when one of your main subjects is essentially inaccessible? Oppenheim and Fielder creatively rise to the task by layering realities onto each other through the inclusion of varying modes of storytelling, like reenactments and even reenactments within reenactments.

This layered reality can have a disorienting and almost psychedelic quality at times – even on the seemingly straight shots. One of the most striking examples is a scene of Evans working on his laptop in the kitchen. A reptile (a blue Argentine tegu) moves slowly across the table. On the other side of the room is a screen playing a life-size AI-generated video of Holmes, talking to nobody in particular.

This trippy scene is as bizarrely haunting and unnerving as some of the intense confrontations with Billy in this final section. Wide eyed and unapologetic, Billy’s small acts of seemingly controlling behaviour (like taking over the whisking of eggs in the first half) are writ larger in Holmes’s absence and tinged by his enthusiasm for conservative politics and figures like Charlie Kirk.

In these scenes it becomes clear that while Holmes might have been the draw for the directors as the perfect documentary subject, Evans turns out to be an even better one.

You Can See Everything is breathtaking cinema. While it’s not a major departure from the pair’s previous work, what’s so special about this film is the qualities they have honed. Oppenheim’s ability to make factual narratives look more fictional than many fictions and Nathan Fielder’s aptitude for slowly building layer upon layer of hyper-reality, that leaves you questioning everything you see.

Sarah Lahm does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Norovirus is spreading – how to recognise the symptoms and what to do
articles.summary:
Prostock-studio/Shutterstock.com

Described as the “Ferrari of the virus world” for the way it races from person to person, norovirus is once again on the move as we head into winter.

Reports from the UK Health Security Agency have highlighted that cases of norovirus – commonly known as the “winter vomiting bug” – have increased by more than 35% in England over the past two weeks, compared with the previous fortnight.

While that sounds alarming, this is still within expected levels for the season. Overall case numbers are about 5% above what’s typical for this time of year. Cases have fallen in Scotland, but Wales has seen a rise.

Norovirus symptoms include sudden-onset nausea, diarrhoea and vomiting, sometimes accompanied by fever, stomach pain, body aches and headaches.

Most healthy adults recover within one to three days. However, those with weakened immune systems, older adults and young children face a higher risk of severe symptoms. When this happens, people can be ill for much longer and may need hospital treatment if they become dehydrated.

Norovirus is highly contagious, with some studies suggesting that as few as ten virus particles can cause an infection. It spreads from person to person when tiny amounts of virus from infected faeces or vomit get on to food, hands or surfaces and are then transferred to the mouth.

Close contact between people can also spread the virus. This may help explain why cases peak in winter, when people spend more time together indoors. However, you can catch it at any time of the year.

The virus is also particularly resilient; it can survive on hard kitchen surfaces such as stainless steel and ceramic for up to two weeks, and it takes temperatures of around 60°C to kill it.

There are no approved vaccines or specific treatments for norovirus. It evolves quickly to escape our immune systems, and has proved notoriously difficult to grow in the lab, which has hampered research efforts. That said, recent breakthroughs in growing norovirus using lab-grown human gut cells may make it easier to develop treatments in future.

How to protect yourself and your household

While alcohol-based hand sanitisers can be effective against other viruses, such as the ones that cause COVID and flu, they don’t work well against norovirus. Instead, the best way to protect yourself is by washing your hands often with soap and hot water, ideally for 15 seconds or more. This is particularly important before or after preparing food, and after going to the toilet.

Norovirus is also frequently spread through contaminated food. Fresh produce such as fruit and vegetables may pick up the virus during harvesting, packaging or handling, so wash these thoroughly before use. Shellfish such as oysters can also be contaminated with concentrated norovirus from the water they live in, so ensure these are thoroughly cooked, rather than steamed or eaten raw.

If someone in your household has norovirus, cleaning surfaces regularly with bleach-based products can help prevent the virus from spreading.

Using a dummy called Vomiting Larry, researchers found that norovirus-containing droplets can spread around ten feet (three metres) when someone vomits. So, it’s important to immediately clean areas that have been contaminated by vomit or faeces.

Vomiting Larry in action.

Frequent cleaning of heavily used surfaces such as door handles, light switches, taps, toilet seats and flush handles, ideally while wearing disposable gloves, can help reduce the chances of the virus spreading.

Washing soiled clothes or bedding separately from other laundry, at a temperature of 60°C or above at the longest cycle time possible, can also help kill the virus on soft surfaces.

If you are unlucky enough to get norovirus yourself, the only solution is to allow the virus to run its short, but deeply unpleasant, course.

Replacing lost fluids is essential, so drink plenty of water, tea or electrolyte drinks, or use oral rehydration sachets. If you feel able to eat, stick to plain foods that are easy to digest, such as toast, rice, pasta or soup, and avoid fatty or salty foods that may make your symptoms worse.

As norovirus is highly contagious, ensure that you stay at home and rest as much as possible. Keep your distance from other people in your household where you can, and avoid preparing food for others while you’re unwell and for at least 48 hours after symptoms stop.

Even after full recovery, infectious virus can still be shed in poo for up to two weeks, so continuing to frequently clean bathroom areas can help prevent further transmission.

With cases rising as winter sets in, the Ferrari of viruses may be doing the rounds for a while yet. A few simple habits could save you, and others, a very unpleasant few days.

Charlotte Lewis receives funding from the UK Medical Research Council.

articles.title: Joanne Young waived her anonymity – my research shows why survivors of sexual violence make this brave choice
articles.summary:
Echoing the case of Gisèle Pelicot in France, Joanne Young waived her right to anonymity following the conviction of her ex-husband for drugging her, raping her and allowing other men to rape her too. Philip Young had routinely drugged his wife over many years, soliciting men online to come into their home and rape her.

In the UK and Ireland, victims of sexual violence are entitled to lifelong anonymity. This reflects an enduring reality: rape and sexual assault remain highly stigmatising experiences.

Yet there is growing evidence that survivors are choosing to forgo that protection. Along with colleagues, I have been systematically studying those who choose to waive their right to anonymity. Though survivors’ experiences are very different, common themes emerge.

By waiving this right, Young and Pelicot have opened up a conversation about violence against women and girls. This conversation is sorely needed.

During their trial, Norman Macksoni, Richard Wilkins, Connor Sanderson-Doyle and Mohammed Hassan argued that their sexual activity with the unconscious Joanne Young was consensual as her then-husband gave consent. Another man, Dean Hamilton, admitted charges including rape in February, and Philip Young also pleaded guilty at an earlier hearing to a string of offences.

Pelicot and supporters of Young have said that shame must change sides. They are not wrong. In the UK case, here is a cohort of men who argued in open court that a husband has the power to decide who has sexual access to his wife. That is both shocking and shameful.

Agency and empowerment

Victims of sexual assault experience domination of their bodily autonomy in the most intimate way. And they often describe their experiences in court as similarly intrusive and violating. Intimate videos are replayed, there can be extensive scrutiny of their sexual history and relentless questions about their consent.

Reasserting their agency is another key motivation of those who waive their anonymity. Speaking can be empowering after a trial where they have had very little control over the outcome. In the all too rare instances when a conviction is secured (unlike when it is not), victims are free to speak. Those who feel they have survived both the abuse and the judicial system often feel compelled to speak on behalf of the many others who don’t seek or get justice.

There is a final reason that survivors can be motivated to waive their anonymity. Doing so can allow them to find solidarity with others who share their experience. Sexual violence is associated with a high burden of ill health compared to other traumatic life events. This might be mental health consequences including depression and post-traumatic stress, and physical issues including cardiovascular, metabolic and immune disorders.

Going public can allow survivors to find solidarity with others.
Steve Travelguide/Shutterstock

Research consistently shows that deliberate, intentional acts of violence disproportionately damage people’s faith in others. This can make it difficult for victims to connect with others. This is amplified in cases where the perpetrator is a family member. Previously trusted husbands and fathers have not only exploited their position in the family unit, they have fractured relationships.

For many, and particularly for women where family roles are heavily emphasised, much of their identity is defined by these relationships: daughter, wife or mother. Alongside shame, sexual abuse corrupts these identity-based relationships, further disconnecting victims when they need support.

Philip Young, a former Conservative councillor in Swindon, Wiltshire, harnessed the power of like-minded others. At short notice, after he had drugged Joanne, he was able to find ample men in a small geographical area willing to assault his unconscious wife.

In going public, Young and Pelicot have both harnessed the power of like-minded others for good. Waiving anonymity can allow victims to connect with others at a very vulnerable point in their lives.

But Lavinia Kerwick, the first woman in Ireland to waive her anonymity after the conviction of her rapist in 1991, has described the burden of doing so. The survivor rather than the perpetrator becomes publicly synonymous with the crime. It can become a lens through which others see victims.

Waiving anonymity is not for everyone and certainly shouldn’t be an expectation placed on survivors. And clearly survivors make their decisions based on their own circumstances and concerns. Either way, it is a difficult decision.

Survivors are acutely aware that waiving anonymity comes at a personal cost. But for those who do, their actions are driven by collective rather than personal concerns. In research with colleagues, we have referred to this phenomenon as collective post-traumatic growth. After their trauma, survivors rebuild a view of the world that includes the need for a different future, a better one for all. Drawing strength from the support and solidarity after their disclosure, they are driven to act on behalf of others.

Sexual violence is not simply a private, personal matter. It is a corrosive social force, the effects of which extend far beyond the family home. It damages relationships and communities, and shatters the integrity of our social, judicial and political institutions. Young, Pelicot and others waive their anonymity to progress social, political and legislative change for everyone. It’s time to trade in the shame and offer them our gratitude.
